<SYSTEM>This is the full developer documentation for Holtdroid</SYSTEM>

# Introduction

> What Holtdroid is, who it is for, and how a session looks from the user's side.

Holtdroid is a self-hosted web portal that launches Android devices on demand for testing APKs. It is built for teams whose builds land in a chat channel and whose apps lean on WebViews: QA engineers, web developers working on hybrid apps, support engineers reproducing a customer bug.

## Why it exists

[Section titled “Why it exists”](#why-it-exists)

I’m a frontend engineer, and I build Holtdroid for my own use first. Most users of the products I’ve worked on open them inside an app’s embedded WebView or in Chrome, and a fair share of them do it on old potato phones 🥔 with cursed combinations of Android and [WebView versions](/concepts/webview-versions/). Their bugs only reproduce on exactly those combinations.

I’m also very lazy, and debugging over ADB through Chrome DevTools is flaky and awkward enough to drain whatever motivation was left. So instead of fighting it I wrote a tool that starts the WebView I need and then digs into what the page actually does: the [network requests](/session-tools/network/) on the critical loading path, how well Cloudflare [caches](/session-tools/cache/) the assets, and more.

Maybe I’m the only weirdo out there who rewrites SVG filters by hand and loses sleep over cache hit rates so that people on a bad connection get a page that loads fast and doesn’t cook their phone. Just in case I’m not, I made it public ^.^ If something should be fixed or added, I’d be glad to hear it: open an [issue](https://github.com/holtdroid/holtdroid/issues).

## Getting around

[Section titled “Getting around”](#getting-around)

The portal’s navigation is a dock floating at the bottom of every page. From left to right: the sections (**Apps**, and **App data**, **Pixel perfect**, **Recordings** and **Computers** when they are enabled); a chip for each device you are running, with a status dot (green: ready, blue: starting, amber: the idle stop or the lifetime ends within 5 minutes, red: failed) and a hover card with the device, its Android version, location, the idle countdown, **Open** and **Stop**; **+** to launch an app; the admin pages (**Inventory**, **Users**, **Audit log**); search; the documentation; the theme switch; and your account menu. On smaller screens the admin pages, documentation and theme fold into a **More** menu, and on narrow ones the sections too.

**⌘K** (Ctrl+K on Windows and Linux) anywhere in the portal opens a search over your running devices (open or stop one), the apps (picking one opens its launch dialog), recordings and pages, plus actions: upload an APK, switch the theme, open the documentation. The documentation link carries the page you were on in its address (`#returnUrl=`), so the documentation’s own dock shows **Open the portal**, which brings you back there, for as long as that tab stays open.

## A session, end to end

[Section titled “A session, end to end”](#a-session-end-to-end)

1. Open the portal. The Apps page shows one row per app (package name) found in your configured sources (a folder or bucket that CI or a Slack sync job fills, plus your own uploads): its latest version, how many builds there are, which sources they come from and how many devices run it now; tabs filter by source and `/` jumps to the search. **Launch** on a row starts the latest build; the arrow at the end opens its builds (version, build number, branch, who posted it, size, age) with a launch button and a menu (download, origin, visibility, delete) each, and the app’s name opens a page with every build’s note and changelog. Builds of one version for different processors (x86 and ARM) share a row, and a launch takes the one the chosen device runs natively. Anyone signed in can give an app a description (what it is for, how to test it): it shows above the builds and, shortened, in the app’s row. Pin the apps you test most: they come first in the list for everyone. Next to the list, the **Devices** card shows each provider’s slots as a bar of ticks (running, starting, about to stop, free) and the running sessions, yours first; **Recent recordings** lists the newest recordings when recording is on.

2. Press **Launch**. The launch dialog puts the device together on the left: where it runs (a virtual device or a physical phone, each with how many are free, the virtual one preselected when the build runs on it), the Android version (versions below the app’s `minSdk` are greyed out), the screen (favourites first, **All devices** opens a searchable picker), the WebView, the VPN location and app data. The right column previews the chosen phone with its size and cutout, sums up the choices and holds **Record from start** and **Launch**. A physical provider lists its phones instead, **Any available** by default. A fresh Android device boots (about a minute) while a progress card shows each real start stage and the time since launch. The ⚡ button next to Launch skips the dialog and launches with the provider and location you used last time (or the defaults). When every device is busy, or the one you picked, the launch waits in line and starts as soon as one frees up.

3. The APK is installed as-is and started with WebView debugging enabled at runtime.

4. The session page has a header, the **Device** panel on the left, the device’s screen in the middle and the tools on the right: Chrome DevTools with a picker for the inspected target (any WebView page, iframe or worker in any process), Logcat, DNS, Routes, Files and Terminal, with WebSockets, Cache and Pixel perfect under **More**. The header shows the app and its build (click the name to switch to another build) with the device, Android, WebView and VPN location under it; the time left, **Extend** and **Stop** sit on its right. By default the screen’s side follows the screen: it grows or shrinks until the screen fills its height or the side reaches 70% of the page. A landscape screen splits the page top and bottom instead, the screen above the tools. Dragging the divider sizes it by hand; the button on the divider turns following back on.

   The screen sits in a frame with a toolbar beside it (under it in landscape): Back, Home, Recent apps, the notifications and quick settings, Rotate (click turns left, shift-click right), Screenshot, the keyboard mode, Volume (the volume keys, the media volume slider and a tile that mutes Android itself), Power (locks the device or turns its screen off, with **Wake and unlock** and the key’s mode in its panel) and **Restart app**. Rotate, Volume and Power open their panel on hover, on a right-click, a long press or the context-menu key; a panel stays open once you click inside it, until you click elsewhere or press Esc. When the device vibrates, the page shows a notification and plays a buzz.

   The Device panel holds the device’s controls as rows in three tabs: **Environment** (Network, Location, Battery, Language, Time, Clipboard, Display), **Media** (Stream, Microphone, Camera, Recording) and **App** (App, Device, SSH). Each row shows a summary and its chevron opens it in place; the search button filters the rows of all tabs by name. A row whose settings differ from the defaults is marked **Changed**, its tab gets a dot, and the open row has a reset button.

   The Network row shows the VPN location, the external IP and the network conditions, with Wi-Fi, mobile data and airplane mode tiles, the VPN locations and a link to the network picker. On emulators with VPN locations the picker holds the emulated network conditions: slow or lossy networks and scenarios such as a subway ride, each with its description, and regions such as Bangladesh that add the round trips to CDN edges and to your servers there. The **DNS** tab lists every name the device looks up and rewrites names to your own addresses, with a TTL limit and saved sets of rewrites (see [DNS log and rewrites](/session-tools/dns/)), and **Routes** shows where every connection goes: each server’s country and network, the location it left through, and far servers or connections that aren’t reused (see [Routes](/session-tools/routes/)).

   The Stream row picks the video codec (H.264, the lightest for the server, by default; H.265 or AV1 where the browser decodes them), quality (the device’s own up to 1080p, then 720p, 480p and 360p; a sharper screen is streamed at 1080p), frame rate (45 fps by default, up to the device’s own and never above 60) and bitrate, switches the device audio (it plays in your browser by default, from your first click on the page unless the browser allows autoplay for the portal; until then the row says “Click anywhere for sound” and the Media tab gets a dot), shows the frames, bitrate and dropped frames the browser decodes right now, and switches the keyboard between text input and a virtual USB keyboard that types in any alphabet with the layout set on the device. The codec, the bitrate and a frame rate below 45 fps are remembered in the browser; quality and faster frame rates last for one session.

   The Clipboard row turns sync on or off with a click (both ways by default, or one direction) and keeps the last 10 synced texts, shown with · for spaces and ↵ for line breaks, each with buttons to copy it or save it as a text file. The Time row shows the device’s clock and is marked while the clock is shifted, not in real time or in a time zone picked by hand; it has real-time sync, shifting the clock back or forward by any amount, an exact moment entered in your own time zone, and the time zone, which follows the VPN location unless you pick another one for the session. The Battery row shows the charge (65% and on battery at start) and has battery saver, charging and the charge level with presets. The Display row has a brightness slider and adaptive brightness (for this session only; the stream itself doesn’t get darker, the device and its apps see the setting), the dark theme (light, dark or matching the portal’s theme, which a device launched in that mode already has when the app first opens), Android’s system navigation on emulators (gestures by default, or the back, home and recent apps buttons), the font size with a preview and the display size, Android’s setting that scales buttons, icons and text by changing the density (the screen picked at launch keeps its resolution); rotation is there too. The Language row picks the system language and the keyboard layouts from a grid of flags: a click on a layout adds or removes it (up to 7, remembered in your browser and guessed from your keyboard where the browser allows). When SSH is on, the SSH row says whether a computer is connected to this device and lists the ADB clients and the ports your computers publish on the device, the `adb` command for this device on each connected computer, or the command that connects a computer. The App row restarts and reinstalls the app and saves its data; recording has its own row ([recordings](/concepts/recordings/)).

   On devices that can fake it, the **Location** row follows the VPN location until you tap the map, drag the dot, paste coordinates or use the locate button on the map for your own position. Under the map, **Route** walks, runs or drives the device through stops you tap on the map, along roads (or in straight lines) and optionally in a loop, speeding up, slowing for turns and drifting around the chosen pace; it keeps going until you stop it, even with the tab closed. Apps see the position move but no speed or bearing.

5. Walk away. After the idle timeout (30 minutes by default) the device is deleted and the slot frees up. The home page shows every active session, its owner and how long it has left.

## What it is not

[Section titled “What it is not”](#what-it-is-not)

* Not a device farm for automated test runs (yet). The contracts allow it, but the first goal is interactive debugging.
* Not a way to modify or re-sign APKs. Anything that needs repackaging is out of scope on purpose.
* Not a Play Store environment: sessions run redroid, a rooted AOSP userdebug build without Google services.

## Requirements

[Section titled “Requirements”](#requirements)

* A Kubernetes cluster (1.31+) with **x86_64 nodes with binder and a Mesa GPU** for sessions, dedicated to them. Each session takes about 1 GB of memory idle and a core while its screen streams.
* Permission to run Pods with extra capabilities (Pod Security level `privileged`) in Holtdroid’s namespace, and a runtime with NRI (containerd 2.0+) on the session nodes.
* A forward-auth proxy in front of the ingress (Authelia, oauth2-proxy, …), unless you run it locally with authentication disabled.
* For builds from Slack: a Slack app with a bot token and a small sync job that copies them into a source.

# A self-hosted alternative to BrowserStack, Appetize and Genymotion

> How Holtdroid compares with BrowserStack, Appetize, Genymotion, DeviceFarmer STF, docker-android, redroid and an emulator on your own machine.

There are many ways to get an Android device in front of a tester. This page says where Holtdroid fits among them, and when another tool is the better choice. Holtdroid is a self-hosted, open-source (Apache-2.0) portal: you run it on your own Kubernetes cluster, there is no hosted service to sign up for.

## At a glance

[Section titled “At a glance”](#at-a-glance)

|                                  | Holtdroid            | Cloud device services            | DeviceFarmer STF | docker-android | Local emulator     |
| -------------------------------- | -------------------- | -------------------------------- | ---------------- | -------------- | ------------------ |
| Where it runs                    | Your cluster         | The vendor’s cloud               | Your hosts       | Your hosts     | Your computer      |
| Builds leave your network        | No                   | Yes                              | No               | No             | No                 |
| Price                            | Free, your hardware  | Per seat or minute               | Free             | Free           | Free               |
| Virtual devices on demand        | Yes, redroid Pods    | Yes                              | No               | Yes            | One at a time      |
| Real phones                      | Yes, over USB        | Large catalogues                 | Yes              | No             | Over USB           |
| WebView DevTools in the browser  | Yes, APK untouched   | Varies, often a debuggable build | No               | No             | `chrome://inspect` |
| VPN country per device           | Yes, switchable live | Some offer geolocation           | No               | No             | A VPN app          |
| Builds from Slack, S3, GitHub    | Yes                  | Upload or CI plugins             | No               | No             | Download by hand   |
| Recordings with network and logs | Yes                  | Video and logs                   | No               | No             | No                 |
| iOS                              | No                   | Yes                              | No               | No             | Xcode              |

## BrowserStack, Sauce Labs, LambdaTest

[Section titled “BrowserStack, Sauce Labs, LambdaTest”](#browserstack-sauce-labs-lambdatest)

Commercial clouds of real and virtual devices. Pick them when you need hundreds of real phone models, iOS, or large automated test grids, and are fine with uploading builds to a third party and paying per seat or minute.

Holtdroid covers the other case: a team that tests its own APKs by hand, wants them to stay inside its network, and cares about what a WebView inside the app does. Every device gets [DevTools](/concepts/devtools/) without a debuggable build, a [VPN country](/concepts/vpn/) of its own, [network presets](/session-tools/network/) and [recordings](/concepts/recordings/) that keep the network, console and logcat next to the video.

## Appetize.io

[Section titled “Appetize.io”](#appetizeio)

Appetize streams emulators to a browser and is good at embedding an app in a web page for demos and support. It is a hosted service. Holtdroid gives a similar browser tab on your own hardware, and adds the debugging tools around the screen: [Logcat](/session-tools/logcat/), [files](/session-tools/files/), a [terminal](/session-tools/terminal/), [DNS](/session-tools/dns/) and [routes](/session-tools/routes/), and ADB on your computer through the [holtdroid client](/concepts/ssh/).

## Genymotion

[Section titled “Genymotion”](#genymotion)

Genymotion’s desktop emulator and its cloud images are mature virtual devices for developers. Holtdroid is not an emulator itself: it runs Android in containers with [redroid](/configuration/emulator/) and puts a portal in front for a whole team, with sign-in, a device pool, limits per person, [idle timeouts](/concepts/sessions/) and an audit log.

## DeviceFarmer STF

[Section titled “DeviceFarmer STF”](#devicefarmer-stf)

STF (formerly OpenSTF) is the classic open-source web UI for a farm of real phones on USB. Holtdroid can run [real phones](/configuration/phones/) too, and also starts virtual devices on demand, picks the [Android and WebView version](/concepts/webview-versions/) at launch, lists builds from your [sources](/sources/overview/) and keeps [app data](/concepts/app-data/) between sessions.

## docker-android and redroid

[Section titled “docker-android and redroid”](#docker-android-and-redroid)

docker-android runs the Android emulator in a container with a noVNC screen; redroid runs Android itself in a container on the host’s kernel. Both are building blocks for one device. Holtdroid uses redroid as its runtime and adds what a team needs around it: scheduling on Kubernetes, a session lifecycle, a scrcpy screen in the browser, DevTools, VPN and the portal.

## Android Studio’s emulator on your machine

[Section titled “Android Studio’s emulator on your machine”](#android-studios-emulator-on-your-machine)

The best choice for the developer who writes the app. For testers, designers and support engineers it means installing Android Studio, a fast computer and a cable or `chrome://inspect` for WebViews. Holtdroid needs only a browser, and the [holtdroid client](/guides/developers/connect-computer/) still puts the devices into `adb` and Android Studio when a developer wants them there.

## When Holtdroid is not the right tool

[Section titled “When Holtdroid is not the right tool”](#when-holtdroid-is-not-the-right-tool)

* You need iOS, or a specific real phone model you don’t own.
* You can’t run privileged Pods: redroid shares the node’s kernel, see [emulator isolation](/operations/emulator-security/).
* You want a hosted service with no cluster to run.
* Your main need is running automated test suites across many devices.

# Installation

> Install Holtdroid on Kubernetes with the Helm chart.

Caution

Pre-alpha: the emulator provider is new and not yet released. Simulated devices (`providers.fake`) are enough to try the UI, uploads, sign-in and storage setups without session nodes.

1. **Pick a sign-in mode** — see [Authentication](/configuration/authentication/). Every mode except `header`/`none` needs a session signing key:

   ```sh
   kubectl create namespace holtdroid
   kubectl -n holtdroid create secret generic holtdroid \
     --from-literal=SESSION_KEY="$(openssl rand -base64 48)"
   ```

   Add whatever else your config references with `env:` (OIDC client secret, shared password, S3 keys) to the same Secret. External Secrets Operator, Sealed Secrets and friends work just as well — the chart only needs the Secret’s name.

2. **Write your values.**

   values.yaml

   ```yaml
   publicURL: https://android.example.com
   existingSecret: holtdroid


   config:
     auth:
       mode: anonymous
       sessionKey: env:SESSION_KEY


   providers:
     emulator:
       enabled: true
       nodeSelector: { holtdroid/sessions: "true" } # nodes with binder and a GPU, dedicated to sessions
       slotsPerNode: 4
       # vpn: { locations: [...] }            # see the emulator provider page


   ingress:
     enabled: true
     host: android.example.com
   ```

3. **Install the chart**, from a release:

   ```sh
   helm install holtdroid oci://ghcr.io/holtdroid/charts/holtdroid -n holtdroid -f values.yaml
   ```

   or straight from git, pinning the image to the checked-out commit:

   ```sh
   git clone https://github.com/holtdroid/holtdroid
   helm install holtdroid holtdroid/deploy/helm/holtdroid -n holtdroid -f values.yaml \
     --set image.tag="$(git -C holtdroid rev-parse HEAD)"
   ```

4. **Open the URL and upload an APK** with the *Upload* button, or drop files into the `local` source directly:

   ```sh
   kubectl -n holtdroid cp app.apk "$(kubectl -n holtdroid get pod -l app.kubernetes.io/component=api -o name | cut -d/ -f2)":/var/lib/holtdroid/apks/
   ```

   For builds that arrive from CI or Slack, point a sync job at an S3 bucket and add it as a [source](/sources/overview/).

5. **Add Chromium and WebView builds** (optional). The project’s [chromium-builds](https://github.com/holtdroid/chromium-builds) releases carry Chromium browser and WebView APKs for every milestone from 83 on, x86_64 and arm64. Copy them into a bucket with the `chromium-builds` job of the [holtdroid-sync](https://github.com/holtdroid/holtdroid-sync) chart:

   chromium-builds-sync.yaml

   ```yaml
   job: chromium-builds
   existingSecret: holtdroid-chromium-builds-sync # S3_ACCESS_KEY, S3_SECRET_KEY
   config:
     target:
       type: s3
       s3:
         endpoint: https://s3.example.com
         bucket: holtdroid
         prefix: chromium-builds
         accessKey: env:S3_ACCESS_KEY
         secretKey: env:S3_SECRET_KEY
   ```

   ```sh
   git clone https://github.com/holtdroid/holtdroid-sync
   helm install holtdroid-chromium-builds-sync holtdroid-sync/deploy/helm/holtdroid-sync \
     -n holtdroid -f chromium-builds-sync.yaml --set image.tag="$(git -C holtdroid-sync rev-parse HEAD)"
   ```

   The job writes the browsers to `chromium-builds/browser` and the WebViews to `chromium-builds/webview`. Add the first as a read-only source, so Chromium shows up in the build list like any app, and the second as the WebView catalog, so the launch dialog offers Chromium WebView versions:

   values.yaml

   ```yaml
   config:
     sources:
       - name: local # listing sources replaces the default one; keep it for uploads
         type: filesystem
         filesystem: { dir: /var/lib/holtdroid/apks }
       - name: chromium
         type: s3
         readOnly: true
         s3:
           endpoint: https://s3.example.com
           bucket: holtdroid
           prefix: chromium-builds/browser
           accessKey: env:S3_ACCESS_KEY
           secretKey: env:S3_SECRET_KEY
     webview:
       storage:
         type: s3
         s3:
           endpoint: https://s3.example.com
           bucket: holtdroid
           prefix: chromium-builds/webview
           accessKey: env:S3_ACCESS_KEY
           secretKey: env:S3_SECRET_KEY
   ```

   All releases take about 55 GB. Without a cluster job, run it once from any computer with Docker, or upload single browser APKs from a release page with *Upload*; see [Chromium versions](/sources/chromium/#prebuilt-releases) and [WebView versions](/concepts/webview-versions/) for what the builds can and can’t do.

## Tracking `main` with Argo CD

[Section titled “Tracking main with Argo CD”](#tracking-main-with-argo-cd)

Every commit to `main` publishes `ghcr.io/holtdroid/holtdroid:<commit sha>`. An Argo CD Application can follow the branch and use the synced commit as the image tag, so new commits roll out on their own:

```yaml
apiVersion: argoproj.io/v1alpha1
kind: Application
metadata:
  name: holtdroid
  namespace: argocd
spec:
  project: default
  destination:
    server: https://kubernetes.default.svc
    namespace: holtdroid
  source:
    repoURL: https://github.com/holtdroid/holtdroid.git
    targetRevision: main
    path: deploy/helm/holtdroid
    helm:
      parameters:
        - name: image.tag
          value: $ARGOCD_APP_REVISION
      valuesObject:
        publicURL: https://android.example.com
        existingSecret: holtdroid
        # …the rest of your values
  syncPolicy:
    automated: { prune: true, selfHeal: true }
    syncOptions: [CreateNamespace=true]
```

Keep it a single-source Application so `$ARGOCD_APP_REVISION` is the holtdroid commit. Extra manifests (an `ExternalSecret`, a Traefik `Middleware`, …) can go into the chart’s `extraObjects` value. Right after a push the new pod may wait in `ImagePullBackOff` for a few minutes until that commit’s image is built.

## Chart values

[Section titled “Chart values”](#chart-values)

| Value                      | Default                       | Meaning                                                                         |
| -------------------------- | ----------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `image.repository` / `tag` | `ghcr.io/holtdroid/holtdroid` | Tag defaults to the chart’s `appVersion`                                        |
| `publicURL`                | –                             | External URL; needed for OIDC and secure cookies                                |
| `existingSecret`           | –                             | Secret exposed as env to every component (for `env:` references)                |
| `config`                   | anonymous, filesystem         | Merged into the api config, see [Configuration](/configuration/overview/)       |
| `api.replicas`             | `1`                           | Safe to raise with a shared `sessionKey`                                        |
| `api.cacheVolume`          | `emptyDir` 25Gi               | Volume for `storage.type: filesystem`                                           |
| `api.persistence.*`        | RWO PVC, 10Gi                 | Mounted at `/var/lib/holtdroid`: the default `local` source and uploads         |
| `providers.fake.enabled`   | `false`                       | Simulated devices                                                               |
| `providers.emulator.*`     | disabled                      | Emulator sessions, see [Emulator provider](/configuration/emulator/#helm-chart) |
| `providers.physical.*`     | disabled                      | Phones on USB, see [Phone provider](/configuration/phones/#helm-chart)          |
| `extraProviders`           | `[]`                          | Out-of-tree providers: `[{name, url}]`                                          |
| `ingress.*`                | disabled                      | Standard Ingress                                                                |
| `telemetry.*`              | off                           | Prometheus metrics and tracing, see [Monitoring](/operations/monitoring/)       |
| `audit.*`                  | stdout                        | Audit log of the api and ssh-gateway, same page                                 |
| `extraObjects`             | `[]`                          | Extra manifests, rendered with `tpl`                                            |

# ADB tools

> Logcat, files, a terminal and the app and device cards in the session page, over ADB in the browser.

The session page talks to the device’s ADB itself, in the browser, so you don’t need `adb`, SSH or a key on your machine. The tools sit in tabs next to DevTools:

* **Logcat** follows the main, system and crash buffers. By default it shows only lines from your app (matched by the app’s user id, so it keeps working across restarts and covers all of its processes); switch to **Everything** for the whole device. Filter by level and text, pause, clear, and download what is shown. When the app crashes, a notification shows the first lines of the stack trace with a link to the log. The log is collected from the moment the device is ready and survives app restarts and installing another build.
* **Files** browses the device: shared storage, the app’s private data (`/data/data/<package>`: shared preferences, databases, WebView cookies and storage), `/data/local/tmp` and the whole file system. Download files, upload them with the button or by dropping them onto the list (handy for testing file pickers), create folders and delete.
* **Terminal** is a shell with a real terminal (colours, `top`, line editing). On emulators it only appears when the provider allows arbitrary commands (`redroid.shell: full`); by default it is off, because that shell is root on the node running the session.

The **App** and **Device** rows of the Device panel use the same connection:

* **App** restarts or reinstalls the app and saves its data (these work without ADB), and over ADB shows the installed version, opens deep links (`myapp://…` or `https://…`, optionally only in your app, with a history kept in the browser), grants and revokes runtime permissions, force-stops the app, clears its data, puts the device into deep doze and moves the app between standby buckets.
* **Device** shows the model, Android version, ABIs and build, switches the WebView provider when the image has more than one (restart the app afterwards), and builds bug reports: **Bundle** is a zip with a screenshot, the logcat collected in the tab, device and app details, ready to attach to a bug; **Full report** runs Android’s own `bugreportz`.

Recording a session is done by the server, with logcat and the device’s state next to the screen: see [Recordings](/concepts/recordings/).

## Configuration

[Section titled “Configuration”](#configuration)

```yaml
adb:
  browser: true # session pages may open ADB
  ownerOnly: true # only a session's owner and admins may
```

On emulators ADB is a root shell without an authorization prompt, so anyone with the tools can run anything on that device, and because redroid shares the node’s kernel, root there reaches the node too (see [Security](/operations/security/)). With `ownerOnly` (the default) other users get only the screen and DevTools of sessions that aren’t theirs; set it to `false` to give everyone the tools, or `browser: false` to turn them off. Each connection is audited as `adb.connect` and `adb.disconnect`; see [Monitoring and audit](/operations/monitoring/).

Requests that would restart adbd or the device or move ADB somewhere else (`reboot`, `unroot`, `remount`, `tcpip`, `usb`, `sideload`, `disable-verity`) are refused here and over [SSH](/concepts/ssh/), because they would cut the session off from its own device. On phones the [phone provider](/configuration/phones/#adb-on-phones) also refuses `root`, reverse forwards and the frida-server ports, and limits shell commands with `adb.shell`.

On emulators the same `redroid.shell` policy applies to the browser and the `holtdroid` client: `allowlist` (the default) runs only the commands behind the Logcat tab and the App and Device rows, plus file transfer, so Files browses, downloads and uploads, without its Delete and New folder buttons; `full` runs anything and shows the Terminal tab and those buttons; `off` refuses every shell command. See [Emulator provider](/configuration/emulator/#users-adb-inside-android).

The browser keeps an ADB key in its storage; emulators don’t ask for it.

# App data

> Keep an app's sign-in, settings and WebView storage between sessions.

Every session starts from a fresh install. With app data turned on, Holtdroid can save the app’s private data from a session, by hand or when it ends, and you can start the next session of the same app from that save instead of signing in and clicking through onboarding again.

## What is saved

[Section titled “What is saved”](#what-is-saved)

The app’s internal storage: `/data/data/<package>` and `/data/user_de/0/<package>`. That covers databases, shared preferences, files, and the WebView’s cookies, local storage and IndexedDB. The cache (`cache/` and `code_cache/`) is saved only when the server allows it and it is small enough. External storage (`/sdcard/Android/data/<package>`) is not saved.

A save is taken when:

* you press **Stop**, or the session is stopped for being idle or reaching its maximum lifetime, and **Save app data when the session ends** was on when it was launched. It is off by default. The launch dialog remembers the checkbox in your browser and applies it to every launch from then on, quick launch and launch links included;
* you press **Save app data now** next to the app’s name in the session header. The app is stopped while it is copied and started again.

A session that dies on its own (its node goes away) leaves no save.

## Starting from a save

[Section titled “Starting from a save”](#starting-from-a-save)

The launch dialog has an **App data** choice: **Fresh install** (the default) or one of your saves of that app, newest first. Tick **Also restore the cache** to bring the cache back too, when the save has one.

The quick launch button (⚡) shows a menu when you hover it:

* **Fresh install**: no app data;
* **With app data**: your newest save of the app;
* **With app data and cache**: the same, with its cache.

A plain click launches the way you picked last time, remembered in your browser. Until you pick, it uses your newest save, or a fresh install when there is none.

## Managing saves

[Section titled “Managing saves”](#managing-saves)

The **App data** page (the database icon in the dock) lists your saves per app with their size, build and when they were last used. You can download a save as a `.tar.zst` archive, unless the server turned that off (`tar --zstd -xf <file>` unpacks it), and delete it. Saves are private: nobody else sees them, admins included.

## Limitations

[Section titled “Limitations”](#limitations)

* Apps that encrypt their data with Android Keystore keys can’t read it on another device, because those keys stay on the device the save came from. Such apps may sign you out or reset parts of their state.
* Data from a newer build may break an older one, for example when its database can’t be downgraded. The launch dialog warns about that.

## Configuration

[Section titled “Configuration”](#configuration)

```yaml
appData:
  enabled: true
  cache: true # allow saving the cache
  maxCacheSize: 256MiB # a bigger cache is left out of the save
  maxSize: 1GiB # the cache is left out when it would push a save over this; bigger data isn't saved
  keep: 6 # saves kept per user and app, the most recently used ones; 0 = no limit
  maxAge: 168h # deleted this long after their last use; 0 = never
  export: true # let users download their saves
  timeout: 5m # how long a save may take before the session is stopped without it
  storage: # optional: where saves go; default is the shared storage under app-data/
    type: s3
    s3:
      endpoint: https://s3.example.com
      bucket: holtdroid
      prefix: app-data
      accessKey: env:S3_ACCESS_KEY
      secretKey: env:S3_SECRET_KEY
```

| Key                    | Default  | Meaning                                                                                                          |
| ---------------------- | -------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `appData.enabled`      | `false`  | Save app data when sessions stop and offer it at launch                                                          |
| `appData.cache`        | `false`  | Also save `cache/` and `code_cache/`                                                                             |
| `appData.maxCacheSize` | `256MiB` | A cache bigger than this is not saved; the rest of the data still is                                             |
| `appData.maxSize`      | `1GiB`   | The cache is dropped when it would push a save over this; data alone over it is not saved at all; `0` = no limit |
| `appData.keep`         | `6`      | Saves kept per user and app, the most recently used first; `0` = no limit                                        |
| `appData.maxAge`       | `168h`   | A save unused this long is deleted; `0` = never                                                                  |
| `appData.export`       | `true`   | Users may download their saves                                                                                   |
| `appData.timeout`      | `5m`     | Longest a save may take                                                                                          |
| `appData.storage.*`    | shared   | Same keys as [`storage`](/configuration/storage/); empty `type` = the shared storage                             |

The shared storage is often an `emptyDir` cache (the chart’s default), which loses saves on every restart of the api. Point `appData.storage` at S3 or a persistent volume to keep them.

Sizes are measured on the device, before compression. Stopping a session waits for its save, so a big save makes **Stop** slower.

# Architecture

> The services that make up Holtdroid and how a request flows through them.

Holtdroid is a handful of small services built from **one Go binary** (`holtdroid <subcommand>`), plus a heavier session image that contains the Android emulator.

```
flowchart LR
  user([Browser]) -->|forward-auth| ingress[Ingress]
  ingress --> api

  subgraph ns[holtdroid namespace]
    api["api<br/>UI + REST + session proxy"]
    prov["provider-emulator"]
    subgraph session["Session Pod"]
      agent["agent + emulator"]
      vpn["vpn (sing-box)"]
    end
  end

  api -- "list + download" --> sources[("Sources<br/>folder / S3")]
  sync["sync jobs<br/>(Slack, CI, …)"] -. "*.apk + .meta.json" .-> sources
  api -- Provider API --> prov
  api -- "Agent API via /s/{provider}/{id}/" --> agent
  prov --> k8s[(Kubernetes API)]
  agent -. shared network namespace .- vpn
  vpn --> internet[(Internet)]
```

| Service               | Role                                                                                                                                                                                                                           |
| --------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| **api**               | Serves the web UI and its REST API, lists APKs from folder/S3 sources and takes uploads, caches and parses APKs, asks providers for sessions, proxies all session traffic, tracks activity and reaps idle sessions. Stateless. |
| **sync jobs**         | Independent of Holtdroid: anything that writes `*.apk` files (and optional `.meta.json` sidecars) into a source, e.g. a Slack channel sync.                                                                                    |
| **provider-emulator** | A *device provider*: owns emulator sessions as Kubernetes Pods, accounts for slots, renders the VPN sidecar.                                                                                                                   |
| **agent**             | Runs inside each session: boots the device, installs and instruments the app, serves the screen, DevTools, clipboard and network controls.                                                                                     |

## Design principles

[Section titled “Design principles”](#design-principles)

* **Contracts between services.** Providers and agents are HTTP APIs with a shared conformance suite; sources are a file layout. The api knows nothing about Slack, Kubernetes or ADB. See [Contracts](/extending/contracts/).

* **Stateless api.** Nothing the api needs to keep sessions running lives only in its memory or on its disk:

  * sessions belong to providers — the emulator provider keeps them as labels and annotations on the session Pods it creates, so listing Pods *is* listing sessions;
  * sign-ins are signed cookies, verifiable by any replica holding the same `auth.sessionKey`;
  * user activity is flushed to the provider every 30 seconds;
  * downloaded APKs are a cache (filesystem or S3) that refills from the sources; uploads and their owner/visibility live as files in a source.

  Kill the api, reschedule it to another node or run three replicas — nobody notices. The api’s [database](/configuration/database/) holds history, not live state: in memory by default, or a SQLite file replicated to S3, which limits the api to one replica.

* **Same origin for everything.** Browser traffic to a device goes through `https://<portal>/s/<session>/…`. That keeps forward-auth cookies working for WebSockets inside iframes and means users need nothing installed locally.

* **No lock-in.** Auth, secrets and VPN are interfaces with vendor-neutral defaults.

## Launching a session

[Section titled “Launching a session”](#launching-a-session)

```
sequenceDiagram
  participant B as Browser
  participant A as api
  participant S as source
  participant P as provider
  participant G as agent

  B->>A: POST /api/v1/sessions
  A->>S: download the APK revision (if not cached)
  A->>A: parse APK metadata
  A->>P: POST /v1/sessions
  P-->>A: session (provisioning)
  A-->>B: session id
  B->>A: GET /s/{provider}/{id}/v1/status (SSE)
  G->>A: fetch APK (internal port)
  G-->>B: booting → installing → instrumenting → ready
```

# Camera

> Give the device a camera that shows a test card, an image or video from your media library, or your own camera.

redroid devices have no camera of their own. Sessions on Android 13, 14 and 15 get one from Holtdroid: a back camera that any app can open (Camera2, CameraX, a WebView’s `getUserMedia`). The **Camera** row of the session’s Device panel (tab **Media**) chooses what it shows.

| Source       | What apps see                                                                          |
| ------------ | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Test card    | SMPTE color bars with the date and a running clock, the default                        |
| No picture   | A black frame, as from a covered lens                                                  |
| A media file | An image (a QR code, a document, a face) or a video from your media library, on repeat |
| Your camera  | This browser’s camera, live, for as long as you keep it on                             |

The clock on the test card shows at a glance whether the picture an app got is live, frozen or late. Images and videos are scaled to fill the frame the app asked for and cut at the center, so any aspect ratio works; the picture is upright on a phone held in portrait, as with a real back camera.

The row says **in use** while an app has the camera open. Your camera asks for the browser’s permission the first time, sends 15 frames a second (about 3–7 Mbit/s up) and stops when you close the session page or pick another source.

## Media library

[Section titled “Media library”](#media-library)

Images and videos come from the same library as the [microphone](/concepts/microphone/)’s files: add them from either row. Each user has `media.quota` (5 GiB by default).

## Load

[Section titled “Load”](#load)

Nothing renders while no app uses the camera: the agent makes frames only for an open camera. On Android 15 the camera HAL itself starts when an app opens the camera and exits a few seconds after it closes it; on 13 and 14 it stays up but idle (about 16 MB of memory, no CPU), because their cameraserver can’t cope with a stopped one. While one is open, a 1080p stream costs about a third of a CPU core (ffmpeg making the picture and the HAL copying it into the app’s buffers).

## How it works

[Section titled “How it works”](#how-it-works)

holtdroid-redroid’s images for Android 13 to 15 carry a small camera HAL (an AIDL camera provider, lazy on 15). When an app configures a stream it connects to the agent over the abstract socket `@holtdroid-camera`, asks for the largest stream’s size and reads raw frames that ffmpeg renders from the chosen source; it scales them into each of the app’s buffers and encodes JPEGs for still captures on the CPU, without the GPU. Android 11 and 12, and phones, have no Holtdroid camera, and the row is not shown.

# WebView DevTools

> How Holtdroid enables WebView debugging without touching the APK, and how DevTools reaches your browser.

Android only exposes a WebView to Chrome DevTools when the app calls `WebView.setWebContentsDebuggingEnabled(true)` or is built as `debuggable`. Release and most test builds do neither, and a debuggable OS build does not change that.

## Enabling debugging at runtime

[Section titled “Enabling debugging at runtime”](#enabling-debugging-at-runtime)

Sessions run redroid, a rooted userdebug build. After the device boots, the agent starts `frida-server`, installs the APK unmodified and **spawns** the app under Frida with a small script that enables WebView debugging on the main thread before the first WebView is created. The clipboard doesn’t need it: it is synced through scrcpy, like the screen.

Note

Apps with root, emulator or instrumentation detection may refuse to run. That is the main limitation of the emulator provider. A [phone without root](/configuration/phones/) runs such apps, but shows DevTools only for debuggable builds: the app turns WebView debugging on by itself there, without Frida.

## Getting DevTools into the browser

[Section titled “Getting DevTools into the browser”](#getting-devtools-into-the-browser)

Each process with debuggable WebViews listens on an abstract UNIX socket named `webview_devtools_remote_<pid>`. The agent:

1. watches `/proc/net/unix` for those sockets (and `chrome_devtools_remote`);
2. forwards each one through ADB;
3. merges their target lists into one, which the toolbar’s **target** selector shows (page, iframe, service worker, grouped by process);
4. proxies the DevTools WebSocket, rewriting the `Host` header to `localhost`, since the DevTools server rejects any other host;
5. reports the DevTools frontend revision matching the WebView; the portal serves that frontend from a cache of its own in its storage, fetched from Google’s frontend host ahead of time for every Chromium and WebView build it lists, so a session’s VPN, bandwidth limit or offline mode doesn’t affect it. While a revision is still being fetched the panel says so above DevTools, with the number of files so far; DevTools opens as its files arrive. Admins see every fetched revision on the **DevTools frontends** tab of the Inventory page, with its state, file count and archive, and can delete one (it is fetched afresh on the next open) or fetch it ahead of the queue. Chromium snapshot builds report no revision, so the agent uses the `frontend` tag of the [WebView build](/concepts/webview-versions/) or of the [Chromium build](/sources/chromium/) the session started with. Built-in WebViews of some Android images report a revision that is no real commit; for those the agent looks up the commit of the WebView’s version in Chromium Dash.

All of this sits under the session’s path on the portal’s own origin, so your auth cookie covers it and nothing has to be installed on your machine. When the app navigates or recreates its WebView, the panel reconnects to the new target automatically.

Next to the target selector, an address bar shows the selected target’s current URL. The bug icon in front of them refreshes the target list. Copy it with the button on the right, or type or paste another one and press Enter to load it in the WebView (a URL without a scheme gets `https://`, or `http://` for `localhost`, `127.x` and `10.0.2.2`); Escape restores the current one. The button on the left reloads the page. Both send `Page.navigate` / `Page.reload` over a second, short-lived DevTools connection to the same target, so they work with the screencast off. Service workers and other non-page targets only show their URL.

Android’s WebView renders every iframe in its page’s process, even one from another site, so an iframe is never a DevTools target of its own. Pick its page, open the **Console** tab and choose the iframe in the context menu at the console’s top left, the one that reads `top ▾`; Elements, Sources and Network already show it as part of the page. The target selector says the same at the bottom of its list.

Next to DevTools are tabs built on the same connection, which work without DevTools open: [WebSockets](/session-tools/websockets/) and [Cache](/session-tools/cache/). The agent keeps the session’s socket traffic and requests, so they also show what happened before they were opened or the page reloaded.

The settings button next to the target selector holds two switches, saved in your browser:

* **Portal font and colors** (on by default): DevTools uses the portal’s font, gray accents instead of Chrome’s blue, and follows the portal’s light or dark theme; in the dark theme its panels are near-black like the portal. Syntax highlighting keeps DevTools’ colors.
* **Screencast on open** (off by default): DevTools’ own preview of the page is off, since the session already shows the screen. The phone icon at the left of the DevTools toolbar still turns it on for the current target.

# Microphone

> Make the device's microphone hear a test signal, a file from your media library or your own microphone.

A redroid device has no microphone of its own: apps that record hear silence. The **Microphone** row of the session’s Device panel (tab **Media**) replaces what they hear, for every app and every kind of recording (voice notes, speech recognition, calls in a WebView), until you turn it off.

| Source          | What apps hear                                                             |
| --------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Off             | Silence, the device’s own microphone                                       |
| Line-up tone    | A steady 1 kHz tone at −18 dBFS, the broadcast test tone                   |
| Beeps           | A 100 ms 1 kHz beep at the start of every second, to measure delay         |
| Pink noise      | Steady noise across all frequencies                                        |
| A media file    | An audio file, or the sound of a video, from your media library, on repeat |
| Your microphone | This browser’s microphone, live, for as long as you keep it on             |

**Turn off** in the row stops whatever plays. Choosing another source stops the one before, including your microphone in another tab. Your microphone asks for the browser’s permission the first time and stops when you close the session page.

The row is there only on devices whose microphone can be replaced: redroid sessions on Android 11 and later. Phones keep their own microphone (and Holtdroid denies it to the app under test, see [Phones](/configuration/phones/#sound-microphone-and-camera)).

## Media library

[Section titled “Media library”](#media-library)

Files you add to the library belong to you, not to a session, so every session can play them. The library also holds the images and videos the [camera](/concepts/camera/) shows. Anything ffmpeg reads works: MP3, AAC, Opus, WAV, FLAC, or a video, whose sound is played. Files keep their format; nothing is converted on upload, and the sound is resampled to what the app records at.

Each user has `media.quota` (5 GiB by default; per role and per user in the `users` auth mode, see [Authentication](/configuration/authentication/)), and one file can be up to `media.maxFileSize` (1 GiB). Files stay until you delete them.

## How it works

[Section titled “How it works”](#how-it-works)

The agent starts a small helper on the device that registers an Android audio policy: every recording is routed to a remote submix that the helper plays into. The agent feeds it with ffmpeg (test signals and files, in real time) or with the samples your browser sends over a WebSocket (16-bit mono at 48 kHz, about 100 KB/s). When the helper exits, Android drops the policy and the microphone is silent again.

## Configuration

[Section titled “Configuration”](#configuration)

```yaml
media:
  enabled: true # the library and its API; on by default
  quota: 5GiB # per user; 0 = no limit
  maxFileSize: 1GiB # largest file
  storage: # optional: where files go; default is the shared storage under media/
    type: s3
    s3: { endpoint: https://s3.example.com, bucket: holtdroid, prefix: media }
```

Test signals and your microphone work with the library turned off.

# Recordings

> Sessions recorded on the server with logcat, the WebViews' network, console and WebSockets, device, network and load next to the screen, to watch, download or share.

With recordings turned on, the server records sessions while they run. A recording keeps more than the picture:

* the **screen**, as the device encoded it;
* **logcat** of the whole device, every line stamped with the time since the recording started;
* the app’s **WebViews**, as DevTools would show them: every request with its headers, body, response and timing, console messages and uncaught exceptions with their objects, and WebSocket and event-stream messages (see [Network, console and WebSockets](#network-console-and-websockets));
* the **device**: model, Android, build, the WebView version, screen size and density, language, theme, battery;
* the **network**: the VPN location with its external IP and country, the emulated network conditions (throttling: added delay, bandwidth, loss, scenarios; a region with what it adds to CDN and server round trips) and which links are on;
* the **DNS** log: every query with its answers and TTLs, and when rewrites, the TTL limit or the cache changed (see [DNS log and rewrites](/session-tools/dns/));
* the **connections**: every server the device talked to, through which location, with its bytes (see [Routes](/session-tools/routes/));
* the **time**: real time next to the device clock, with its time zone and how far it was set off real time;
* the **load** every two seconds: device and app CPU, memory, frames and jank, traffic, the container’s CPU and throttling, temperatures;
* whether the app was running, and when another build was installed;
* whether the **display** was awake, off or locked, however it happened: the power button in the portal, the screen timing out or the app turning it off;
* what the person at the screen did: taps, long presses and swipes, and the buttons of the phone beside the screen (Back, Home, Recents, volume, rotate, the notification shade and so on). Only what was done in the portal is seen; input from `adb` over SSH or from the app itself isn’t. Typed text and other keys are never recorded.

Nothing is rendered on the server: the agent copies the video the device already encodes and writes the rest as small text files next to it. The portal draws the page from that data: cards on the left for the moment, the network, the device and the load, the phone in the middle, tools on the right (findings, logcat and the WebViews’ network, console and WebSockets), and under them a timeline: one track with the markers above it and, along it, where the screen, the app and the network changed and what happened.

## Recording a session

[Section titled “Recording a session”](#recording-a-session)

What gets recorded is set by `recordings.mode`:

* **`always`** (the default): every session is recorded from the moment it is ready, and a recording can’t be stopped. There is no switch in the launch dialog and no Stop button.
* **`auto`**: sessions are recorded unless you untick **Record from start** in the launch dialog (the choice is remembered in the browser and used by the quick launch button). A recording can be stopped from the session page.
* **`manual`**: sessions are recorded only when you tick **Record from start** at launch or start it from the session page.

On the session page the header has **Record** (unless the mode is `always`). While a recording runs the button shows the elapsed time instead, and **a click on it pins a marker** on the recording’s timeline at that moment; **Share** next to it makes a link and copies it, and the **…** menu adds a marker, opens the recording, stops sharing or stops recording. The **Recording** row of the Device panel (tab **Media**) has the same marker click and, opened, the rest: how long it has run, its size and how much of your space is used; **Keep forever**, which exempts the recording from the retention period; **Share**, which makes a link and copies it (sharing keeps the recording too); a button to open the recording; and, unless the mode is `always`, to stop or start recording. Stopping and starting again makes a new recording. A recording ends when the session stops; the last few seconds are uploaded before the device goes away.

The screen is taken from what a viewer of the session already streams in H.264, so watching and recording cost one encoder on the device. When nobody watches, or the viewer picked H.265 or AV1, the agent runs a stream of its own for the recording: H.264, at most 1280 pixels on the long side, 30 fps, 2 Mbit/s. A static screen costs next to nothing either way.

The sound is taken the same way: the stream of a viewer who listens, or a capture of its own for the recording when nobody does (phones capture sound all session long anyway). It is written as a separate track, 10 seconds a segment, 40 to 60 MB an hour, as Opus, or as AAC on Android 11, whose Opus encoder doesn’t start. A device that can’t capture sound is asked once and then left alone: its recordings are silent. When the device is silent, the recording is too.

## The recordings list

[Section titled “The recordings list”](#the-recordings-list)

**Recordings** in the dock (the clapperboard) lists your recordings, newest first, one row each: a preview, the app’s icon and the recording’s name, its version, how many markers it has, **Shared** or **Kept**, when it was made, its length and size, and when retention deletes it. The preview is the screen just before the touch nearest to the fifth second of the recording, so it shows what someone was about to tap, or the screen at the fifth second when nobody touched it. A recording still in progress is marked and can be watched while it grows.

The buttons on a row **keep** the recording past the retention period (or let it expire again), make and copy a **share link**, stop sharing, rename it, **delete** it and open it. The **Storage** card beside the list shows how much of your space is used and the server’s rules: how long recordings are kept, the shortest one that is kept and whether share links are allowed. **Open a file** plays a `.holtdroid` file from your disk (see [Recording file](#recording-file-holtdroid)).

## The player

[Section titled “The player”](#the-player)

A recording opens on a page of its own:

* **the header**: back to the list, the app’s icon, the recording’s name (with the pencil to rename it), its version, the screen it was recorded on, the VPN location, who recorded it, when, how long it is and its size. On the right: when retention deletes it (or **Kept**, **Shared, kept**), **Keep**, **Link at 04:09**, **Share** (see [Sharing](#sharing)), stop sharing, and **Export** (see [Downloads](#downloads));
* **cards on the left** with the state at the playhead: **At 04:09** (real time, the device clock with how far it was set off, its time zone, the screen, whether the app runs, the battery), **Network** (the VPN exit and IP, the emulated network, the region and the traffic, with bars for the last minute), **Device** (the package, version, model, Android, WebView, screen and the quick settings that were on) and **Load** (CPU, memory, the app, frames, the container and temperatures). They change as the video plays;
* **the phone** in the middle, playing the screen, with taps and swipes drawn over it. Above it a badge says what the screen showed and since when (**Landscape since 03:52**, **Off since 01:14**), next to the button that hides taps and swipes and full screen. **Marker** (or `M`) sits in the corner on your own recordings;
* **the tools on the right**: **Findings**, Logcat, and, when the app had WebViews, Network, Console, WebSockets and Cache, plus DNS and Routes when the session had them and Pixel perfect for signed-in viewers. The tabs that don’t fit in the column’s width go under **More**, the open one always stays in view. Every tab shows what had happened up to the moment you are at.

Everything beside the phone is ordinary page text, so you can select and copy it.

### Findings

[Section titled “Findings”](#findings)

**Findings** collects what went wrong up to the playhead, newest first: requests that failed or answered 4xx or 5xx, console errors and uncaught exceptions in the WebViews, the app’s crashes and ANRs found in logcat (`FATAL EXCEPTION`, tombstones, `ANR in`), and the app closing without a crash. The last one before the playhead is highlighted. Click one to jump there; a request offers **Open in Network** and **Copy as cURL**, a console error **Open in Console**. The tab’s counter turns red when there are errors.

### Timeline and controls

[Section titled “Timeline and controls”](#timeline-and-controls)

The card under the phone starts with five seconds back, play and pause, five seconds forward, the time, the speed (**0.5×**, **1×**, **2×**, **4×**), the sound, and **Jump to** **Error**, **Marker** or **Tap**, each going to the next one after the playhead.

Under them, one track shows the whole recording, with the time under it:

| On the track        | Shows                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                               |
| ------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| flags above it      | the markers, with their note (see [Markers](#markers)); near the end they open to the left                                                                                                                                                                                          |
| round icons         | where something changed: the **screen** (portrait, landscape, off, locked, no video), the **app** (running, closed, starting), the **network** (the emulated network, region or VPN exit; amber when throttled, red when offline) and DNS rewrites, TTL or a cleared cache (violet) |
| red and amber icons | crashes (a bug) and ANRs (an hourglass)                                                                                                                                                                                                                                             |
| short ticks         | taps and swipes (grey), errors (red) and closes and 4xx answers (amber)                                                                                                                                                                                                             |

The part already played is shaded, and a line marks the playhead. Hover the track to see the time under the pointer, what changed or happened there and what the screen, the app and the network were doing; click or drag to go there. With the keyboard, focus the track: the arrows move five seconds, `Page Up` / `Page Down` a tenth of the recording (at least thirty seconds), `Home` / `End` to either end, and the same readout follows the playhead.

| Key            | Does                                    |
| -------------- | --------------------------------------- |
| `Space` or `K` | play or pause                           |
| `←` / `→`      | five seconds back / forward             |
| `M`            | pin a marker here (your own recordings) |

Taps and swipes show on the phone as green circles with a fading trail, and the navigation keys as a label at the bottom. The pointer button hides them (it only appears when something was touched); the downloaded video always has them.

When a recording has sound, a speaker button next to the speed turns it on or off. It plays at 1× only, since at other speeds it would change its pitch; at 0.5×, 2× and 4× the player is silent. The downloaded video carries the sound (AAC, or Opus where the browser has no AAC encoder) and so does the `.holtdroid` file.

### Markers

[Section titled “Markers”](#markers)

A marker is a pin on the timeline with an icon (pin, bug, flag, star, warning or done) and a short note. Click the elapsed time in the session header (or the **Recording** row) while it records, or press **Marker** (or `M`) in the player: the marker lands at that moment and a small field opens over the phone to say what happened. `Enter` saves it, `Esc` leaves it unnamed. Click a pin to jump there, rename it, change its icon or delete it. Anyone with a share link sees the markers but can’t change them. The downloaded video shows each marker as a label over the phone for a few seconds, and a recording with a marker is never deleted for being too short.

### Logcat

[Section titled “Logcat”](#logcat)

The **Logcat** tab has the whole device’s logcat, each line with its time in the recording:

* the level menu hides quieter lines (for example **Warnings and above**) and the filter box searches tags and messages;
* click a line’s time to jump to it in the recording;
* while you hold a selection the panel stops following the video, so the text doesn’t scroll away; click elsewhere to follow again;
* the copy button puts the lines on screen on the clipboard.

The live tab is described in [Logcat](/session-tools/logcat/).

### Network, console and WebSockets

[Section titled “Network, console and WebSockets”](#network-console-and-websockets)

The agent watches the app’s WebViews over a DevTools connection of its own, whether or not anyone has DevTools open: every tab, every iframe (nested ones too) and every worker and service worker, from their very first request. It follows them for the whole session, so a socket the app opened before the recording started is still recorded from then on, with its address. The tabs next to **Logcat** show what it saw up to the moment you are at; when there is more than one tab, iframe or worker, a menu narrows Network and Console to one of them, and lines from iframes and workers say where they came from. Android’s WebView runs an iframe in its page’s process, even one from another site, so it is not a context of its own: its requests, console and sockets are recorded with the page’s. In a live session’s DevTools you reach it the same way, through the page: pick it in the Console’s context menu (`top ▾`), or find it in Elements and Sources. Counters on the tabs turn red when requests failed or the page logged errors.

* **Network** lists requests as they were sent: status (pending until the response is complete at that moment), method, name, host, size and time. Filter by URL, by type (Fetch/XHR, Doc, JS and so on) or to errors only. Click a request for its headers, query string and body (**Payload**), the **Response** and its **Timing**, or copy it as cURL or as a `fetch()` call. **Timing** splits the request’s time into **Queued, stalled**, **DNS**, **Connect** (TLS included), **Send**, **Waiting (TTFB)** and **Download**, so you can tell a slow server from a slow network or a queue in the app. Bodies are kept up to 1 MB; images, media and fonts are recorded without theirs.
* **Console** has `console.*` calls, uncaught exceptions with their stack and the WebView’s own messages (failed loads, violations, deprecations), with level filters and search. Click a message to open the objects it logged and its stack.
* **WebSockets** lists the sockets and event streams; pick one for its frames, sent ↑ and received ↓, and click a frame for its contents. A socket that carries video or another media stream (its frames look like H.264, MP4, WebM, JPEG and the like, or it moves a steady flow of data) is marked **media stream**: from then on its frames are counted but not recorded.
* **Cache** checks how the requests up to that moment use the WebView’s cache and a CDN in front of the server (see [Cache](/session-tools/cache/)).

JSON is shown as a tree you can open and close, also when it sits in a string field. Messages and bodies in common framings are split into their parts, each a tree: **Socket.IO** and **Engine.IO** packets (the event name as a label, `2`/`3` as ping and pong), **SignalR** and Engine.IO polling records separated by `\x1e`, **Server-Sent Events** and **JSON Lines**. Frames show their label and a one-line preview in the list; a binary frame is marked **bin**, and one that holds UTF-8 text shows that text (and parses it) rather than base64. Forms are name and value pairs, binary payloads a hex dump. **Pretty** and **Raw** switch between the parsed view and the text as it was sent, and the copy button copies it.

Values that look like a point in time get two chips: the first (a clock with an arrow back) says how far they were from the **device clock when the line was recorded**, the second how far they are from it **at the player’s position** (“now”, “3.2 s ago”, “in 1 h”), so a timestamp that was “now” when it arrived keeps “now” in the first chip and reads “3 s ago” in the second three seconds of video later. The live WebSockets tab of a session shows the same two chips, the second against the clock right now. Times are found in Unix time in seconds, milliseconds, microseconds or nanoseconds, ISO 8601 and HTTP dates. Hover it for its distance from the device clock both now and when it was recorded, the same moment in UTC, in the device’s time zone and in yours, as Unix seconds and milliseconds (click one to copy), and, when the device clock was set off real time, how it compares with real time. When that moment lies within the recording, **Go to 00:12** jumps there, back or ahead. A value without a time zone is read as UTC. Plain numbers count as seconds only when the field’s name says it is a time (`expiresAt`, `created_at`, `exp`, `ts`…) or they fall within five years of the recording.

Caution

Headers, cookies and bodies are recorded as the app sent and received them, tokens included, and anyone with a share link or the `.holtdroid` file sees them.

### Cache

[Section titled “Cache”](#cache)

The Cache tab runs the same checks as in a live session, on what was recorded up to the moment you are at. It reads the recorded requests’ headers and says where caching goes wrong: the request time in the URL, parameters that change on every request, the same file downloaded again, CDN misses and hits that shouldn’t be, and weak headers. See [Cache](/session-tools/cache/).

In a finding, a request’s time seeks there and **Open in Network** shows it on the Network tab.

### Pixel perfect

[Section titled “Pixel perfect”](#pixel-perfect)

Signed-in viewers get a **Pixel perfect** tab next to the others, with the same panel as in a session (see [Pixel perfect](/session-tools/pixel-perfect/)): the reference is laid over the video, and **Find differences** pauses playback and compares the frame at the playhead. **Skip what moves** takes the next few frames of the recording. A recording has no device behind it, so differences aren’t named by native views or WebView elements, Detect only finds plain bars, and there is no Freeze: the paused frame is already still. Frames come from the stream’s video, so a higher stream quality while recording gives a cleaner comparison. Recordings made since this was added keep the device’s screen size and density, so dp are exact; older ones take the screen as 360 dp wide.

### DNS and Routes

[Section titled “DNS and Routes”](#dns-and-routes)

**DNS** lists the names the device looked up up to that moment, with their answers, and **Routes** where the connections went, as in a session (see [DNS log and rewrites](/session-tools/dns/#recordings) and [Routes](/session-tools/routes/#in-recordings)).

## Downloads

[Section titled “Downloads”](#downloads)

**Export** in the player’s header offers:

| Item                            | What you get                                                           | Who has it                                |
| ------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------- |
| **Video (.mp4)**                | the screen with the device’s cards beside it, rendered in your browser | your own recordings, once they have ended |
| **Recording file (.holtdroid)** | everything in one file, to watch again without the server              | your own and shared recordings            |
| **Network (.har)**              | the WebViews’ requests with their bodies and the WebSocket messages    | when the app had WebViews                 |
| **Logcat, colored (.log)**      | the whole logcat with levels and colours as ANSI codes                 | everyone                                  |
| **Logcat, plain text (.txt)**   | the same lines without colour codes                                    | everyone                                  |

The **HAR** file opens in Chrome DevTools’ Network panel (drop it there), and in Charles, Fiddler or HAR viewers.

In both logcat files each line starts with its time in the recording, followed by the usual `threadtime` line. The colored one keeps the level letter in bold and colours tags and the lines of warnings and errors, so it reads well with `less -R`, `bat`, `lnav` or an editor with ANSI support.

### Video (.mp4)

[Section titled “Video (.mp4)”](#video-mp4)

**Export → Video (.mp4)** renders the recording into an MP4 file in your browser, frame by frame, with the Holtdroid logo on top (the text is part of the picture, so it can’t be selected). It opens with a three-second card about the app (name, version, package) and the device (model, Android, WebView, screen), when it was recorded and how long it is; then the phone plays with a narrow column beside it for what changes: the device clock and the recording time, whether the app runs, the battery, quick settings, the network and the load. Logcat and the WebViews’ tabs stay on the page, where they can be read and searched. It is 1296 pixels tall and 30 fps: 1262×1296 for a phone held upright. If the screen turned sideways in the recording or it is a tablet, the phone’s column is made wider and so is the video (up to about 2160 pixels), so the picture stays readable; the phone’s frame turns smoothly when the device does. A progress bar over the recording’s timeline shows how far it got, how fast it goes and how long is left; keep the tab open until it finishes.

The video is never held in memory. In Chrome and Edge you first pick where to save it and it is written straight into that file as it renders; cancelling removes the half-written file. Other browsers collect it in their private storage as they go and download it at the end. It needs a browser with WebCodecs (Chrome, Edge, Safari 17+, Firefox 130+) that can encode a video this size.

### Recording file (.holtdroid)

[Section titled “Recording file (.holtdroid)”](#recording-file-holtdroid)

This saves everything in one file: the video segments, the events (device state, network, load, taps), the logcat, the WebViews’ requests, console and WebSockets, the markers, the preview and the app’s icon. It is an ordinary ZIP archive whose video and logs are stored as they are, so any archiver opens it. It points back at nothing on the server.

Open it again, on any machine and without signing in, on the **Open** page (**Recordings → Open a file**, or `/open`): drop the file on the page or pick it. It plays exactly like a recording on the server, with the logcat, panels, taps, markers and the video download, and **nothing is uploaded**. The browser reads only the pieces it plays (the segment under the playhead, the logcat around it) from your disk, so the file never sits in memory whole, however big it is. Keep, sharing and editing markers are only for recordings on the server.

In the archive: `holtdroid.json` (the format, the recording’s details and its markers), `manifest.json`, `init-N.mp4` and `seg-N.m4s` (the video, as fragmented MP4), `ainit-N.mp4` and `aseg-N.m4s` (the sound, as Opus or AAC in fragmented MP4), `events-N.jsonl.gz` (one JSON event per line), `logcat-N.log.gz`, `devtools-N.jsonl.gz` (one JSON line per request, console message, socket change or frame), `thumb.jpg` and `icon.png`. To get a plain video of a recording without a new epoch (the screen didn’t turn or restart), join an init file and its segments in order: `cat init-0.mp4 seg-1.m4s seg-2.m4s … > video.mp4`.

## Naming

[Section titled “Naming”](#naming)

A recording is named after its app. The pencil next to the name, on a recording’s card and on its page, gives it a name of your own (up to 120 characters); leaving it empty goes back to the app’s. The name shows to anyone with the share link, in the `.holtdroid` file and in the video’s header.

## Sharing

[Section titled “Sharing”](#sharing)

**Share** in the player’s header (or the link button on a row in the list) makes a link that opens the recording without signing in, and copies it. Once shared, the button reads **Copy share link** and gives the same link, at the moment you are at; **Stop sharing** turns it off. A shared recording is kept, so the link doesn’t die after `recordings.maxAge`; it stays kept when you stop sharing, until you let it expire yourself. People with the link can watch and download the logcat, but the page has no video download. The shared page shows the recording’s name and who recorded it (their display name).

The link you copy carries the moment you are at, like a video link with a time: `#t=46.2&tab=network&request=…` opens the recording there, on the same tab (Findings, Logcat, Network, Console, WebSockets, DNS, Routes or Cache), with the request, console message, socket frame, name or finding you had open opened and scrolled to. `t` also takes `1m20s`. **Link at 00:46** copies such a link for the page you are on: for your own recording that is the portal’s page, which only signed-in people can open, and it doesn’t share anything. Someone signed in to the portal who opens a share link sees it inside the portal, with its dock and menus.

## Keeping and space

[Section titled “Keeping and space”](#keeping-and-space)

A recording that ends in under `recordings.minDuration` (20 seconds by default) is deleted as soon as it ends: a session stopped at once or one that failed to start leaves nothing to watch. A recording you kept or shared, or one with a marker on it, stays.

Recordings are deleted `recordings.maxAge` after they were made unless you **Keep** them. Each user has `recordings.quota` bytes: when a new recording doesn’t fit, the oldest recordings that aren’t kept are deleted first; when only kept ones are left, new sessions start without a recording and a running one stops. Kept recordings count against the quota too.
