As a rough guide, a recording takes 0.2 to 2 GB per hour of an app in use (the viewer’s stream quality decides), less for mostly static screens; logcat and the device data add a few megabytes per hour, and the WebViews’ traffic as much as its bodies weigh (a page busy with JSON APIs can add tens of megabytes).

## Configuration

[Section titled “Configuration”](#configuration)

```yaml
recordings:
  enabled: true
  mode: always # always: every session, can't be stopped; auto: unless the launch says no; manual: only on request
  maxAge: 168h # deleted this long after recording unless kept; 0 = never
  minDuration: 20s # a finished recording shorter than this is deleted unless kept or marked; 0 = keep all
  quota: 50GiB # per user; 0 = no limit
  share: true # allow share links
  maxFileSize: 64MiB # largest file an agent may upload
  sweepInterval: 10m # how often retention runs
  storage: # optional: where recordings go; default is the shared storage under recordings/
    type: s3
    s3:
      endpoint: https://s3.example.com
      bucket: holtdroid
      prefix: recordings
      accessKey: env:S3_ACCESS_KEY
      secretKey: env:S3_SECRET_KEY
```

Agents upload to the api’s internal listener (`internalURL`), so session Pods need to reach it, as they already do for APKs. Each upload URL carries a secret only that session’s agent knows.

# Sessions and slots

> Session states, activity, idle timeout, TTL and slot accounting.

A **session** is one device running one APK for one user. A **slot** is a place a session can run: for the emulator provider, one of a node’s `slotsPerNode` places; for the [phone provider](/configuration/phones/), a phone.

## States

[Section titled “States”](#states)

```
stateDiagram-v2
  [*] --> starting
  state starting {
    direction LR
    provisioning --> booting
    booting --> installing
    installing --> restoring
    installing --> instrumenting
    restoring --> instrumenting
  }
  starting --> ready: instrumented
  starting --> failed: any step fails
  ready --> stopping
  failed --> stopping
  stopping --> [*]
```

`failed` sessions keep their slot until they are stopped or reaped, so the reason stays visible on the home page.

## The session page

[Section titled “The session page”](#the-session-page)

The browser tab of a session page is titled with the app’s name, so several open sessions are easy to tell apart. The page has a header and three columns.

The **header** has the app’s icon, name, version and state, and badges for the device (model or screen and its size in pixels), the Android version, the WebView and the VPN location, then the slot’s label. On the right:

* **Stops when idle in** (or **Stops in**, when the session’s lifetime ends first) with the time left and a bar of five segments that empty as the deadline nears; it turns amber in the last five minutes;
* with [recordings](/concepts/recordings/) on: **Record**, or while recording the elapsed time, which adds a marker when clicked; **Share** copies the recording’s link, and the **…** menu adds a marker, opens the recording, stops sharing or stops recording;
* **Extend** and **Stop**.

The **Device** panel on the left holds the device’s controls as rows in three tabs: **Environment** (Network, Location, Battery, Language, Time, Clipboard, Display), **Media** (Stream, Microphone, Camera, Recording) and **App** (App, Device, SSH). Each row shows a summary; the chevron opens it in place with all of its controls, and a row with something changed from the default is marked **Changed**. The search button filters the rows of all three tabs by name. Rows a session can’t use (a camera on a device without one) aren’t shown.

In the middle is the **stage**: the device’s screen in its frame, with a toolbar beside it (under it while the screen is in landscape): Back, Home, Recent apps, Notifications, Quick settings; Rotate (click turns left, shift-click right), Screenshot, the keyboard mode (text input or a USB keyboard), Volume (click for the volume keys, the slider and mute), Power (click for the key; its panel has wake, lock and screen off and what the key does); and **Restart app**. Rotate, Volume and Power open their panel on hover, and on a right-click, a long press or the context-menu key too. The stage and the tools card on the right share the space; drag the handle between them, or let the stage fit the screen.

On the right are the [session tools](/session-tools/overview/).

## The app inside a session

[Section titled “The app inside a session”](#the-app-inside-a-session)

When the app is closed or crashes it stays closed: the device stays `ready` and a card over the screen says so, with **Reopen**. After a crash the card names the exception and has **Logcat**, which opens the stack trace, and can be dismissed. Restart, reinstall and **Save app data now** are in the App row too. Starting it from the device’s app drawer works as well; DevTools and clipboard sync attach either way.

On emulator sessions the home screen holds only the app under test, on a wallpaper with the Holtdroid logo; the system apps are in the app drawer and there is no search bar. Text pasted from the browser lands in the device’s clipboard without Android’s clipboard preview popping up.

**Switch version** (click the app’s name in the session header) lists every build with the same application ID that the device runs (of the x86 and ARM builds of one version, the device’s own) and installs the chosen one into the running device:

* with **Keep app data** on (default) it is installed over the current build, upgrade or downgrade, so you can test how the app’s storage migrates. Builds signed with another key can’t be installed this way;
* with it off, the current build and its data are removed first.

If the install fails, the previous build keeps running.

## The screen

[Section titled “The screen”](#the-screen)

States of the device show as a small card over the last frame instead of hiding it. Taps and swipes pass through the cards to the screen; only their buttons catch the pointer:

* **Screen is off**, since when and for how long, with **Wake**; right-clicking the screen wakes it too;
* **Locked**, with **Unlock**; swiping up on the screen works as well;
* **Reconnecting to the device**, with how old the last frame is: the frame turns grey and input pauses until the stream is back;
* **… crashed** or **… is closed** at the top (see above).

## Metrics

[Section titled “Metrics”](#metrics)

The App and Device rows show the load every two seconds. The App row has the app’s own CPU and memory, per process too (WebView renderers included), and the frames it renders with how many of them are janky. The Device row has the device’s CPU and memory, free space on `/data`, temperatures and, for emulators, the CPU, memory and throttling of the session Pod (Android, the agent and the VPN sidecar together). Android in redroid runs on the node’s kernel, whose `/proc` shows the whole node, so an emulator’s device CPU and memory are the Pod’s: its cores are the Pod’s CPU limit, its memory the Pod’s memory limit, and the app’s CPU is a percent of that limit. Its sensor readings and the total of `/data` are the node’s. The screen stream’s own numbers (frames shown, bitrate and dropped frames, as decoded in this browser) are in the Stream row, and the device’s network traffic with the external IP in the Network row.

The device is only measured while a session page is open and visible.

## Activity and reaping

[Section titled “Activity and reaping”](#activity-and-reaping)

A session counts as active when someone actually uses it:

* keyboard, mouse, wheel or touch input anywhere on its session page, including the device screen and the DevTools panel, while the tab is visible (reported every 30 seconds);
* a clipboard action, location switch, app restart, device button or device setting change;
* the user presses **Extend**.

An open tab that nobody touches does **not** keep the device alive.

The api deletes a session when it has been idle longer than `sessions.idleTimeout` (default `30m`), or when it is older than `sessions.maxTTL` (default `8h`) regardless of activity. The home page shows both deadlines as countdowns.

## Slots

[Section titled “Slots”](#slots)

Each provider reports its slots as `free`, `busy`, `offline` or `maintenance`. The emulator provider runs `slotsPerNode` sessions per node (or a per-node count) and at most `slots` sessions overall. Nodes are chosen with the chart’s `nodeSelector` and `tolerations`. When nothing is free, a launch waits in line on the launch page and starts as soon as a slot frees up, first come first served; leaving the page gives up the place. The line lives in the api replica’s memory, so a restart drops it.

Admins see every slot on the **Inventory** page (the server icon in the dock): the device’s or node’s model, system, battery, memory, storage and temperature sensors, and the session running on it. **Hold** keeps new sessions off a slot, or off a whole provider, while someone works on it; a running session keeps going, and the slot shows `maintenance` once it ends until an admin releases it. Holds are kept by the provider, so restarts don’t lose them.

## Ownership

[Section titled “Ownership”](#ownership)

The user who launched a session is its owner. Every signed-in user can see all sessions; only the owner and members of `auth.adminGroups` can stop or extend them or use their ADB tools (`adb.ownerOnly`). Your [connected computer](/concepts/ssh/) reaches only your own sessions.

# Connecting your computer

> Publish your computer's ports on your devices and reach their ADB with the holtdroid client.

`holtdroid` is a small client you run on your own computer. While it runs, every device you have running in the portal reaches the ports you pick as `http://localhost:<port>`, and each device’s ADB gets a port on your computer. It works over SSH through the portal’s gateway, but you don’t need SSH keys or an `ssh` command.

## What it looks like

[Section titled “What it looks like”](#what-it-looks-like)

holtdroidzsh

```
          
              ╭──────────────────────╮╭────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────╮
            
              │ holtdroid            ││ Settings                                                           │
            
              │ ● connected          ││                                                                    │
            
              │                      ││ Client      v0.4.0                                                 │
            
              │   Overview           ││ Portal      https://android.example.com                            │
            
              │   Devices     1      ││ User        otter                                                  │
            
              │   Ports       2      ││ Computer    otters-mac · 4ma52uwpbqwcbtbp                          │
            
              │   Log                ││ Key         SHA256:Zru7u9KFnruNN8vZsTaJL9hayAphx7lrZ0uGzIib12k     │
            
              │ › Settings           ││ Config      ~/.config/holtdroid/connect/android.example.com        │
            
              │                      ││ Binary      ~/.cache/holtdroid/holtdroid-6557e34d57c7f6f9          │
            
              │                      ││ Enrolled    until 17 Nov 2026, extended on every renewal           │
            
              │                      ││                                                                    │
            
              │                      ││ The holtdroid command                                              │
            
              │                      ││ ▸ ✓ installed ~/.local/bin/holtdroid → ~/.cache/holtdroid/holtdro… │
            
              │                      ││                                                                    │
            
              │                      ││ Updates                                                            │
            
              │                      ││   [ ] Update automatically when the portal has a newer client      │
            
              │                      ││   This is the portal's current client.                             │
            
              │                      ││                                                                    │
            
              │                      ││                                                                    │
            
              │                      ││                                                                    │
            
              │                      ││                                                                    │
            
              ╰──────────────────────╯╰────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────╯
            
               ↑↓ move · enter choose · ← back · q quit
            
        
```

```
          
              adb devices
            
              List of devices attached
            
              127.0.0.1:15555	device
            
               
            
              adb -s 127.0.0.1:15555 shell getprop ro.product.model
            
              sdk_gphone64_arm64
            
        
```

Meanwhile, in another terminal, adb already knows the device.

## Connecting a computer

[Section titled “Connecting a computer”](#connecting-a-computer)

Open **Computers** (the laptop button in the dock), click **Get the command** and run what it shows in a terminal on your computer:

```sh
curl -fsSL https://android.example.com/tunnel.sh | sh -s -- eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiIs…
```

The script finds the client build for your system (macOS or Linux, Intel or Arm), downloads it from the portal, checks its SHA-256 and runs it with the code from the command. There is no Windows build: on Windows run the command in [WSL](https://learn.microsoft.com/windows/wsl/install). Its published ports and per-device ADB ports reach Windows through WSL’s localhost forwarding, so a Windows `adb` connects with `adb connect 127.0.0.1:<port>`; opening the browser from the client may not work there. The client then:

* makes its own key for this portal (it never touches `~/.ssh`) and trades the code for this computer’s enrollment, named after its hostname;
* connects to the gateway and opens its full-screen UI;
* keeps running until you press `q`, and reconnects by itself when the network drops or the laptop wakes up.

The code works once and only for 10 minutes, so a command in your shell history is useless afterwards. Next time, run the client without a code:

```sh
~/.cache/holtdroid/holtdroid
```

or install the `holtdroid` command from **Settings** and just run `holtdroid`.

## The client’s screens

[Section titled “The client’s screens”](#the-clients-screens)

The sections are on the left; `↑`/`↓` or `1`–`5` pick one, `→` or Enter goes into it, `←` or Esc comes back, `q` quits.

The mouse works too: click a section or a hint in the bottom line (`y yes`, …) to do what its key does, and scroll lists with the wheel. One click on a port or a setting acts on it; a device opens on the second click. While the client has the mouse, hold Option (macOS) or Shift (most Linux terminals) to select text.

The client doesn’t manage devices: launching, restarting, reinstalling and stopping them, logcat, a shell and the device’s details are on the portal’s session page. **Launch a device** (`n` or a click, on Overview and Devices) opens the portal in the browser.

* **Overview**: whether the computer is connected, as whom, how many devices run, what is published and how long the certificate is valid.

* **Devices**: your running devices with their local ADB address and whether they are already in `adb devices`; Enter, `o` or a second click opens one’s session page in the browser. Chrome’s `chrome://inspect/#devices` lists the WebViews of every device in `adb devices` (keep **Discover USB devices** on), with full DevTools; `w` or a click on the plate under the devices opens it in Chrome. With ADB turned off on the portal the plate says it’s unavailable.

* **Ports**: the published ports and the ports of programs that look like dev servers (`node`, `bun`, `python`, `java` and the like). Space publishes or unpublishes the one under the cursor, `n` publishes a port by number (also one nothing listens on yet), `a` shows every other listener too: system services and desktop apps. A port the gateway refused shows why. The **Mode** line on top (`m` or a click switches it) picks how ports get published, see [Publish modes](#publish-modes).

* **Log**: what the client did, newest at the bottom.

* **Settings**: the client’s version, the portal, user, computer and key, where the enrollment and the binary are, and **Install**: it links `holtdroid` into the first writable directory on your `PATH` among `~/.local/bin`, `~/bin`, `/opt/homebrew/bin` and `/usr/local/bin` (`~/.local/bin` otherwise, with the line to add it to your `PATH`). The link points at `~/.cache/holtdroid/holtdroid`, which `tunnel.sh` moves to the newest client whenever you run it again; an existing `holtdroid` that isn’t this client is never replaced.

## Updates

[Section titled “Updates”](#updates)

On every start the client asks the portal which builds it serves and compares their SHA-256 with its own. When the portal has a different one, the client offers to update:

```text
  holtdroid  A newer client is available from android.example.com.


  ▸ Update now  and start again
    Skip  keep this one; it may not work correctly with the portal


    [ ] Update automatically from now on
```

**Update now** downloads the portal’s build into `~/.cache/holtdroid`, checks its SHA-256, points `~/.cache/holtdroid/holtdroid` (and so the `holtdroid` command) at it and starts it with the same arguments. With the box ticked it updates without asking from then on; the setting is in **Settings** under **Updates**, next to **Update now** while this client is outdated, and is kept in `holtdroid/client.json` in your user config directory. **Skip** keeps the running client; the Overview then warns that it may not work correctly. Without a terminal an outdated client only prints a warning, unless automatic updates are on. `--no-update-check` skips the check.

Without a terminal (in a script, a service or with `--plain`) the client prints the banner and a short status block instead, whenever the connection, the devices or the published ports change.

Options: `--portal <url>` when the computer is enrolled with several portals, `--publish 3000,5173` to replace the list of published ports, `--publish-mode manual|dev|all` to switch the [publish mode](#publish-modes), `--no-adb-connect` to leave `adb` alone, `--plain` for status lines instead of the full-screen UI, `--insecure` to accept a self-signed certificate of the portal (remembered for that portal), `-v` for debug logs. The key and the enrollment are in your user config directory (`~/Library/Application Support/holtdroid/connect` on macOS, `~/.config/holtdroid/connect` on Linux); delete the portal’s folder there to forget it.

## Publishing ports

[Section titled “Publishing ports”](#publishing-ports)

The client watches which TCP ports listen on your computer’s loopback and reports them to the portal. Publish them in the client’s **Ports** section or on the **Computers** page, which lists each connected computer’s published ports and dev servers (**Show all** adds the other listeners); click a port to publish it on your devices, click again to stop. You can also publish a port nothing listens on yet, for a dev server you are about to start. The choice is saved on the computer, so it survives restarts of the client.

### Publish modes

[Section titled “Publish modes”](#publish-modes)

* **Manual**: only the ports you pick.
* **Dev servers** (the default): also every port of a program that looks like a dev server (`node`, `bun`, `python`, `java`, `vite` and the like), as soon as it starts listening, and until it stops.
* **Everything**: also every other listener on the loopback, system services and desktop apps included.

The ports you picked stay published in every mode. The client’s TUI asks before it switches to an automatic mode: anything on your devices, including any page in a WebView, then reaches those services as `localhost`. The automatic modes never publish the `adb` server (5037), local emulators or another `holtdroid` client, which would let a device control other devices; the client’s own ADB ports aren’t listeners it reports in the first place. The mode is saved per portal on the computer. The **Computers** page shows it and greys out the ports it published; to stop one of those, switch back to **Manual** in the client.

A published port goes to every device you run, including ones you start later, and only to yours. Apps and WebViews reach it as `http://localhost:<port>`. Plain HTTP to `localhost`, `127.0.0.1` and `::1` is allowed even when the app’s network security config forbids cleartext traffic; every other host still follows the app’s policy. Ports are bound on the device’s loopback only, so 80 and 443 are fine on emulators. If another connection already published a port on a device, it is skipped there and tried again later.

Android in an emulator session shares its network with the session’s own programs, so their ports can’t be published there: adb (5555, 5038), Frida (27042), the agent (18580, 18581), the VPN sidecar (7890, 9090) and the metrics port when metrics are on.

## ADB

[Section titled “ADB”](#adb)

Every running device gets its own port on your computer, from 15555 up, kept for as long as the client runs. If `adb` is on your `PATH`, the client runs `adb connect` for each device and `adb disconnect` when it stops, so they just show up in `adb devices`:

```sh
adb -s 127.0.0.1:15555 shell
```

The **Computers** page and the **SSH** row of a session’s Device panel show which port belongs to which device. On emulators `adb connect` needs no authorization prompt and `adb shell` is root (redroid is a userdebug build and the agent restarts adbd as root), with the node’s kernel underneath. `adb reboot`, `adb unroot`, `adb remount`, `adb tcpip` and `adb usb` are refused: they would cut the session off from its device. For logcat, files and a shell without any of this, use the [ADB tools](/concepts/adb/) on the session page.

## What is open right now

[Section titled “What is open right now”](#what-is-open-right-now)

The **SSH** row of a session’s Device panel shows the ADB clients and published ports of that device. While its panel is open, each port is checked through its own tunnel: green means your server answers, red means nothing listens on that port on your computer. Clicking a port copies `http://localhost:<port>` (`http://localhost` for 80, `https://localhost` for 443). The **Computers** page also lists every device you have tunnels to, and the laptop button in the dock shows how many of your computers are connected.

## How it is secured

[Section titled “How it is secured”](#how-it-is-secured)

* The api is an SSH certificate authority. For the code (and later for the computer’s refresh token) it signs the computer’s public key into a certificate valid for 15 minutes, for your SSH user name only. The gateway trusts nothing but certificates from that authority, so it keeps no keys.
* The client renews the certificate in the background, and each renewal also replaces the refresh token. A refresh token is tied to the computer’s key: someone who copies the token without the key gets nothing. A computer that isn’t used for 30 days (`refreshTTL`) has to be connected again with a new command.
* The portal tells the client the gateway’s host key, so the client refuses a gateway that presents a different one.
* For the portal’s API (launching and stopping devices, restarting apps) every renewal also brings an access token, valid as long as the certificate, that the portal accepts as `Authorization: Bearer` with the rights the user has in the browser.
* The gateway runs no commands: shells, `exec`, SFTP, agent forwarding and forwarding to anything but your devices’ ADB are refused. It announces itself as OpenSSH and greets only enrolled computers.
* Tokens are not stored on the server yet, so a single computer can’t be revoked. Until the persistent database lands, an administrator revokes every computer at once by changing `sshGateway.caKey`; a stolen key and refresh token work until the refresh token expires.

Traffic through a tunnel counts as activity of the device it went to, so a device you use only from your computer is not reaped as idle.

## Running the gateway

[Section titled “Running the gateway”](#running-the-gateway)

With the Helm chart, turn on `sshGateway.enabled` and point a TCP entry at the `…-ssh-gateway` Service on port 2222. You can use a LoadBalancer or NodePort (`sshGateway.service.type`), or an ingress TCP route such as a Traefik `IngressRouteTCP` on a dedicated entrypoint. Give it a stable host key and certificate authority key, PEM private keys referenced as secrets:

```yaml
existingSecret: holtdroid # SSH_HOST_KEY and SSH_CA_KEY, each from ssh-keygen -t ed25519 -N '' -f key
sshGateway:
  enabled: true
  hostKey: env:SSH_HOST_KEY
  caKey: env:SSH_CA_KEY
```

Without `hostKey` the gateway makes a new one on every restart, and without `caKey` the api makes a new authority on every restart; either way every computer has to be connected again. The chart wires the rest: the api finds every gateway replica through a headless Service, the gateway fetches the authority and your sessions from the api’s internal port, and the session NetworkPolicy lets only the gateway reach the agents’ tunnel port (18581). The api image carries the client builds and serves them with `/tunnel.sh`.

## Operator settings

[Section titled “Operator settings”](#operator-settings)

| Setting                   | Default   | Meaning                                                              |
| ------------------------- | --------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `allowADB`                | `true`    | Forward each device’s ADB to the client                              |
| `allowReverse`            | `true`    | Publish client ports on the devices’ `localhost`                     |
| `reversePorts`            | `1-65535` | Device ports that may be published, e.g. `80,443,1024-65535`         |
| `maxTunnelsPerConnection` | `32`      | ADB channels plus published ports one computer may hold              |
| `codeTTL`                 | `10m`     | How long the code in the portal’s command works                      |
| `certificateTTL`          | `15m`     | Lifetime of a computer’s certificate, renewed in the background      |
| `refreshTTL`              | `720h`    | How long an unused computer stays enrolled                           |
| `insecureTLS`             | `false`   | The command and the client accept the portal’s certificate unchecked |

The client learns `allowADB` and `allowReverse` from the gateway when it connects. With ADB off it opens no local ADB ports, runs no `adb connect` and marks `chrome://inspect` as unavailable. With publishing off it keeps your chosen ports but doesn’t ask for them, and both the client and the Computers page say so.

`insecureTLS` is for a portal with a self-signed certificate, such as a development setup: the command becomes `curl -fsSLk …` and the client starts with `--insecure`. Anyone between the computer and the portal could then read and change its traffic, the enrollment code included, so leave it off wherever the portal has a real certificate. The SSH connection itself stays protected by the gateway’s host key either way.

Behind a forward-auth proxy (`auth.mode: header`), let `/tunnel.sh`, `/connect/` and `/api/v1/connect/enroll` and `/refresh` through without a login, and requests that carry `Authorization: Bearer`: the portal checks those itself.

The gateway drops a client that stops answering its keepalives after about 30 s (`keepaliveInterval`, 15 s), which frees its ports for the next connection.

# Per-session VPN

> How each device gets its own switchable egress location.

Every emulator session can route all of the device’s traffic (TCP, UDP and DNS) through a VPN, and the user can switch the location from the session toolbar at any time.

## How it works

[Section titled “How it works”](#how-it-works)

The session Pod has a `vpn` sidecar running [sing-box](https://sing-box.sagernet.org/) in the Pod’s network namespace, which Android shares:

* sing-box opens a `tun` interface, and the agent adds policy routing inside Android that sends every app’s traffic into it (Android’s own network daemon manages the routing there, so sing-box can’t);
* cluster and LAN ranges (`vpn.bypassCIDRs`) are excluded, and so is everything running as root (the agent, sing-box itself, Android’s root daemons), so the portal can still reach the agent;
* each location is a sing-box outbound, plus `direct`, behind a selector;
* switching location changes the selector through sing-box’s local API, so the switch is instant and needs no restart;
* the device’s DNS queries are captured from the tunnel and handed to the session’s agent, which logs them, answers your rewrites and resolves the rest through the selected location, so lookups don’t leak (see [DNS log and rewrites](/session-tools/dns/));
* those lookups return IPv4 addresses only (`AAAA` answers are empty), so the device never tries IPv6 through a location that can’t carry it.

The launch dialog shows a location’s flag when its `id` or `label` is a country code or name. An app listed in a location’s `defaultFor` starts in that location. Otherwise the dialog and the quick-launch button use the location you used last time with that provider, or with **Any** (remembered in the browser’s `localStorage`, also when you switch during a session). If there is none, or it is no longer offered, it falls back to the configured default (`vpn.default`). With `vpn.direct: false` there is no VPN-less option at all.

The same tunnel carries the session’s [network conditions](/configuration/emulator/#network-conditions): latency, bandwidth limits, packet loss and outages applied with `tc netem`, and regions with their own round trips to CDN edges and to servers.

Android itself is barely configured (only Private DNS is turned off, so lookups stay visible to the agent); to apps it looks like a normal network. Port forwarding (`adb reverse`, [your connected computer](/concepts/ssh/)) runs over loopback and is unaffected by the VPN.

## Locations are sing-box outbounds

[Section titled “Locations are sing-box outbounds”](#locations-are-sing-box-outbounds)

Holtdroid has no code for any particular VPN vendor. A location is an id, a label and a [sing-box outbound](https://sing-box.sagernet.org/configuration/outbound/) (or endpoint, such as WireGuard): SOCKS, Shadowsocks, VLESS, Hysteria, WireGuard, anything sing-box speaks. Holtdroid only tags it with the location id and puts it behind the selector.

Every session Pod runs its own copy of these outbounds. That is fine for proxies that accept many connections with the same credentials, but not for WireGuard: VPN services usually give one key per account, and the same key connected from several Pods at once makes the peers knock each other off.

## Recommended: a shared VPN gateway

[Section titled “Recommended: a shared VPN gateway”](#recommended-a-shared-vpn-gateway)

Run one sing-box yourself as a **VPN gateway**. It holds the real VPN connection, one tunnel per location, and offers a SOCKS server where the username selects the location. Each Holtdroid location is then just “SOCKS to the gateway, user `de`”:

```
flowchart LR
  subgraph s1["Session Pod 1"]
    e1["emulator"] --> v1["sing-box sidecar"]
  end
  subgraph s2["Session Pod 2"]
    e2["emulator"] --> v2["sing-box sidecar"]
  end
  v1 -- "socks, user de" --> gw["VPN gateway<br/>(your sing-box)"]
  v2 -- "socks, user nl" --> gw
  gw -- "WireGuard" --> de[(VPN server DE)]
  gw -- "WireGuard" --> nl[(VPN server NL)]
```

* One key per location serves any number of sessions.
* Switching stays per session: each sidecar has its own selector.
* Sessions on the same location share its egress IP.
* Adding a vendor or a country is a change to the gateway, not to Holtdroid.

[Shared VPN gateway](/operations/vpn-gateway/) has a complete setup. Configuration keys are on the [emulator provider](/configuration/emulator/#vpn) page.

# WebView versions

> Start a virtual device with a chosen Chromium or Google WebView instead of the one built into Android.

Many WebView bugs depend on the WebView version, not on the Android version. Each virtual device comes with the WebView built into its Android image: Chromium 125 on Android 11 up to 128 on Android 15. With a WebView catalog, the launch dialog offers other versions too. The agent installs the chosen build over the built-in WebView before the app starts, so every app on the device, including yours, uses it.

## Choosing a version

[Section titled “Choosing a version”](#choosing-a-version)

On a virtual device, the launch dialog has a **WebView** section under the screen. Its cards are the kinds of WebView:

* **Built-in**, the WebView shipped with the Android image;
* **Chromium WebView** (`com.android.webview`), the open-source builds;
* with a Google WebView catalog, **Chrome WebView** (`com.google.android.webview`), with the proprietary codecs (H.264, AAC).

Picking a kind selects its newest Stable build and lists its versions below the cards, newest first: one row per build with its version, the release channels it is on today (Stable, Beta, Dev, Canary), its release date and size. The four newest are shown; the rest open with **N older versions**. The preview column on the right repeats the chosen version.

The launch dialog preselects the newest Stable build of the default kind, `webview.defaultPackage` (Chromium WebView unless configured), and restores nothing. When that kind has no build for the chosen Android version, it takes the other kinds. Quick launch uses the version you last launched with, or the same default. Built-in is never remembered: picking it applies to that launch only.

Only builds that work on the chosen Android version are shown. Chromium 149 and later need Android 14 or 15. On Android 11, 12 and 13 they abort as soon as an app creates a WebView, so there the newest choice is Chromium 145 (148 with `extra: [148]`). The choice is remembered per provider and reused by quick launch, except Built-in. While the session starts, the progress shows “Installing WebView …”, which adds a few seconds. The session header then shows the installed version. To compare versions, start one session per version.

The Device row still shows the WebView provider and can switch it during a session. Uninstalling the update with `pm uninstall com.android.webview` (over ADB, or in the Terminal tab where it is offered) brings back the built-in WebView.

## Prebuilt releases

[Section titled “Prebuilt releases”](#prebuilt-releases)

The [chromium-builds](https://github.com/holtdroid/chromium-builds) releases go back to Chromium 83, with proprietary codecs, for x86_64 and arm64. [holtdroid-chromium-builds-sync](/sources/chromium/#prebuilt-releases) fills the catalog from them. The launch dialog offers only the builds an Android version accepts as its WebView, which depends on the build’s `targetSdk`:

| `targetSdk`   | Works on          |
| ------------- | ----------------- |
| 33 and higher | every version     |
| 31 and 32     | Android 11 and 12 |
| 30 and lower  | none, not listed  |

## Where the snapshot builds come from

[Section titled “Where the snapshot builds come from”](#where-the-snapshot-builds-come-from)

The builds are Chromium’s own snapshot builds of Android System WebView for x86_64, published in the public `chromium-browser-snapshots` bucket. They are `com.android.webview`, signed with Chromium’s public debug key. The [holtdroid-redroid](https://github.com/holtdroid/holtdroid-redroid) images re-sign the built-in WebView with the same key. Without that, Android would refuse to install a snapshot as an update of the built-in WebView.

For each milestone, the catalog holds the snapshot closest before that milestone’s last Canary release. Compared with what users get from the Play Store:

* it is a main-branch build, so fixes merged into the release branch later are missing;
* it has no Google-only parts such as Safe Browsing;
* it carries the same Blink, V8 and WebView code, which is what page behaviour depends on.

Snapshots for x86_64 go back to Chromium 129, so older versions are only available as the built-in WebView of some Android image.

DevTools work as usual. Snapshot builds don’t report which DevTools frontend fits them, so the catalog records the commit of that milestone’s Canary release and the agent serves that frontend.

## Google WebView

[Section titled “Google WebView”](#google-webview)

Chromium’s snapshots are built without proprietary codecs: H.264, AAC and HEVC in `<video>` and Media Source Extensions don’t play in them. The WebView built into the Android images does play them, and so does Google’s Android System WebView, `com.google.android.webview`, which a second catalog can hold: the APKs of Google WebView from APKMirror, with the same tags as the Chromium catalog plus `package` and `abis`.

A Google WebView build doesn’t replace the built-in one. The agent installs it next to `com.android.webview` and makes it the device’s WebView with `cmd webviewupdate set-webview-implementation`. Android accepts it because the [holtdroid-redroid](https://github.com/holtdroid/holtdroid-redroid) images list it as a WebView provider (not a default one, so a session without a choice keeps the built-in WebView). Uninstalling `com.google.android.webview` brings the built-in one back.

### On phones

[Section titled “On phones”](#on-phones)

A phone’s Android takes only WebViews signed by Google, so the launch dialog offers phones only Google WebView builds for their processor (`arm64-v8a`), never Chromium snapshots. The agent installs the build as an update of the phone’s own `com.google.android.webview`, which works only for a version newer than the phone’s: a failed install fails the session. When the phone is cleaned (before a session and after it ends) every system WebView with an update installed over it goes back to its factory version, including an update the Play Store installed. Quick launch keeps a phone’s built-in WebView unless one was picked for it before.

Fill it with a job of your own that writes APKs and sidecars to a prefix of its own (each job prunes its prefix), and list that prefix under `webview.catalogs`:

```yaml
# holtdroid chart, config:
webview:
  storage: { type: s3, s3: { …, prefix: webview } }
  catalogs:
    - { type: s3, s3: { …, prefix: apkmirror/google-inc/android-system-webview } }
```

A build’s sidecar needs the tags `version` and `milestone`, `package: com.google.android.webview`, `minSdk` or `requiresSdk` for the Android versions it runs on, and `abis` (comma-separated, e.g. `arm64-v8a,armeabi-v7a`). A device is offered only builds whose `abis` it runs natively; WebView crashes under ARM translation. Without `abis` a build is offered everywhere. Android 15 and later refuse to install a WebView with only 32-bit libraries, so a build whose `abis` has no 64-bit ABI is offered up to Android 14. ARM builds for phones go to a prefix of their own, listed as one more catalog.

## Filling the catalog

[Section titled “Filling the catalog”](#filling-the-catalog)

The catalog is a folder or S3 prefix written by [holtdroid-webview-sync](https://github.com/holtdroid/holtdroid-sync/blob/main/docs/webview.md) (`job: webview` in the chart `deploy/helm/holtdroid-sync`). It reads [Chromium Dash](https://chromiumdash.appspot.com) and keeps:

* the milestones on the Stable, Beta, Dev and Canary channels now;
* the newest `milestones.latest` (6);
* every milestone divisible by `milestones.every` (5);
* any `milestones.extra`.

From each snapshot zip (about 500 MB) it downloads only the WebView APK, using HTTP range requests. Each build takes about 420 MB in storage, about 4.5 GB with the defaults. Builds of milestones that drop out of the selection are deleted.

```yaml
# holtdroid-sync chart
job: webview
existingSecret: holtdroid-webview-sync
config:
  milestones: { latest: 6, every: 5 }
  target:
    type: s3
    s3:
      endpoint: https://s3.example.com
      bucket: holtdroid
      prefix: webview
      accessKey: env:S3_ACCESS_KEY
      secretKey: env:S3_SECRET_KEY
```

Then point the api at the same place:

```yaml
# holtdroid chart, config:
webview:
  storage:
    type: s3
    s3:
      endpoint: https://s3.example.com
      bucket: holtdroid
      prefix: webview
      accessKey: env:S3_ACCESS_KEY
      secretKey: env:S3_SECRET_KEY
```

The catalog is not an APK source: its builds don’t appear in the build list. The api lists them from their sidecars alone and streams the chosen one to the session’s agent over its internal port, without putting it in the APK cache.

## Limits

[Section titled “Limits”](#limits)

* Phones take only Google WebView builds for ARM, newer than their own WebView. Chromium snapshots are virtual devices only.
* Chromium builds have no proprietary codecs; Google WebView builds do.
* Snapshot builds: x86_64 from Chromium 129 on; earlier versions only as a built-in WebView.
* Chromium 149 and later only on Android 14 and 15. The sync job’s `requirements` rules record this as `requiresSdk` in the catalog, and the api refuses a build the chosen Android version can’t run.
* A WebView that fails to install fails the session, and the reason says why.

# Authentication

> Sign-in modes — anonymous names, a shared password, OIDC, a forward-auth proxy, or users with passkeys and invite links.

Holtdroid always knows *who* owns a session, but how people sign in is up to you. Pick one mode with `auth.mode`.

| Mode        | Who gets in                              | Identity                                      |
| ----------- | ---------------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------- |
| `anonymous` | Everyone who can reach the URL (default) | A random name like `big-cute-otter`           |
| `password`  | Everyone who knows one shared password   | A random name, assigned after the password    |
| `oidc`      | Users of your identity provider          | Username, name, email and groups from the IdP |
| `users`     | People with an invite link and a passkey | A user in the api’s database, with a role     |
| `header`    | Whoever your forward-auth proxy lets in  | Taken from headers the proxy sets             |
| `none`      | Everyone, as one local admin             | `local` — for development only                |

## Signed session cookies

[Section titled “Signed session cookies”](#signed-session-cookies)

`anonymous`, `password`, `oidc` and `users` keep the signed-in identity in an HttpOnly cookie holding a JWT signed with `auth.sessionKey`. Nothing is stored on the server, so any number of api replicas can verify it and it survives restarts and rescheduling — as long as they all share the same key.

```yaml
auth:
  mode: anonymous
  sessionKey: env:SESSION_KEY # at least 32 bytes; generate with: openssl rand -base64 48
  sessionTTL: 720h # sessions are refreshed after half of this
  cookieName: holtdroid_session
```

Caution

Without `sessionKey` the api generates a random key at startup and warns: every restart signs everybody out and each replica rejects the others’ cookies.

The same key encrypts the Figma tokens users save on the Pixel perfect page (see [Pixel perfect](/session-tools/pixel-perfect/)); with `mode: header` it is optional and used only for that.

The cookie is marked `Secure` when `publicURL` starts with `https://`. Switching modes invalidates existing cookies.

## Anonymous

[Section titled “Anonymous”](#anonymous)

Visitors are signed in on their first request with a random `size-mood-animal` name, so everyone can tell whose session is whose without accounts. **Get a new name** in the user menu draws another one.

## Shared password

[Section titled “Shared password”](#shared-password)

```yaml
auth:
  mode: password
  sessionKey: env:SESSION_KEY
  password: env:HOLTDROID_PASSWORD
```

The sign-in page asks for the password once, then hands out a random name just like the anonymous mode. Failed attempts are slowed down.

## OIDC

[Section titled “OIDC”](#oidc)

Any OpenID Connect provider works (Authelia, Keycloak, Authentik, Dex, Google, Entra ID, …). Holtdroid uses the authorization code flow with PKCE and reads the user’s claims from the ID token and the userinfo endpoint.

```yaml
publicURL: https://android.example.com
auth:
  mode: oidc
  sessionKey: env:SESSION_KEY
  allowedGroups: [qa, developers] # optional
  adminGroups: [admins]
  oidc:
    issuer: https://auth.example.com
    clientID: holtdroid
    clientSecret: env:OIDC_CLIENT_SECRET
    scopes: [openid, profile, email, groups]
    usernameClaim: preferred_username
    groupsClaim: groups
    pictureClaim: picture
```

Register the client at your provider with:

* redirect URI `https://<publicURL>/api/v1/auth/oidc/callback` (override with `auth.oidc.redirectURL`);
* grant type `authorization_code`, PKCE `S256`;
* token endpoint authentication `client_secret_basic`.

Authelia client example

```yaml
identity_providers:
  oidc:
    clients:
      - client_id: holtdroid
        client_name: Holtdroid
        client_secret: "$pbkdf2-sha512$…" # digest of the secret given to Holtdroid
        authorization_policy: two_factor
        require_pkce: true
        pkce_challenge_method: S256
        redirect_uris:
          - https://android.example.com/api/v1/auth/oidc/callback
        scopes: [openid, profile, email, groups]
        token_endpoint_auth_method: client_secret_basic
```

## Users and passkeys

[Section titled “Users and passkeys”](#users-and-passkeys)

The `users` mode keeps its own user directory in the api’s [database](/configuration/database/). People sign up through an invite link with their name and email and sign in with a **passkey** (Touch ID, Face ID, Windows Hello, a security key or a password manager); there are no passwords. Admins get a **Users** page: everyone’s role, limits and passkeys, invite links, recovery links, and the people waiting for approval.

```yaml
publicURL: https://android.example.com # passkeys are bound to this host
database:
  type: sqlite # users must survive restarts
auth:
  mode: users
  sessionKey: env:SESSION_KEY
  users:
    allowedDomains: [example.com, example.org] # optional: who may sign up
    oidcRole: "" # role for new SSO sign-ins: "" waits for approval, or user
    limits: # optional defaults per role
      user: { maxSessions: 2, maxSessionTTL: 4h, recordingsQuota: 20GiB, appDataMaxSize: 512MiB }
      admin: { maxSessions: 0 }
```

Caution

With the in-memory database every restart forgets all users and passkeys. Use `database.type: sqlite`, ideally with a replica.

**The first admin.** While there is no admin, the api logs a single-use invite link with the admin role at startup, valid for 24 hours. Open it, enter your name and email and register a passkey. Every restart replaces the link until the first admin exists:

```sh
kubectl -n holtdroid logs deploy/holtdroid-api | grep "first admin"
```

**Roles.** `admin` manages users and sees the inventory and the audit log, `user` launches devices, and an empty role means *waiting for approval*: the person is signed in but sees only a waiting screen until an admin gives them a role. Holtdroid keeps at least one admin.

**Invite links.** An admin creates them on the Users page with a role, single-use or reusable, expiring after a day, a week, a month or never, and optionally limited to some email domains (on top of `allowedDomains`). A reusable link with the *waiting for approval* role is an open sign-up page whose newcomers you approve by hand. Each link stays in the list with a copy button until it expires or is used up; revoke it there when it leaks.

**Creating users.** Instead of an invite, an admin can add someone directly with **New user** on the Users page: name, email and role. The account starts without a passkey, and the dialog shows a single-use link, valid for an hour to 30 days (a week by default), that you send them; opening it registers their first passkey and signs them in. It is a recovery link, so a lost one is replaced from the user’s page.

**Domains.** `allowedDomains` and an invite’s domains check the email’s domain when someone signs up, but nothing sends mail to verify the address: treat the check as a guard against typos and the wrong people using a shared link, not as proof of who someone is.

**Passkeys and recovery.** Under **Account and passkeys** in the user menu, people add more passkeys, rename them and remove them; the last one stays. An admin can remove any passkey and create a **recovery link**, single-use and valid for up to 30 days, with which the user registers a new passkey on a new device. Creating one cancels earlier recovery links.

**From the command line.** `holtdroid users` runs in the api’s container, writes to the api’s database file and leaves replicating the change to the running api. It is for operators who can already exec into the api:

```sh
alias hd='kubectl -n holtdroid exec deploy/holtdroid-api -- holtdroid --config /etc/holtdroid/config.yaml'
hd users list                                   # id, role, email, name
hd users recover --email you@example.com        # locked out: a recovery link
hd users create --email bot@example.com --name "CI bot" --max-sessions 0
hd users session --email bot@example.com        # a session cookie value
```

`create` adds a user without a passkey, such as a bot or an AI agent, which then calls the API with a cookie from `session`:

```sh
curl -b "holtdroid_session=$(hd users session --email bot@example.com)" \
  https://android.example.com/api/v1/sessions
```

A session lasts `auth.sessionTTL` (`--ttl` to change it) and ends early when the user is deleted.

**Signing in with SSO as well.** Set `auth.oidc` as for the `oidc` mode and the sign-in page also offers **Sign in with SSO**. The provider’s email finds the user; an unknown email signs up with `auth.users.oidcRole`, or as admin when the user is in one of `auth.adminGroups`. `allowedDomains` applies to SSO sign-ups too. After that the role comes from the Users page, not from the provider’s groups.

### Limits

[Section titled “Limits”](#limits)

Every user has five limits. An admin can set them per user on the Users page; an empty field uses the role’s default from `auth.users.limits`, and a role without one uses the server-wide setting.

| Limit             | Server-wide setting   | Meaning                                                         |
| ----------------- | --------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `maxSessions`     | `sessions.maxPerUser` | Devices the user may run at once; 0 for no limit                |
| `maxSessionTTL`   | `sessions.maxTTL`     | How long a session lives before it is reaped                    |
| `recordingsQuota` | `recordings.quota`    | Storage for the user’s recordings; 0 for no limit               |
| `appDataMaxSize`  | `appData.maxSize`     | Largest app data save; 0 for no limit                           |
| `referencesQuota` | `pixelPerfect.quota`  | Storage for the user’s Pixel perfect references; 0 for no limit |
| `mediaQuota`      | `media.quota`         | Storage for the user’s media library; 0 for no limit            |

Deleting a user signs them out at once and removes their passkeys. Devices they run keep going until stopped or reaped, and their recordings, app data and references stay until they expire; their media library stays until an admin deletes it from the storage.

## Forward-auth headers

[Section titled “Forward-auth headers”](#forward-auth-headers)

With `mode: header` Holtdroid trusts identity headers set by a proxy in front of it, and refuses requests without them.

Danger

The api must then only be reachable through that proxy — anyone who can reach it directly can claim any identity.

```yaml
auth:
  mode: header
  header:
    user: Remote-User
    groups: Remote-Groups
    name: Remote-Name
    email: Remote-Email
    picture: "" # optional header with an avatar URL
```

Traefik + Authelia

A `forwardAuth` middleware on the portal’s route, copying Authelia’s `Remote-*` headers into the request:

```yaml
apiVersion: traefik.io/v1alpha1
kind: Middleware
metadata:
  name: authelia
  namespace: holtdroid
spec:
  forwardAuth:
    address: http://authelia.authelia.svc.cluster.local/api/authz/forward-auth
    trustForwardHeader: true
    authResponseHeaders: [Remote-User, Remote-Groups, Remote-Name, Remote-Email]
```

```yaml
# Helm values
ingress:
  enabled: true
  className: traefik
  host: android.example.com
  annotations:
    traefik.ingress.kubernetes.io/router.middlewares: holtdroid-authelia@kubernetescrd
config:
  auth:
    mode: header
    adminGroups: [admins]
```

Authelia sends `Remote-Groups` comma-separated, which is what Holtdroid expects.

ingress-nginx + oauth2-proxy

Run oauth2-proxy with `--set-xauthrequest` (and `--reverse-proxy`), then let ingress-nginx ask it about every request:

```yaml
# Helm values
ingress:
  enabled: true
  className: nginx
  host: android.example.com
  annotations:
    nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/auth-url: http://oauth2-proxy.auth.svc.cluster.local/oauth2/auth
    nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/auth-signin: https://auth.example.com/oauth2/start?rd=$scheme://$host$escaped_request_uri
    nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/auth-response-headers: X-Auth-Request-User,X-Auth-Request-Groups,X-Auth-Request-Email
config:
  auth:
    mode: header
    header:
      user: X-Auth-Request-User
      groups: X-Auth-Request-Groups
      email: X-Auth-Request-Email
      name: ""
```

The api and the ssh-gateway must not be reachable around the proxy: keep the Services `ClusterIP` and, if other workloads share the cluster, add a NetworkPolicy that only lets the ingress controller reach the api’s port 8080.

## Groups and admins

[Section titled “Groups and admins”](#groups-and-admins)

| Key                  | Applies to       | Meaning                                       |
| -------------------- | ---------------- | --------------------------------------------- |
| `auth.allowedGroups` | `oidc`, `header` | If set, only members of these groups get in   |
| `auth.adminGroups`   | `oidc`, `header` | Members can stop and extend anyone’s sessions |

In the `users` mode roles come from the directory instead; `adminGroups` only decides the role of a first SSO sign-in.

Everyone can see all sessions. Only the owner or an admin can stop or extend one.

## Avatars

[Section titled “Avatars”](#avatars)

When the identity provider supplies a picture (the OIDC `picture` claim, or `header.picture` in the header mode), the UI shows it. Otherwise — and in the anonymous and password modes — it draws a deterministic [DiceBear](https://www.dicebear.com) **Voxel Art** avatar from the username, in the browser, so `big-cute-otter` always gets the same little voxel figure. Only absolute `http(s)` picture URLs are accepted.

# Database

> The api's SQL database — in memory, or a SQLite file replicated to S3 with Litestream.

The api keeps a small SQL database: session events and, in the [`users` auth mode](/configuration/authentication/#users-and-passkeys), users, passkeys and invite links, everyone’s saved [DNS rewrite sets](/session-tools/dns/#saved-sets) and backends for [network regions](/configuration/emulator/#regions), and the last [route measured](/configuration/emulator/#the-sessions-route) through each VPN location (gone after a restart with `memory`; the backends are then kept in the browser instead). Sessions, APKs, uploads and recordings don’t live there, so losing it never stops sessions; in the `users` mode it does lose every account.

## In memory (default)

[Section titled “In memory (default)”](#in-memory-default)

```yaml
database:
  type: memory
```

SQLite in RAM. Every restart and every api replica starts empty. Fine for trying Holtdroid and for deployments that don’t need history.

## SQLite file

[Section titled “SQLite file”](#sqlite-file)

```yaml
database:
  type: sqlite
  path: /var/lib/holtdroid/holtdroid.db
```

A SQLite file in WAL mode. The Helm chart mounts the api data volume (`api.persistence`) at `/var/lib/holtdroid`, so the default path survives restarts as long as that volume does.

SQLite allows one writer, so the api runs as **one replica**: the chart refuses `api.replicas` above 1 and stops the old pod before starting a new one.

## Replication to S3

[Section titled “Replication to S3”](#replication-to-s3)

```yaml
database:
  type: sqlite
  path: /var/lib/holtdroid/holtdroid.db
  replica:
    type: s3
    s3:
      endpoint: https://s3.example.com
      region: us-east-1
      bucket: holtdroid
      prefix: database
      accessKey: env:DB_S3_ACCESS_KEY
      secretKey: env:DB_S3_SECRET_KEY
      pathStyle: true
```

[Litestream](https://litestream.io), built into the api, streams every change to the bucket within about a second. When the api starts and the file is missing (a new node, a lost volume, an `emptyDir` data volume) the database is restored from the bucket first. If the bucket is empty too, the api starts with an empty database.

`replica.s3` takes the same keys as [S3 artifact storage](/configuration/storage/#s3-and-compatible-stores), except `credentialsURL`: use static keys, or leave both keys empty for the AWS default credentials (environment, IAM roles). `prefix` defaults to `database`; give the database a prefix of its own, not one shared with sources or the cache. The keys need `GetObject`, `PutObject`, `DeleteObject` and `ListBucket` on it.

`replica.type: filesystem` with `replica.filesystem.dir` replicates to a directory instead, e.g. a second volume.

| Key                     | Default                           | Meaning                                                      |
| ----------------------- | --------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------ |
| `database.type`         | `memory`                          | `memory` or `sqlite`                                         |
| `database.path`         | `/var/lib/holtdroid/holtdroid.db` | The SQLite file, for `sqlite`                                |
| `database.replica.type` | –                                 | Empty (no replica), `s3` or `filesystem`; only with `sqlite` |

To start over, stop the api and delete the file together with the replica’s prefix; deleting only the file restores it from the replica.

The schema is migrated automatically when the api starts. Downgrading the api to a version older than the database’s schema isn’t supported.

# Emulator provider

> Run sessions as redroid Pods (Android on the node's kernel) on Kubernetes, several per node.

The `provider-emulator` service runs every session as a Pod with [redroid](https://github.com/remote-android/redroid-doc), Android 15 in a container on the node’s own kernel, so several sessions share a node. It creates the Pods in its own namespace and needs a ServiceAccount allowed to manage Pods and Secrets there, to create and update its maintenance ConfigMap, and to list Nodes cluster-wide (the Helm chart creates all of it).

```yaml
listen: ":8080"
kubeconfig: "" # empty: the Pod's service account
namespace: holtdroid
slots: 0 # cap over all nodes; 0: no cap
slotsPerNode: 1
nodeSelector: "holtdroid/sessions=true" # a label selector
tolerations:
  - { key: dedicated, operator: Equal, value: nas, effect: NoSchedule }
image: ghcr.io/holtdroid/holtdroid-session:0.1.0 # the agent
imagePullPolicy: IfNotPresent
imagePullSecrets: []
agentPort: 18580
tunnelPort: 18581
redroid:
  images: # Android version → image; the newest is the default
    "15": ghcr.io/holtdroid/holtdroid-redroid:15
  screens: [] # the built-in presets; see below
  fps: 60
  gpu: /dev/dri/renderD128
  dataSize: 8Gi
  shell: allowlist # what users' ADB may run inside Android: allowlist | full | off
  privileged: false # true: a privileged Android container, for runtimes without NRI
  args: [] # more redroid boot arguments
resources: # the Android container
  requests: { cpu: 500m, memory: 1536Mi }
  limits: { memory: 3Gi }
agentResources:
  requests: { cpu: 100m, memory: 256Mi }
  limits: { memory: 1Gi }
nodes:
  big-node: # a node name
    slots: 6
    names: [Fox, Owl, Lynx] # what users see for slots 1–3; the rest show their ids, big-node-4, …
    resources: # replaces resources above on this node
      requests: { cpu: "1", memory: 2Gi }
      limits: { memory: 4Gi }
vpn:
  locations: [] # see below; empty means no VPN sidecar
maintenance: holtdroid-emulator-maintenance # ConfigMap for maintenance holds; empty turns them off
nodeInfo:
  selector: "app.kubernetes.io/component=node-info" # node-info Pods in the namespace; empty: none
  port: 8090
```

| Key                        | Meaning                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                             |
| -------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `kubeconfig`               | Path to a kubeconfig. Empty uses the in-cluster service account                                                                                                                                                                                                                                     |
| `namespace`                | Where session Pods and their Secrets are created                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                    |
| `nodeSelector`             | [Label selector](https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/overview/working-with-objects/labels/#label-selectors) for nodes that may run sessions. See [Node requirements](#node-requirements)                                                                                                            |
| `tolerations`              | Taints session Pods tolerate. Nodes with other `NoSchedule`/`NoExecute` taints are not used                                                                                                                                                                                                         |
| `slots`                    | Maximum concurrent sessions over all nodes; `0` means no cap                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        |
| `fillOrder`                | Node names, one per slot, in the order free slots are handed out: the nth occurrence of a node is its slot n. `[core, core, k3s-1, k3s-2, k3s-3, core, core, core, core]` fills two slots on `core`, then one on each k3s node, then the rest of `core`. Slots beyond the list follow, by node name |
| `slotsPerNode`             | Sessions per node, unless `nodes.<name>.slots` says otherwise                                                                                                                                                                                                                                       |
| `image`, `imagePullPolicy` | Session image: the agent with adb, Frida, scrcpy-server and ffmpeg (the replaced microphone and camera). The pull policy applies to the redroid image too                                                                                                                                           |
| `imagePullSecrets`         | Secret names for pulling the images                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                 |
| `agentPort`                | Port the agent listens on inside the Pod; the api reaches it at the Pod IP. Android shares the Pod’s network, so a device can’t use this port (decision #161)                                                                                                                                       |
| `tunnelPort`               | Port of the agent’s tunnel endpoints, reachable only by the ssh-gateway; taken on the device as well                                                                                                                                                                                                |
| `redroid.images`           | Android version → image, [holtdroid-redroid](https://github.com/holtdroid/holtdroid-redroid) tagged by version: redroid with software video encoders and ARM64 translation. The launch dialog offers the versions; the newest is the default                                                        |
| `redroid.screens`          | Screens the launch dialog offers (`id`, `label`, `like`, `width`, `height`, `dpi`, `cutout`); the first is the default. Empty takes the built-in presets, see [Screens](#screens-and-android-versions)                                                                                              |
| `redroid.fps`              | Refresh rate, fixed at boot                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                         |
| `redroid.shell`            | What users’ ADB may run inside Android: `allowlist` (default), `full` or `off`, see [Users’ ADB](#users-adb-inside-android)                                                                                                                                                                         |
| `redroid.gpu`              | DRI render node Android renders on                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                  |
| `redroid.dataSize`         | Size limit of the `emptyDir` holding Android’s `/data`                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              |
| `redroid.privileged`       | `false` (default): the Android container gets a fixed set of capabilities, a default seccomp profile and only the devices Android needs, from the [session-devices plugin](#session-devices). `true`: a privileged container, for runtimes without NRI                                              |
| `resources`                | Android container resources. Leave out a CPU limit: a busy session may borrow idle cores                                                                                                                                                                                                            |
| `agentResources`           | Agent container resources                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                           |
| `nodes`                    | Per-node overrides by node name: `slots`, `resources`, and `names`, the labels users see for its slots, in order (Inventory shows the id too)                                                                                                                                                       |
| `vpn`                      | Per-session VPN, see below                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                          |
| `sessionTelemetry`         | Metrics port and tracing settings passed to session agents, see [Monitoring](/operations/monitoring/)                                                                                                                                                                                               |
| `maintenance`              | Name of the ConfigMap in `namespace` that keeps maintenance holds. The provider creates it on the first hold. Empty turns holds off                                                                                                                                                                 |
| `nodeInfo`                 | Label `selector` and `port` of the `holtdroid node-info` Pods that describe session nodes on the Inventory page. Empty selector: Node objects only                                                                                                                                                  |

Every matching node has `slotsPerNode` slots, named `<node>-1`, `<node>-2`, …, and labelled with those ids unless `nodes.<name>.names` gives them labels; the Inventory page shows both. A session takes the first free slot, or the one picked in the launch dialog, and its Pod is pinned to that slot’s node; slots of nodes that are not Ready or are cordoned show as offline. Session state lives on the Pod, so restarting the provider loses nothing. Run one provider replica per namespace.

## Sizing

[Section titled “Sizing”](#sizing)

An idle session takes about 1 GB of memory and 0.05 of a core. Streaming a screen that keeps changing costs about one core per 720p stream (video is encoded in software inside Android), and WebGL in all sessions of a node shares its GPU evenly. Measured on a Ryzen 7 5825U with Radeon graphics: six sessions run side by side. Count on 1 core and 1.5 GB per slot, plus room for whatever else the node runs.

## Node requirements

[Section titled “Node requirements”](#node-requirements)

* Linux with binder (`CONFIG_ANDROID_BINDERFS`); ashmem is not needed.
* A GPU with a Mesa driver and a render node (`/dev/dri/renderD128`): Intel and AMD integrated graphics work. WebGL runs on it; WebGPU is not available in WebView.
* For [network conditions](#network-conditions): the `sch_netem`, `sch_htb`, `ifb`, `cls_u32`, `act_mirred` and `cls_matchall` kernel modules (stock distribution kernels have them; they load on first use).
* containerd and Kubernetes that support `securityContext.supplementalGroupsPolicy` (1.31 or newer); the pre-pull DaemonSet also uses an image volume (1.35, or the `ImageVolume` feature gate).
* A runtime with [NRI](https://github.com/containerd/nri) enabled for the [session-devices plugin](#session-devices): containerd 2.0 or newer (on by default), or CRI-O 1.26 or newer. Without it set `redroid.privileged: true`.
* **Nodes dedicated to sessions.** The Android container shares the node’s kernel and keeps `CAP_SYS_ADMIN` in the node’s user namespace, which Android’s init and zygote need for their mounts, so root inside a session — frida-server, the agent’s adb, and users’ ADB with `redroid.shell: full` — can still reach the node (by mounting a fresh `/proc` and changing node-wide settings, for one). Keep session nodes free of anything else (taint them and set `nodeSelector`/`tolerations`). The provider narrows what Android gets and keeps the rest of the cluster out of its reach: the Android container isn’t privileged (see [Session devices](#session-devices)), the chart’s egress NetworkPolicy lets sessions reach only cluster DNS, the api and the internet (the LAN, node IPs and other Pods are carved out), the agent container runs without privileges (only `NET_ADMIN` in the Pod’s network namespace, for network conditions), users’ ADB runs only allowlisted commands by default, and the image’s init wrapper keeps Android from rewriting the node’s sysctls. See [Emulator isolation](/operations/emulator-security/) for the risks, what is enforced and what to add (AppArmor, kernel updates, separate nodes for untrusted APKs).

Sessions run `x86_64` and 32-bit `x86` apps natively. Apps with only `arm64-v8a` native code run through `libndk_translation`; separate ARM executables don’t (that would need `binfmt_misc` on the node). When a version of an app has both an x86 and an ARM build, a launch on a virtual device takes the x86 one; an ARM-only version of an app that has x86 builds (Chrome 157 from APKMirror, say) can’t be launched there.

## Pod layout

[Section titled “Pod layout”](#pod-layout)

Each session Pod has three containers sharing one network namespace:

* `android`: the redroid image of the launch’s Android version, as root, with an `emptyDir` on `/data`. Its boot arguments set the GPU and the launch’s screen. It isn’t privileged: see [Session devices](#session-devices).
* `agent`: the session image, without privileges (all capabilities dropped, except `NET_ADMIN` when VPN locations are configured: it shapes the VPN tunnel for [network conditions](#network-conditions)). It reaches Android’s adbd at `127.0.0.1:5555` and frida-server at `127.0.0.1:27042`, roots adbd, enables the screen’s cutout overlay, installs and instruments the app and serves the Agent API. The node’s `/sys/fs/cgroup` is mounted read-only at `/host/cgroup` so the device card shows the `android` container’s CPU and memory (its limits, or the node’s without them), and `/data` against `redroid.dataSize` rather than the node’s disk.
* `vpn`: the sing-box sidecar, when locations are configured.

adbd listens on every address of the Pod; keep `networkPolicy` on so only the api and the ssh-gateway reach the Pod, and its `egress` rules on so Android reaches only cluster DNS, the api and the internet. Anything in-cluster a sidecar needs, such as a shared VPN gateway, goes into `networkPolicy.egress.extraEgress`.

## Session devices

[Section titled “Session devices”](#session-devices)

Unless `redroid.privileged` is set, the Android container runs with:

* the capabilities Android’s init and services ask for, and no others: `CHOWN`, `DAC_OVERRIDE`, `DAC_READ_SEARCH`, `FOWNER`, `FSETID`, `KILL`, `SETGID`, `SETUID`, `SETPCAP`, `NET_BIND_SERVICE`, `NET_ADMIN`, `NET_RAW`, `IPC_LOCK`, `SYS_CHROOT`, `SYS_PTRACE`, `SYS_ADMIN`, `SYS_BOOT`, `SYS_NICE`, `SYS_RESOURCE`, `WAKE_ALARM`, `BLOCK_SUSPEND` and `BPF`. It can’t load kernel modules, set the clock, read the kernel log or use raw I/O, and holtdroid-redroid trims every init service’s capabilities to this set (logd runs without its kernel-log and audit readers);
* Docker’s default seccomp profile for these capabilities plus `userfaultfd`, which ART’s garbage collector on Android 15 and 16 needs (without it every Java process rebuilds the boot image in memory and the container runs out of it); AppArmor unconfined (Android mounts filesystems all the time);
* `/sys` read-only except the virtual block devices’ queues, which APEX activation tunes;
* only these devices, which `holtdroid session-devices` adds when the container is created: binder (any minor, since every container mounts its own binderfs), `/dev/loop-control` and `/dev/loop0`…`/dev/loop511` (APEX activation takes about 36 loop devices per session, numbered across the node), `/dev/fuse`, `/dev/net/tun`, `redroid.gpu`, and `/dev/kmsg` pointed at `/dev/null` so Android’s logging stays out of the node’s kernel log.

`holtdroid session-devices` is an [NRI](https://github.com/containerd/nri) plugin: the chart runs it as a DaemonSet on the session nodes, as root without capabilities, with the runtime’s NRI socket (`/var/run/nri`) and the GPU’s render node mounted. It only touches the `android` container of session Pods in the provider’s namespace that carry the `holtdroid/devices` annotation, which the provider sets on unprivileged sessions, and replaces that container’s seccomp profile with the one above (the Pod asks for `RuntimeDefault`, which blocks `userfaultfd`). A session started while the plugin isn’t running gets no devices and fails to boot. What these limits do and don’t protect is in [Emulator isolation](/operations/emulator-security/).

## Screens and Android versions

[Section titled “Screens and Android versions”](#screens-and-android-versions)

The launch dialog offers the provider’s screens and Android versions (`Screen` and `Android` selects, remembered per provider). Versions older than the build’s `minSdk` or `requiresSdk` tag are greyed out with the reason in a tooltip, and the newest one it runs on is picked instead. Quick launch does the same: it keeps the Android version used last when the build runs on it, otherwise takes the newest one that fits, and shows the version in its tooltip; when no version fits, the button is disabled and says why. A screen is fixed for the session: width, height and density in pixels, as a popular phone reports them, plus an emulated display cutout. Android ships overlays for cutouts — `corner` (a hole in the top-left corner), `double` (notches top and bottom), `hole` (a centered punch hole), `tall` (a tall notch) and `waterfall` (curved edges) — which the agent enables after boot with `cmd overlay`, so apps see `WindowInsets` with a real cutout. Android doesn’t draw the black shape in the stream, so the session page paints it over the screen (with a speaker and camera) together with the display’s rounded corners; the cutout fades to 30% under the pointer and passes clicks through to the device.

In the launch dialog four screens show as cards, next to a live preview of the chosen one with its size in px and dp and its cutout, and **All devices** opens a picker of all of them with search, brand chips and filters for the cutout (notch, punch hole, none) and narrow screens (360 dp or less); a star marks a favorite (kept in your browser), and favorites come first in both places. Besides the generic screens below, the provider ships a catalog of about fifty real phones and tablets (Pixel, Galaxy A and S, Redmi, Poco, Moto, OnePlus, Realme, Fairphone and others), searchable in the launch dialog. Each has its size, density, corner radius and a cutout shape: a punch hole, a capsule, a waterdrop or a wide notch, placed in dp from the top edge. The numbers are approximations from public specifications and measurements, good enough to see how an app’s header sits next to a cutout, not to the pixel.
