| `holtdroid_ssh_bytes_total`                 | counter   | ssh-gateway      |                                                                            |
| `holtdroid_http_requests_total`             | counter   | every API        | `api`, `operation`, `code`                                                 |
| `holtdroid_http_request_duration_seconds`   | histogram | every API        | `api`, `operation`                                                         |
| `holtdroid_audit_events_total`              | counter   | api, ssh-gateway | `action`, `result`                                                         |
| `holtdroid_audit_dropped_total`             | counter   | api, ssh-gateway | `sink`                                                                     |

Plus the standard Go runtime and process metrics. Session counts and slots are refreshed by the reaper (`sessions.reapInterval`). The launch duration is measured from the launch request to the session being ready, by the replica that launched it. Streaming operations (server-sent events, the screen) count in the request duration until the stream ends.

## Tracing

[Section titled “Tracing”](#tracing)

```yaml
telemetry:
  tracing:
    enabled: true
    endpoint: http://otel-collector.monitoring:4318 # OTLP over HTTP
    insecure: false
    sampleRatio: 1
```

Requests are traced from the api through the provider to the session’s agent: every contract call carries the W3C `traceparent` header, and every service continues the trace it receives. Without `endpoint` the exporter reads the standard `OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_*` environment variables. The chart passes the same settings to session agents.

## Audit log

[Section titled “Audit log”](#audit-log)

The api and the ssh-gateway write one JSON line per action to **stdout**, while their regular logs go to stderr. Every audit line has `"log":"audit"` and a `schema` version, so a collector can route them apart:

```json
{
  "time": "2026-01-01T12:00:00Z",
  "level": "INFO",
  "msg": "audit",
  "log": "audit",
  "schema": 1,
  "service": "api",
  "action": "session.launch",
  "result": "ok",
  "actor": "otter",
  "provider": "emulator",
  "session": "3f9c1a2b7e",
  "artifact": "slack/C1/F1/app.apk@1f2e",
  "clientIp": "10.42.0.17",
  "forwardedFor": "203.0.113.7",
  "userAgent": "Mozilla/5.0 …",
  "details": { "location": "pl", "package": "com.example.app" }
}
```

| Field                 | Meaning                                                                    |
| --------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `schema`              | Version of this format; bumped on any incompatible change                  |
| `service`             | `api` or `ssh-gateway`                                                     |
| `action`              | What happened, see below                                                   |
| `result`              | `ok`, `denied` (not allowed) or `failed` (allowed, but it didn’t work)     |
| `actor`               | User name; `admin: true` when they acted as an admin. Empty for the reaper |
| `provider`, `session` | The session acted on                                                       |
| `artifact`            | `source/path` of the build, with `@revision` once it was resolved          |
| `clientIp`            | The peer address the service saw (often your ingress)                      |
| `forwardedFor`        | The raw `X-Forwarded-For` header: only as trustworthy as your proxy        |
| `userAgent`           | The browser or client                                                      |
| `reason`              | Why it was denied or failed, or why the reaper stopped the session         |
| `details`             | Action-specific strings                                                    |

| Action                     | Details                                                       | Notes                                                                                                                     |
| -------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `auth.signin`              | `method` (`anonymous`, `password`, `oidc`, `passkey`)         | Header mode has no sign-in: your proxy did it                                                                             |
| `auth.signout`             |                                                               |                                                                                                                           |
| `session.launch`           | `package`, `location`, `appData`, `appDataCache`, `recording` | `appData` is the id of the save the session started from; `recording` the recording that started with it                  |
| `session.stop`             |                                                               | Stopped by a user                                                                                                         |
| `session.reap`             | `owner`                                                       | `reason`: `idle timeout` or `max TTL reached`                                                                             |
| `session.extend`           |                                                               |                                                                                                                           |
| `session.install`          | `package`, `keepData`                                         | Another build installed into a running session                                                                            |
| `session.location`         | `location`                                                    | VPN location switch                                                                                                       |
| `session.microphone`       | `source`, `media`                                             | What the session’s microphone hears was changed; the browser’s own microphone streams through the session proxy           |
| `session.camera`           | `source`, `media`                                             | What the session’s camera shows was changed; the browser’s own camera streams through the session proxy                   |
| `session.clipboard`        |                                                               | Clipboard writes through the agent API; never the content. Clipboard sync inside the scrcpy stream is not seen by the api |
| `artifact.upload`          | `package`, `version`, `visibility`, `temporary`               |                                                                                                                           |
| `artifact.update`          | `visibility`, `temporary`                                     |                                                                                                                           |
| `artifact.delete`          |                                                               |                                                                                                                           |
| `app.update`               | `package`                                                     | Someone changed or removed an app’s description                                                                           |
| `artifact.download`        |                                                               | Denied for non-admins with `downloads.adminOnly`                                                                          |
| `ssh.enroll`               | `computer`, `hostname`, `fingerprint`, `os`                   | A computer was enrolled with a code from the portal; denied for invalid, expired or reused codes                          |
| `ssh.connect`              | `computer`, `hostname`                                        | From the ssh-gateway; denied for a rejected certificate from the portal’s authority                                       |
| `ssh.disconnect`           | `computer`, `hostname`, `seconds`, `bytes`                    |                                                                                                                           |
| `ssh.tunnel`               | `computer`, `hostname`, `kind` (`adb`, `reverse`), `port`     | Every ADB connection and port published on a device                                                                       |
| `appdata.save`             | `owner`, `package`, `trigger`, `id`, `cache`, `size`          | `trigger`: `stop`, `reap` or `manual`; nothing is recorded when the app had no data                                       |
| `appdata.download`         | `package`, `id`                                               |                                                                                                                           |
| `appdata.delete`           | `package`, `id`                                               | Deleted by the user; retention deletions are only logged                                                                  |
| `recording.start`          | `recording`                                                   | Started from the session page; recordings started at launch show up as `recording` in `session.launch`                    |
| `recording.stop`           | `recording`                                                   | Stopped from the session page; stopping the session ends its recording too                                                |
| `recording.delete`         | `recording`                                                   | Deleted by the user; retention and quota deletions are only logged                                                        |
| `recording.marker`         | `recording`                                                   | A marker was pinned from the session page                                                                                 |
| `recording.rename`         | `recording`                                                   | The owner gave it a name                                                                                                  |
| `recording.share`          | `recording`                                                   | A share link was made                                                                                                     |
| `recording.unshare`        | `recording`                                                   |                                                                                                                           |
| `reference.upload`         | `reference`, `name`, `source` (`figma` for an import)         | A Pixel perfect reference was added or imported from Figma                                                                |
| `reference.delete`         | `reference`, `name`                                           |                                                                                                                           |
| `media.upload`             | `media`, `name`                                               | A file was added to the user’s media library                                                                              |
| `media.delete`             | `media`, `name`                                               |                                                                                                                           |
| `devtools.frontend.delete` | `rev`                                                         | An admin dropped a cached DevTools frontend from the Inventory page                                                       |
| `adb.connect`              |                                                               | The session page’s ADB connection; denied per `adb.browser` / `adb.ownerOnly`                                             |
| `adb.disconnect`           | `seconds`                                                     |                                                                                                                           |
| `audit.export`             | `events`, `q`                                                 | An admin downloaded events from the audit page                                                                            |
| `provider.maintenance`     | `slot`, `enabled`, `reason`                                   | An admin held or released a slot (empty `slot`: the whole provider) on the Inventory page                                 |
| `user.signup`              | `email`                                                       | Someone signed up with an invite link (`actor` is the new user)                                                           |
| `user.create`              | `user`, `email`, `role`                                       | An admin created a user without a passkey on the Users page                                                               |
| `user.update`              | `user`, `role`                                                | An admin changed a user’s profile, role or limits                                                                         |
| `user.delete`              | `user`                                                        | An admin deleted a user                                                                                                   |
| `user.recovery`            | `user`, `step`                                                | An admin created a recovery link (`step: link`), or a user registered a passkey with one                                  |
| `invite.create`            | `invite`, `role`                                              | An admin created an invite link                                                                                           |
| `invite.delete`            | `invite`                                                      | An admin revoked an invite link                                                                                           |
| `passkey.add`              | `user`                                                        | A user added a passkey                                                                                                    |
| `passkey.delete`           | `user`                                                        | A user or an admin removed a passkey                                                                                      |

Session actions are also kept in the api’s [database](/configuration/database/).

### Other destinations

[Section titled “Other destinations”](#other-destinations)

```yaml
audit:
  stdout: true
  otlp:
    enabled: true
    endpoint: http://otel-collector.monitoring:4318 # empty: OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_* variables
  webhook:
    url: env:AUDIT_WEBHOOK_URL # a secret reference
    authorization: env:AUDIT_WEBHOOK_AUTH # optional Authorization header value
    batchSize: 100
    flushInterval: 5s
    retries: 5
    timeout: 10s
```

* **OTLP logs** carry the same fields as attributes, with the action as the event name.
* **The webhook** receives `POST` requests with a JSON array of events (the fields above, without `level`/`msg`/`log`), at most `batchSize` at a time and at least every `flushInterval`. Failed batches are retried with backoff; after `retries` they are dropped and counted in `holtdroid_audit_dropped_total`, as are events that arrive while 4096 are already waiting. Events still queued are sent on shutdown.

Durability is the destination’s job. For a complete trail, collect stdout: it is written synchronously.

### Audit log in the portal

[Section titled “Audit log in the portal”](#audit-log-in-the-portal)

Admins (members of `auth.adminGroups`) get an **Audit log** page: events newest first, filters by action or action group, user, result, service, time range and free text, a live mode that refreshes every 5 seconds, a detail view per event and an export of the filtered events as JSON lines. Clicking a user, an action or a session in the table filters by it.

```yaml
audit:
  store:
    enabled: true
    maxEvents: 10000 # the oldest events are dropped beyond either limit
    maxAge: 720h # 0: no age limit
    path: /var/lib/holtdroid/audit/events.jsonl # empty: memory only
```

The api keeps the events in memory; 10 000 of them take about 5 MiB. With `path`, they are also appended to a JSON lines file, read back on start, and the file is rewritten whenever it holds twice as many lines as events are kept, so it stays bounded. The ssh-gateway sends its events to the api in batches when its `audit.forward` is on (the chart does that whenever `audit.store.enabled` is set).

In the chart, `audit.store.persistence` decides where the file lives:

| Value            | Where                                               | Survives                                      |
| ---------------- | --------------------------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------- |
| `data` (default) | the api data volume (`api.persistence`)             | restarts and new pods, if the volume is a PVC |
| `volume`         | `audit.store.volume`, by default a tmpfs `emptyDir` | container restarts, not a new pod             |
| `none`           | nowhere, memory only                                | nothing                                       |

A tmpfs volume counts against the api container’s memory limit.

The page is a convenience, not an archive: each api replica keeps its own events (with several replicas, each page load shows one replica’s view), and it never replaces collecting stdout or the sinks above.

# Security

> Threat model and hardening notes for running Holtdroid.

## What you are running

[Section titled “What you are running”](#what-you-are-running)

* **Session Pods on the node’s kernel.** Android runs in a redroid container on the node’s own kernel, and the VPN sidecar needs `NET_ADMIN` and a TUN device. The Android container isn’t privileged: it gets only the devices Android needs and a fixed set of capabilities (no kernel modules, clock, kernel log or raw I/O), under Docker’s default seccomp profile plus `userfaultfd` ([Session devices](/configuration/emulator/#session-devices)). It still holds `CAP_SYS_ADMIN` on the node’s kernel, which Android’s init and zygote need, so root inside a session can still reach the node, by mounting a fresh `/proc` and changing node-wide settings for one: treat it as root on the node. The agent’s adbd runs as root, and so does the ADB shell users get in the browser and over SSH. Dedicate nodes to sessions (`nodeSelector`/`tolerations`), run Holtdroid in its own namespace, and let only people you trust with those nodes open sessions (`allowedGroups`), or turn the ADB tools off (`adb.browser: false`, no SSH gateway). [Emulator isolation](/operations/emulator-security/) covers what the session Pod can do, what is enforced and what to add.
* **Untrusted code.** APKs are third-party binaries running in a rooted Android. Apps don’t get root themselves, but their network traffic is real: without a VPN (or on the `direct` location) it leaves from your nodes’ network. Keep `vpn.bypassCIDRs` minimal, set `vpn.direct: false` if devices must never egress directly, and keep the chart’s egress NetworkPolicy on (`providers.emulator.networkPolicy.egress`): it stops session Pods from reaching the LAN, the nodes and other Pods.
* **The VPN gateway** holds your VPN credentials and relays plain SOCKS inside the cluster. Only session Pods should reach it; see [Shared VPN gateway](/operations/vpn-gateway/).
* **The SSH gateway** (optional) lets a user’s connected computers reach their own devices’ ADB, which on redroid is a root shell on the node’s kernel without an authorization prompt, and publish ports on their loopback. It never runs commands or forwards anywhere else, and accepts only short-lived certificates the api signs with `sshGateway.caKey`. Anyone who runs a user’s connect command within its 10 minutes enrolls a computer as that user, so the command is as sensitive as a password while it is fresh. Single computers can’t be revoked yet; changing `caKey` revokes all of them. Each computer also gets 15-minute bearer tokens for the portal’s API with its user’s rights. A computer in the client’s **Dev servers** (the default) or **Everything** publish mode exposes its local services to every device of its user without asking per port. Leave `sshGateway.insecureTLS` off unless the portal has a self-signed certificate. See [Connecting your computer](/concepts/ssh/).
* **ADB tools in the browser** (on by default) give a session’s owner and admins ADB on its device. On emulators that ADB is root on the node’s kernel, so by default it only runs the commands behind the Logcat and Files tabs and the app and device cards (`redroid.shell: allowlist`); `redroid.shell: full` adds a root Terminal and should stay off unless the session nodes hold nothing else. `adb.ownerOnly: false` extends the tools to everyone who may open the session, `adb.browser: false` turns them off; see [ADB tools](/concepts/adb/).
* **APK downloads** (on for everyone by default): anyone who can see a build can save it to their computer. Set `downloads.adminOnly: true` when builds must not leave the portal; see [Downloads](/sources/overview/#downloads).
* **The GPS map** makes the api fetch tiles from `map.url` (OpenFreeMap by default) for signed-in users. Only the path is forwarded, with the api’s own User-Agent and no cookies; set `map.url: ""` if the api must not reach the internet. GPS routes along roads send the clicked points to `routing.url` (the public FOSSGIS Valhalla by default) the same way; set `routing.url: ""` to keep them in.
* **Who can get in.** The default `anonymous` mode lets anyone who reaches the URL launch devices. Put it on a private network, or use `password`, `oidc` or `header` — see [Authentication](/configuration/authentication/). With `header` the api trusts the forward-auth proxy completely, so never expose it without that proxy.
* **The session key signs every identity.** Treat `auth.sessionKey` like a password: whoever has it can mint sessions for any user name.

## What the chart does for you

[Section titled “What the chart does for you”](#what-the-chart-does-for-you)

* The api’s internal port (artifact downloads for agents, session lookups for the SSH gateway) is a separate Service and is never routed by the ingress.
* Session agents accept connections only from the api, and on their tunnel port only from the SSH gateway (NetworkPolicy).
* Every service except the session’s `android` and `agent` containers runs as non-root with a read-only root filesystem.
* Secrets are only referenced in config and resolved in memory; they are never logged.

## Reporting vulnerabilities

[Section titled “Reporting vulnerabilities”](#reporting-vulnerabilities)

Please use GitHub’s private vulnerability reporting on the repository rather than public issues.

# Troubleshooting

> Common problems with redroid nodes, ARM translation, Frida, DevTools and VPN.

## Session stuck in `provisioning`

[Section titled “Session stuck in provisioning”](#session-stuck-in-provisioning)

* `kubectl -n holtdroid describe pod <session>`: usually the redroid image is still being pulled (about 1.5 GB) or no node matches `nodeSelector`/ `tolerations` with a free slot.
* Enable the pre-pull DaemonSet to avoid the pull on first use.

## Session fails in `booting`

[Section titled “Session fails in booting”](#session-fails-in-booting)

* `CreateContainerError: … path escapes from parent`: the cluster doesn’t honour `supplementalGroupsPolicy: Strict` (Kubernetes 1.31+, containerd 2.x).
* Android never boots: the node’s kernel needs binder (`CONFIG_ANDROID_BINDERFS`). The `android` container’s log is Android’s own (`kubectl -n holtdroid logs <session> -c android`); Android also writes to the node’s kernel log.
* No screen, or a black one: the node needs a GPU with a Mesa driver at `redroid.gpu` (`/dev/dri/renderD128`).
* The agent’s log: `kubectl -n holtdroid logs <session> -c agent`.
* Images built for one architecture: the session and redroid images are `linux/amd64` only. arm64 nodes can’t run them.

## Install fails with `INSTALL_FAILED_NO_MATCHING_ABIS`

[Section titled “Install fails with INSTALL_FAILED_NO_MATCHING_ABIS”](#install-fails-with-install_failed_no_matching_abis)

The redroid images are x86_64 with ARM translation (`libndk_translation`), which runs `arm64-v8a` libraries. APKs that ship only 32-bit ARM libraries (`armeabi-v7a` without `arm64-v8a`) can’t be installed: no Android 12–16 x86_64 image translates 32-bit ARM. Ask for a build that includes `arm64-v8a` (or `x86_64`).

## App installs but crashes immediately

[Section titled “App installs but crashes immediately”](#app-installs-but-crashes-immediately)

* ARM-only native libraries run through Android’s ARM translation layer; a few libraries (heavy NEON assembly, JIT engines, some DRM) don’t work under it. `adb logcat` from your [connected computer](/concepts/ssh/) shows `libndk_translation` in the crash’s backtrace.
* The app may detect root, an emulator or Frida and exit. The agent log shows the Frida spawn and the app’s exit. Holtdroid never repackages an APK, so such apps need a build without the checks.

## Frida doesn’t attach

[Section titled “Frida doesn’t attach”](#frida-doesnt-attach)

The agent starts the app under Frida to turn on WebView debugging; nothing in the APK changes.

* The session fails with `adb root: …` or `start frida-server: …`: after boot the agent runs `adb root`, pushes `frida-server` and starts it. The redroid images are userdebug builds, so `adb root` works; a different image in `redroid.images` must be one too.
* Only the app’s main process is instrumented. A WebView in another process of the app may show up without debugging enabled.
* Apps started from the launcher are instrumented too: the agent notices the new process within about a second and attaches to it. A WebView created in that first second gets debugging once the script loads.
* Upgrading Frida means bumping `frida-go` and `FRIDA_VERSION` in `images/session.Dockerfile` together: the agent’s devkit and the device’s `frida-server` must be the same version.
* Building the session image on Apple Silicon works, running the agent there under Rosetta doesn’t (Frida needs `eventfd`). Test on an amd64 node.

## DevTools shows no targets

[Section titled “DevTools shows no targets”](#devtools-shows-no-targets)

* The app has not created a WebView yet; targets appear as soon as it does.
* If the app starts WebViews in a separate process, pick that process in the target selector.
* Check the agent’s `/v1/devtools/targets` through the portal: `https://<portal>/s/<session>/v1/devtools/targets`.

## DevTools panel stays blank

[Section titled “DevTools panel stays blank”](#devtools-panel-stays-blank)

The portal fetches the DevTools frontend from Google’s frontend host and keeps it in `devTools.storage` (the api’s `storage` when unset; a cache volume there means a crawl after every restart, so point it at an S3 prefix). It does so ahead of sessions for every Chromium and WebView build it lists, and on the first open of any other revision, which can take a minute. The api needs outbound HTTPS for that; session Pods don’t.

## VPN location doesn’t change the IP

[Section titled “VPN location doesn’t change the IP”](#vpn-location-doesnt-change-the-ip)

* `bypassCIDRs` must not contain the address range of the VPN servers.
* The sidecar logs `lookup ….cluster.local: … mdns: query timeout`: sing-box sends `*.local` names to mDNS. Set `vpn.resolver` to your cluster DNS IP (`kubectl -n kube-system get svc kube-dns`).
* A WireGuard tunnel that drops whenever another session starts: the same key is in use from several places (other session Pods, or a client outside Holtdroid on the same server). Move WireGuard into a [shared VPN gateway](/operations/vpn-gateway/) and give it servers nobody else uses with that key.
* WireGuard logs `sendmmsg: message too long`: lower its `mtu` to 1280 on overlay networks.

## No metrics or audit lines

[Section titled “No metrics or audit lines”](#no-metrics-or-audit-lines)

* Metrics are off until `telemetry.metrics.listen` is set (chart: `telemetry.metrics.enabled`). `curl <pod>:9090/metrics` from inside the cluster; session pods only accept scrapes from `telemetry.metrics.from`.
* The `PodMonitor` needs the Prometheus Operator CRDs, and your Prometheus usually only picks monitors with its own release label (`telemetry.metrics.podMonitor.labels`).
* Audit lines go to **stdout**, regular logs to stderr. A collector that only reads one stream misses the other. Filter on `"log":"audit"`.
* `holtdroid_audit_dropped_total{sink="webhook"}` growing: the webhook is down or slow; the api log says why (`audit webhook dropped a batch`).

# Shared VPN gateway

> One sing-box that holds the VPN tunnels for all sessions, so one WireGuard key serves any number of devices.

Holtdroid gives every session its own sing-box sidecar, and each location is a plain sing-box outbound (see [Per-session VPN](/concepts/vpn/)). Putting WireGuard straight into those outbounds breaks as soon as two sessions use the same location: VPN services hand out one key per account, and one key connected from several places at once makes the peers fight.

The fix is a gateway you run once: a single sing-box that keeps one tunnel per location and offers a SOCKS server where the **username picks the location**. Holtdroid’s sidecars only talk SOCKS to it. The gateway is not part of Holtdroid; it is an ordinary sing-box deployment, so any vendor or protocol sing-box supports works.

```
flowchart LR
  side["session sidecars"] -- "socks user=de / nl / us" --> gw["vpn-gateway<br/>sing-box"]
  gw -- "auth_user de" --> de[(WireGuard DE)]
  gw -- "auth_user nl" --> nl[(WireGuard NL)]
  gw -- "auth_user us" --> us[(any outbound)]
```

## Gateway config

[Section titled “Gateway config”](#gateway-config)

One SOCKS inbound, one user per location, one tunnel per location, and a route rule per user. Anything that matches no user is rejected.

```json
{
  "log": { "level": "warn", "timestamp": true },
  "dns": { "servers": [{ "type": "local", "tag": "local" }] },
  "inbounds": [
    {
      "type": "socks",
      "tag": "socks",
      "listen": "::",
      "listen_port": 1080,
      "users": [
        { "username": "de", "password": "holtdroid" },
        { "username": "nl", "password": "holtdroid" }
      ]
    }
  ],
  "endpoints": [
    {
      "type": "wireguard",
      "tag": "de",
      "mtu": 1280,
      "address": ["10.5.0.2/32"],
      "private_key": "<your WireGuard private key>",
      "peers": [
        {
          "address": "de1234.nordvpn.com",
          "port": 51820,
          "public_key": "<server public key>",
          "allowed_ips": ["0.0.0.0/0", "::/0"]
        }
      ]
    },
    {
      "type": "wireguard",
      "tag": "nl",
      "mtu": 1280,
      "address": ["10.5.0.2/32"],
      "private_key": "<your WireGuard private key>",
      "peers": [
        {
          "address": "nl987.nordvpn.com",
          "port": 51820,
          "public_key": "<server public key>",
          "allowed_ips": ["0.0.0.0/0", "::/0"]
        }
      ]
    }
  ],
  "route": {
    "rules": [
      { "auth_user": ["de"], "outbound": "de" },
      { "auth_user": ["nl"], "outbound": "nl" },
      { "inbound": ["socks"], "action": "reject" }
    ],
    "default_domain_resolver": "local"
  }
}
```

* `mtu: 1280` keeps WireGuard packets under the MTU of overlay networks (flannel VXLAN is 1450); the default 1420 fails with `sendmmsg: message too long`.
* sing-box runs WireGuard in userspace, so the gateway needs no `NET_ADMIN` or TUN device.
* The SOCKS password only has to match Holtdroid’s config. The hop is unencrypted, so keep it inside the cluster and let only session Pods in (the NetworkPolicy below). If it has to cross an untrusted network, use an encrypted inbound (Shadowsocks, VLESS + TLS) with the same `auth_user` rules instead.
* Using the same key elsewhere (another gateway, a laptop)? Give each place different servers.

### NordVPN

[Section titled “NordVPN”](#nordvpn)

NordVPN’s WireGuard (“NordLynx”) uses one private key per account and the interface address `10.5.0.2/32`. With an access token from the Nord Account dashboard:

```sh
# the private key
curl -s -u "token:$NORD_TOKEN" https://api.nordvpn.com/v1/users/services/credentials \
  | jq -r .nordlynx_private_key


# a recommended server and its public key, per country (81 = Germany)
curl -s 'https://api.nordvpn.com/v1/servers/recommendations?filters[country_id]=81&filters[servers_technologies][identifier]=wireguard_udp&limit=1' \
  | jq '.[0] | {hostname, key: (.technologies[] | select(.identifier == "wireguard_udp") | .metadata[] | select(.name == "public_key") | .value)}'
```

Other WireGuard services (Mullvad, Proton, your own server) give you the same three things: a private key, an interface address, and per server a host and public key.

## On Kubernetes

[Section titled “On Kubernetes”](#on-kubernetes)

Store the config in a Secret (it holds the private key; an `ExternalSecret` or sealed secret works the same) and run it as a small Deployment with a Service:

```yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata: { name: vpn-gateway, namespace: vpn }
spec:
  replicas: 1
  selector: { matchLabels: { app: vpn-gateway } }
  template:
    metadata: { labels: { app: vpn-gateway } }
    spec:
      securityContext: { runAsNonRoot: true, runAsUser: 65532, runAsGroup: 65532 }
      containers:
        - name: sing-box
          image: ghcr.io/sagernet/sing-box:v1.14.2
          args: [run, -c, /etc/sing-box/config.json]
          ports: [{ name: socks, containerPort: 1080 }]
          readinessProbe: { tcpSocket: { port: socks } }
          resources: { requests: { cpu: 50m, memory: 64Mi } }
          volumeMounts: [{ name: config, mountPath: /etc/sing-box, readOnly: true }]
      volumes:
        - name: config
          secret: { secretName: vpn-gateway } # key: config.json
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata: { name: vpn-gateway, namespace: vpn }
spec:
  selector: { app: vpn-gateway }
  ports: [{ name: socks, port: 1080, targetPort: socks }]
---
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata: { name: vpn-gateway, namespace: vpn }
spec:
  podSelector: { matchLabels: { app: vpn-gateway } }
  policyTypes: [Ingress]
  ingress:
    - from:
        - namespaceSelector:
            matchLabels: { kubernetes.io/metadata.name: holtdroid }
      ports: [{ port: 1080, protocol: TCP }]
```

Keep one replica: each replica would open its own tunnels with the same key.

Check it from a throwaway Pod in the Holtdroid namespace:

```sh
kubectl -n holtdroid run vpn-check --rm -it --restart=Never --image=curlimages/curl -- \
  curl -s --socks5-hostname de:holtdroid@vpn-gateway.vpn.svc.cluster.local:1080 https://ipinfo.io/json
```

## Holtdroid config

[Section titled “Holtdroid config”](#holtdroid-config)

Each location is SOCKS to the gateway with the location as username. With `udp_over_tcp` the device’s UDP (DNS, QUIC) is carried inside the TCP connection, so the Service needs only TCP:

```yaml
vpn:
  resolver: 10.43.0.10 # your cluster DNS: kubectl -n kube-system get svc kube-dns
  locations:
    - id: de
      label: Germany
      outbound: &gateway
        type: socks
        server: vpn-gateway.vpn.svc.cluster.local
        server_port: 1080
        username: de
        password: env:VPN_GATEWAY_PASSWORD # any string field may be a secret reference
        udp_over_tcp: true
    - id: nl
      label: Netherlands
      outbound: { <<: *gateway, username: nl }
```

`vpn.resolver` is needed because sing-box’s system resolver sends `*.local` names, `*.cluster.local` included, to mDNS. Alternatively use the Service’s ClusterIP as `server`. The gateway’s address must be inside `vpn.bypassCIDRs` (the default private ranges cover usual clusters). All keys are on the [emulator provider](/configuration/emulator/#vpn) page.

## Without Kubernetes

[Section titled “Without Kubernetes”](#without-kubernetes)

The gateway is a single container: `docker run -v ./config.json:/etc/sing-box/config.json ghcr.io/sagernet/sing-box:v1.14.2 run -c /etc/sing-box/config.json` on a network the session containers can reach, with that host or IP as `server`.

# Cache

> How the WebViews' requests use the HTTP cache and a CDN in front of the server, as findings with the requests and headers behind each.

An app that downloads the same files on every start is slow on a mobile network and costs its users data. The **Cache** tab reads the headers of every request the app’s WebViews finish and says where caching goes wrong: files without caching headers, URLs that change on every request, a CDN that doesn’t cache what it could, or caches what it shouldn’t. Each finding lists the requests behind it and the headers to fix.

## When the tab is there

[Section titled “When the tab is there”](#when-the-tab-is-there)

The tab sits next to DevTools whenever the session has WebView DevTools: always on emulators, and on [phones](/configuration/phones/) only for debuggable builds (see [WebView DevTools](/concepts/devtools/)). The agent follows every page, iframe, worker and service worker of the WebViews for the whole session, so the tab sees requests made before you opened it, and fills again after a reload of the portal page.

The headers are the ones that went over the wire, `Set-Cookie` and the network stack’s own request headers included.

## What you see

[Section titled “What you see”](#what-you-see)

### The toolbar

[Section titled “The toolbar”](#the-toolbar)

**Pause** stops updating the tab, **Resume** catches up. **Clear** empties it (a reload of the page brings back what the agent kept). On the right, how many finished requests the tab has.

### The numbers

[Section titled “The numbers”](#the-numbers)

The top row sums up the requests a cache could keep at all: `GET` and `HEAD` requests that finished without an error with a status of 200, 203, 204, 206, 300, 301, 304, 308, 404 or 410. Preflights, WebSockets, event streams, pings, CSP reports, signed exchanges and `data:` or `blob:` URLs don’t count.

| Number                 | What it says                                                                                                                                                   |
| ---------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| **Cacheable requests** | how many requests that is                                                                                                                                      |
| **From the WebView**   | the share the WebView answered itself: from its memory or disk cache, a service worker, the prefetch cache, or a `304` revalidation. Hover it for the split    |
| **CDN hits**           | the share of a CDN’s hits among its hits and misses; only when responses came through a CDN. Hover it for the counts, and how many the CDN didn’t cache at all |
| **Downloaded**         | the bytes of those requests that came over the network                                                                                                         |
| **Could be cached**    | bytes downloaded again that a cache could have served; only when there are any                                                                                 |

A CDN is recognised by its headers. Cloudflare’s `cf-cache-status` counts `HIT`, `REVALIDATED`, `UPDATING` and `STALE` as hits, `MISS` and `EXPIRED` as misses, and anything else (`BYPASS`, `DYNAMIC`) as not cached. `x-cache`, `x-cache-status` and `cdn-cache` count for other CDNs, named CloudFront, Fastly or nginx when their other headers say so.

### Findings

[Section titled “Findings”](#findings)

Below the numbers are the findings, errors first, then the ones that waste the most bytes, then the ones with the most requests. The chips above them filter by severity: **All**, **Errors**, **Warnings** and **Hints**, each with its count.

* a red circle is an **error**: the app breaks caching, or a CDN may hand one user’s response to another;
* an amber triangle is a **warning**: something is downloaded more often than it needs to be;
* a grey **i** is a **hint**: worth a look, often harmless.

A row shows the finding, how many bytes a cache could have saved (when it knows) and `×N`, the number of requests behind it. When the requests leave nothing to report, the list says **Nothing to improve in how these requests are cached**.

Click a finding for its details:

* what is wrong and what to do about it;
* **Requests**: up to the last 200 of them, each with the time it was sent, its status, its name and host, the CDN’s status (`HIT`, `MISS`, `DYNAMIC`…) and where it came from: its size when it came over the network, or **memory cache**, **disk cache**, **service worker**, **prefetch cache** or **304**;
* **Response headers** and **Request headers** of the request you pick, only the ones that change caching: `Cache-Control`, `CDN-Cache-Control`, `Cloudflare-CDN-Cache-Control`, `Expires`, `Pragma`, `ETag`, `Last-Modified`, `Vary`, `Age`, `Date`, the CDN’s status headers and `Set-Cookie` in the response; `Cache-Control`, `Pragma`, `If-None-Match`, `If-Modified-Since` and whether there was an `Authorization` (its value is hidden) in the request.

## What it looks for

[Section titled “What it looks for”](#what-it-looks-for)

A file counts as **static** when it is a script, stylesheet, image, media file, font or web app manifest. Its name has a **content hash** when the last part of the path ends in eight or more letters and digits before the extension (`app.3f9a8c1d.js`, `chunk-BX2KQ7aZ.css`), or a query value is a hex string of eight or more characters that mixes digits and letters.

* **Request time in the URL of …**: a query parameter or path segment holds the time the request was sent (within an hour; a date within a day and a half), such as `_=1730032212345` or `/feed/2026-10-27/`. *Error when the headers or a CDN would have cached the response, else warning.* Leave it out, or put a version or a content hash there instead.
* **`name` changes on every request to …**: three or more requests to the same path where one parameter is new every time (six characters or more, with a digit). *Warning.* If it is a cache-buster or a nonce, every response is a miss: drop it.
* **… downloaded N times**: the same URL came over the network in full twice or more. *Warning.* Depends on the reason it gives: add `Cache-Control`; add an `ETag` or `Last-Modified`; answer revalidations with `304`; or find why the request asked for a fresh copy.
* **Cloudflare missed … N times** (or another CDN). *Warning.* A lifetime under a minute for the CDN, a `Vary` header, another edge or a purge; give it a longer `s-maxage`.
* **… serves a cached copy of … that is marked private / no-store / sets a cookie**. *Error.* Another user may get this response; a cache rule likely overrides the origin’s headers.
* **… bypassed its cache for …** (`BYPASS`). *Warning for static files, else hint.* It names the header that caused it (`Cache-Control: private`, `no-store`, `no-cache`, `max-age=0`, `Set-Cookie`, an `Authorization` header); with none, a cache rule or Page Rule says to bypass.
* **… doesn’t cache …** (`DYNAMIC`) on a static file or on a response whose headers allow caching. *Warning.* Send `Cache-Control` with a `max-age`, or add a cache rule: Cloudflare doesn’t cache HTML or JSON, and only some extensions, by default.
* **… served … past its lifetime**: a CDN hit whose `Age` is over the lifetime the headers give. *Hint.* `stale-while-revalidate`, an edge TTL override, or a stale copy.
* **No caching headers on …**: a static file or a page without `Cache-Control` or `Expires`. *Warning for static files, hint for pages.* Send `Cache-Control`. With only `Last-Modified` the WebView guesses a lifetime of a tenth of the file’s age.
* **… is no-store** on a static file. *Warning.* `no-cache` with an `ETag`; a hashed file can be cached for a year with `immutable`.
* **… must be revalidated but has nothing to revalidate with**: `no-cache` or a zero lifetime without `ETag` or `Last-Modified`. *Warning for static files, else hint.* Add a validator, so a short `304` replaces the whole body.
* **… has a content hash but a short lifetime** (under seven days). *Hint.* `Cache-Control: public, max-age=31536000, immutable`.
* **… sets a cookie** on a static file or a response marked `public` or `s-maxage`. *Warning when marked for shared caches, else hint.* Most CDNs, Cloudflare included, don’t cache responses with `Set-Cookie`; move the cookie elsewhere.
* **… varies by …** `*`, `Cookie`, `User-Agent` or `Authorization`. *Error for `*`, else warning.* `Vary: *` means no cache may reuse it; the others split the cache into many copies, and Cloudflare ignores `Vary` except `Accept-Encoding`.
* **… has only Pragma: …** in a response without `Cache-Control`. *Hint.* Caches ignore `Pragma` in responses; send `Cache-Control`.
* **Almost every request asked for a fresh copy** (80% or more of at least five), or **N requests asked for a fresh copy**. *Warning, or hint for a few.* The requests carried `Cache-Control: no-cache` or `Pragma: no-cache`. When almost all do, DevTools’ **Disable cache** is probably on (see below).

**Could be cached** adds up the bytes downloaded again in the first three: the request time in the URL, a parameter that changes every time, and the same file downloaded again.

## Common tasks

[Section titled “Common tasks”](#common-tasks)

**See what the second start reuses.** Use the app once so it fills its cache, then go through the same screens again, or reload the page from DevTools. Requests answered from the cache move **From the WebView** up; the ones that don’t come back as **downloaded N times**.

**Check that the CDN caches the API.** Pick a request in a CDN finding and read `cf-cache-status` (or `x-cache`) and `Cache-Control` side by side in **Response headers**. `DYNAMIC` with a `max-age` means the CDN needs a cache rule; `BYPASS` says which header turned it off.

**Make sure the tab shows how the app caches.** Turn off **Disable cache** in the DevTools tab’s Network panel. While it is on, every request asks for a fresh copy and the tab warns **Almost every request asked for a fresh copy**.

**Find a cache-buster.** The **Request time in the URL** and **changes on every request** findings name the parameter and its value; the **Requests** list shows that every request had a URL of its own.

## In recordings

[Section titled “In recordings”](#in-recordings)

A [recording](/concepts/recordings/#cache) has the same Cache tab, checked over the requests up to the playhead. There a request’s time seeks the video to it, and **Open in Network** opens the request you picked on the recording’s Network tab with all its headers and the body.

## Limits

[Section titled “Limits”](#limits)

* Only the WebViews’ requests are seen; native code that talks to the network on its own (an HTTP client in Kotlin or Java) isn’t.
* The tab keeps the last 5000 finished requests; for a reload or another browser the agent keeps about 8 MB of them (without bodies), dropping the oldest first.
* The findings read headers only. Whether a file really changed between two downloads, and what the CDN’s own rules say, the tab can’t know.
* Requests still loading show up once they finish.
* The live tab has no **Open in Network**: find the request in the DevTools tab’s Network panel.

# DNS log and rewrites

> Every name a session's device looks up, rewrites of names to other addresses, a TTL limit and saved sets of rewrites.

Sessions with a [VPN](/concepts/vpn/) answer the device’s DNS themselves: the sidecar hands every query to the session’s agent, which logs it, answers the names you rewrote and sends the rest to `vpn.dns` through the selected location. Each session starts with an empty cache and no rewrites, so nothing carries over from another session.

The **DNS** tab next to DevTools has two views.

## Queries

[Section titled “Queries”](#queries)

Every name the device looks up, as it happens. Apps ask for a name’s `A`, `AAAA` and `HTTPS` records at once, so those queries share one row: the time, the name, the record types it asked for, the addresses it got (or where a `CNAME` points, or what an `HTTPS` record offers, such as `alpn h3, h2`), the TTL and how long the slowest answer took. A TTL like `0s / 5m` is what the device got next to what the upstream sent. The list survives a reload of the page (the agent keeps the last 2000 queries). Filter it by name or answer, or show only rewritten, failed or `NXDOMAIN` lookups.

An ordinary answer has no marks; what stands out does:

* **rewrite** (violet): a rewrite answered it;
* **NXDOMAIN** (amber): the name doesn’t exist;
* **SERVFAIL** (red): the upstream didn’t answer;
* **no records**: the name exists but has none of these types;
* **far** (amber): every address answered is on another continent than the session’s exit (see [Routes](/session-tools/routes/)).

A dashed type means an empty answer: `AAAA` is always empty because the sidecar resolves IPv4 only, so apps connect over IPv4. A click on a row shows each query’s records, with the `CNAME` chain and every `HTTPS` parameter, and the country and network of each address.

The wand at the end of a row, or **Rewrite this name…** in its details, opens a new rewrite for that name.

## Rewrites

[Section titled “Rewrites”](#rewrites)

A rewrite answers a name with your own answer instead of the real one:

| Answer with   | What the device gets                                                          |
| ------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| IP address    | the IPv4 addresses you enter for `A` queries; other types get an empty answer |
| Block         | `0.0.0.0`, so connections fail at once                                        |
| Other name    | a `CNAME` to that name and its addresses, looked up through the location      |
| Doesn’t exist | `NXDOMAIN`                                                                    |

A name is either exact (`api.example.com`) or a wildcard (`*.example.com`, every name under `example.com` but not `example.com` itself). An exact name wins over a wildcard and a longer wildcard over a shorter one. When you start from a query, the dialog offers the name itself, its siblings and everything under it, and shows which names seen in the session would match.

A rewrite’s TTL is 0 by default, so Android doesn’t cache it and turning the rewrite off takes effect at once. Every rule has a switch to turn it off without deleting it, and counts how many queries in the list it answered.

Changing the rewrites clears Android’s DNS cache. Connections that are already open keep their address until they close, and an app’s own cache can keep a name a little longer (a WebView up to a minute); restart the app when a rewrite has to apply to everything.

## TTL limit and the cache

[Section titled “TTL limit and the cache”](#ttl-limit-and-the-cache)

The TTL menu caps every TTL the device gets: **TTL 0 s** keeps Android from caching answers at all, so every lookup shows up in the list; 5, 30, 60 or 300 seconds keeps lookups fresh without that many queries. The limit also applies to negative answers (through the `SOA` record). **Clear DNS cache** empties Android’s resolver cache right away.

The agent turns Android’s Private DNS (DNS over TLS) off in these sessions: lookups over TLS would bypass the log and the rewrites.

## Encrypted DNS in apps

[Section titled “Encrypted DNS in apps”](#encrypted-dns-in-apps)

Browsers and some apps resolve names themselves over DNS over HTTPS (DoH), which the log and the rewrites never see. Two things keep them on the device’s DNS:

* **Chrome and Chromium** get the policy `DnsOverHttpsMode: off` on their command line, next to the flags that skip their welcome screens. Chrome reads command-line policies only on debuggable devices (redroid is) and not in its Stable and Beta channels; Chromium builds, Dev and Canary obey it.
* **Block DoH** in the toolbar (on by default) answers the names of well-known DoH and DNS-over-TLS servers (Cloudflare, Google, Quad9, OpenDNS, NextDNS, AdGuard, the rest of Chrome’s upgrade list) with `NXDOMAIN`. Chrome Stable in its automatic mode, and most apps that bundle DoH, then fall back to the device’s DNS. Those lookups are marked **DoH blocked**, and Chrome’s retries of its server (about one a second) fold into one row with a count; a rewrite of the same name wins over the block. Turn the switch off to test an app’s own DoH.

WebViews never use DoH: in Chromium only the browser turns it on, so the WebView of any provider resolves through the device.

## Saved sets

[Section titled “Saved sets”](#saved-sets)

**Sets** saves the current rewrites and TTL limit under a name, for you alone, in the portal’s [database](/configuration/database/). A set is never loaded into a new session by itself: pick it from **Sets** and choose to use it instead of the current rewrites or to add it to them (a name in both takes the set’s rewrite). The same menu overwrites, renames or deletes a set, and imports and exports sets as JSON files to share them.

## Recordings

[Section titled “Recordings”](#recordings)

A [recording](/concepts/recordings/) keeps the DNS log: its DNS tab lists the queries up to the playhead, with rows where the rewrites or the TTL limit changed and where the cache was cleared. Those moments are violet ticks on the timeline.

## Limits

[Section titled “Limits”](#limits)

* Only sessions with a VPN sidecar have the tab; physical phones don’t yet.
* Chrome picks up its flags when it starts: one that was already running before a new install keeps its DoH until it restarts. An app that reaches a DoH server by IP address (`https://1.1.1.1/dns-query`) isn’t blocked.
* An app that hard-codes an IP address, or resolves names over its own DNS-over-HTTPS, isn’t affected by rewrites.
* Addresses are IPv4 only, like everything the sidecar resolves.

# Files

> Browse the device's file system from the session page, download and upload files, and, where ADB runs any command, create folders and delete.

The **Files** tab is a file browser for the session’s device. Use it to grab a file the app wrote (a database, a log, an export), to put a file on the device for the app to pick, or to look at what an app keeps in its private data. It works over [ADB in the browser](/concepts/adb/), so you need nothing installed on your computer.

## When the tab appears

[Section titled “When the tab appears”](#when-the-tab-appears)

The tab sits next to **Logcat** and **Terminal**, after the DevTools tabs. It is there when the portal lets you use ADB on this session:

* the server allows ADB in the browser (`adb.browser`, on by default);
* with `adb.ownerOnly` (the default), the session is yours or you are an admin; other users see only the screen and DevTools;
* the device supports ADB (every emulator and phone does).

There is nothing to click or allow: the page connects to the device’s ADB once the device is first ready, and keeps that one connection for Logcat, Files and Terminal. The browser keeps an ADB key in its storage, and the device doesn’t ask to authorize it. While the connection is being set up the tab shows **Connecting to ADB…**. If it fails or drops, the tab shows **Could not reach the device over ADB** with the reason and a **Reconnect** button.

## What you see

[Section titled “What you see”](#what-you-see)

A toolbar, then the list of the current folder. The tab opens in the device’s Downloads folder, `/sdcard/Download`.

* **Go to…** jumps to one of five places:

  | Entry           | Path                                                     |
  | --------------- | -------------------------------------------------------- |
  | Downloads       | `/sdcard/Download`                                       |
  | Shared storage  | `/sdcard`                                                |
  | App data        | `/data/data/<package>`, the session’s app’s private data |
  | /data/local/tmp | `/data/local/tmp`, a folder ADB may always write to      |
  | Root            | `/`, the whole file system                               |

* **Up** goes to the parent folder.

* The **path field** shows where you are; type another path and press Enter to go there.

* **Refresh** lists the folder again. The list doesn’t update by itself when the app writes a file.

* **New folder** and **Upload files**, described below. **New folder** is only there where ADB runs any shell command (see [Limits](#limits)).

Each row has the name, the size (files only) and the time it was last modified, in your browser’s time zone. Folders come first, then files, both in alphabetical order. Click a folder’s name to open it. **Download** and, where ADB runs any shell command, **Delete** show up when you hover a row.

`App data` holds what the app keeps for itself: `shared_prefs`, `databases`, `files`, and the WebView’s cookies and storage under `app_webview`. The [App data](/concepts/app-data/) feature saves and restores this folder between sessions.

## Common tasks

[Section titled “Common tasks”](#common-tasks)

**Download a file.** Hover the row and click **Download**; the browser saves it under its own name. Folders and symbolic links have no download button: download the files in them one by one.

**Upload files.** Click **Upload files** and pick one or more files, or drop them anywhere on the list. They go into the folder you are looking at, one after another, with a progress line (`photo.jpg: 1.2 MB of 3.4 MB`). A file with the same name is replaced. Dropping a picture into Downloads is the quickest way to test an app’s file picker or share sheet.

**Create a folder.** Click **New folder**, type a name and press **Create**. Missing parent folders in the name (`a/b/c`) are created too.

**Delete.** Hover the row and click **Delete**. The page asks first; for a folder it asks to delete it *and everything in it*, and removes the whole tree.

**Look inside the app’s data.** Pick **App data** in **Go to…**, open `databases` or `shared_prefs` and download the file. Open a SQLite database with any SQLite viewer on your computer. The file is a snapshot of that moment: an app that keeps the database open may still have changes in its `-wal` file next to it, so download that too.

## Recordings

[Section titled “Recordings”](#recordings)

[Recordings](/concepts/recordings/) don’t keep anything of this tab: the player has no Files tab, and browsing, uploads and deletions are not recorded. What you do in the app with an uploaded file shows up on the recorded screen like anything else.

## Limits

[Section titled “Limits”](#limits)

* **Delete** and **New folder** run shell commands (`rm` and `mkdir`), so they are only shown where the provider lets ADB run any command, which is also when the [Terminal](/session-tools/terminal/) tab shows up (`redroid.shell: full` on emulators, `adb.shell: full` on phones, see [Emulator provider](/configuration/emulator/#users-adb-inside-android) and [ADB on phones](/configuration/phones/#adb-on-phones)). By default both run only an allowlist of read-only commands and package operations, and the tab browses, downloads and uploads. Those are file transfer and work under every setting, even `off`.
* On emulators ADB runs as root, so every folder can be read and written. Uploaded files belong to root with mode `644`: an app can read a file you put into its private data, but may not be able to change it.
* On phones ADB runs as Android’s `shell` user, also on rooted phones. The app’s private data and most of the system can’t be listed (the tab shows **Could not list** with the reason); shared storage and `/data/local/tmp` work.
* There is no preview, editing, renaming, moving or copying of files. To change a file, download it, edit it on your computer and upload it again.
* A download is read into the browser’s memory before it is saved, so very large files take a while and a lot of memory.
* Symbolic links are listed like folders. A link to a file can’t be opened or downloaded from the tab.
* Everything is gone when the session ends, except what [App data](/concepts/app-data/) saves.

# Logcat

> The device's log in the session page, filtered to your app by default, with levels, search, pause, download and a notice when the app crashes.

The **Logcat** tab is Android’s log, live, in the session page: what `adb logcat` would print, without `adb` on your machine. By default it shows only your app’s lines, so QA can see the error behind a broken screen and developers can follow their own tags without the rest of the system.

The session page reads it over [ADB in the browser](/concepts/adb/), from the device’s `main`, `system` and `crash` buffers.

## When the tab appears

[Section titled “When the tab appears”](#when-the-tab-appears)

Logcat, [Files and Terminal](/concepts/adb/) are the tabs that need ADB. They appear when the portal lets the session page open ADB (`adb.browser`, on by default) and you may use it: with `adb.ownerOnly` (the default) only the session’s owner and admins get them; everyone else sees the screen and DevTools only. See [ADB tools](/concepts/adb/#configuration).

Collecting starts once the device is first ready, whether or not the tab is open, and keeps going while the app restarts or another build is installed. The first lines are the last 2000 the device already had, so what happened during start-up is there too.

## What you see

[Section titled “What you see”](#what-you-see)

### The toolbar

[Section titled “The toolbar”](#the-toolbar)

* **This app** / **Everything**: only your app’s lines, or the whole device. Your app is matched by its Linux user id, so all its processes count and a restart doesn’t lose it. If the id couldn’t be found, a line says *The app’s user id is unknown, so every line is shown.*
* The level menu: **Verbose** (everything, the default), **Debug**, **Info**, **Warn** or **Error**, each showing that level and above. Fatal lines always show.
* **Filter tag or message**: keeps lines whose tag or message contains the text, ignoring case.
* **Pause** / **Resume**: freezes the list at the last line; lines keep coming in underneath and show up on resume.
* **Scroll to the newest** (an arrow to a line): the list follows new lines while you are at the bottom and stops when you scroll up; this button takes you back and follows again.
* **Clear** (the eraser): empties the list.
* **Download what is shown**: a text file `logcat-<package>-<date and time>.txt` with exactly the lines that pass the filters, in the usual `threadtime` form (time, PID, TID, level, tag, message).

### The lines

[Section titled “The lines”](#the-lines)

Each line has the time (`MM-DD HH:MM:SS.mmm`, in your browser’s time zone), the process id, the level letter, the tag (cut short; hover for the whole tag) and the message, wrapped. The letter and the tag are coloured by level:

| Letter | Level   | Colour         |
| ------ | ------- | -------------- |
| `V`    | Verbose | grey           |
| `D`    | Debug   | blue           |
| `I`    | Info    | green          |
| `W`    | Warn    | amber          |
| `E`    | Error   | red            |
| `F`    | Fatal   | dark red, bold |

Lines from the `crash` buffer have a red tint behind them. While ADB connects the tab shows **Connecting to ADB…**; if that fails or the connection drops, **Could not reach the device over ADB** with the reason and a **Reconnect** button. Before the first line arrives the tab says *Waiting for log lines…*; when the filters hide everything, *No line matches the filters.*

### The crash notice

[Section titled “The crash notice”](#the-crash-notice)

When your app crashes (a `FATAL EXCEPTION` from `AndroidRuntime`, or a native crash’s `*** *** ***` from `DEBUG` in the crash buffer) and the report names the app’s process (`Process: <package>` for Java, `>>> <package> <<<` or the app’s uid for a native one), a notice *The app crashed* pops up on any tab with the first five lines of the stack trace. It stays for 15 seconds; its **Logcat** button opens this tab. A card over the device’s screen says *… crashed* with the exception’s line and the time until you dismiss it, with **Logcat** and **Reopen**, which starts the app again.

## Common tasks

[Section titled “Common tasks”](#common-tasks)

**Catch the error behind a bug.** Reproduce it, set the level to **Error** or **Warn**, and download what is shown to attach to the report.

**Follow your own tags.** Type the tag into the filter, or a word from your messages. Switch to **Everything** when the cause may be outside the app, such as `ActivityManager` killing it or the WebView’s own process.

**Read a crash.** Click **Logcat** in the crash notice and scroll to the red lines; switch the level to **Error** to see the stack trace alone.

**Start from a clean log.** **Clear** before reproducing, so the download holds only what happened since.

For a bug report with a screenshot, device and app details and this log (the whole device, whatever the filters), use **Bundle** in the **Device** row: see [ADB tools](/concepts/adb/).

## In recordings

[Section titled “In recordings”](#in-recordings)

A [recording](/concepts/recordings/#logcat) keeps its own logcat, written on the server: the whole device, each line stamped with its time in the recording. Its player has a logcat panel with the same level and text filters, follows the playhead, and downloads the whole log as plain text or with colours. It doesn’t depend on this tab: a recording has its logcat even when nobody had the session page open.

## Limits

[Section titled “Limits”](#limits)

* The tab keeps the last 20,000 lines in the browser; older ones drop out, also while paused. Reloading the session page starts over with the last 2000 lines the device has.
* Only the `main`, `system` and `crash` buffers; not `events` or `radio`.
* The log lives in the browser tab, not on the server. Two people watching the same session each collect their own.
* Logcat runs as a shell command: with `redroid.shell: off` on emulators, or `adb.shell: off` on [phones](/configuration/phones/#adb-on-phones), the tab stays empty. See [Emulator provider](/configuration/emulator/#users-adb-inside-android).
* When the ADB connection drops, the tab stops getting lines. **Reconnect** opens it again, and logcat carries on from the last line it had.

# Network

> Slow, lossy or dropping networks for the whole device, and a region's round trips to CDNs and servers, on top of the session's own route.

Apps are built on fast office Wi-Fi and used on a train. **Network conditions** put the device on a slower network: a named link such as 3G or weak 4G, a scenario that changes the link over time (a subway ride, an elevator), and optionally a **region**, the round trips that users in a country have to a CDN and to your servers. Use it to see whether the app shows loaders, retries and clear errors instead of a blank screen.

## Where to find it

[Section titled “Where to find it”](#where-to-find-it)

Network conditions are there in emulator sessions with a [VPN](/concepts/vpn/): the conditions are applied to the VPN tunnel, so without VPN locations configured there are none. Phones don’t have them (see [Phones](/configuration/phones/)).

The **Network** row of the **Device** panel (tab **Environment**) shows the current conditions and, opened, everything for a quick change:

* **Conditions**: chips for **No limits**, **Typical 4G**, **3G**, **2G (EDGE)** and **Subway** (plus the current network when it is another one), and **All…**, which opens the picker;
* **Ping**, **Mbit/s** and **Loss** of what is applied right now: the network’s own numbers, or the current step’s while a scenario runs (`Subway · step 2 of 3: 3G`);
* **VPN exit**, the [VPN location](/concepts/vpn/) with the external address;
* **Wi-Fi**, **Mobile data** and **Airplane mode**, and the device’s traffic;
* **Network conditions**, a row with the current summary that opens the picker too.

The row is marked **Changed** while anything is emulated or a radio is off; **Reset** in it turns everything back.

## What it affects

[Section titled “What it affects”](#what-it-affects)

The conditions apply to **the whole device**: every app, the WebView, native code, DNS lookups. They are not DevTools’ throttling, which slows down one page only. What Holtdroid itself uses to reach the device (the screen, DevTools, ADB, the agent) isn’t slowed down, and neither are the addresses in `vpn.bypassCIDRs`.

An outage in a scenario drops every packet while Android still sees a connected network, so requests hang until they time out, as on a dead cell. For a network that Android knows is gone, turn on **Airplane mode**, or turn **Wi-Fi** and **Mobile data** off, in the Network row.

The conditions stay when you switch the VPN location; the agent then measures the new route (see [The session’s route](#the-sessions-route)).

## The picker

[Section titled “The picker”](#the-picker)

The picker opens over the session. Its header says what is on: a running scenario and its step (`Subway · step 2 of 3`), or the network’s name, or the region with its link (`🇩🇪 Germany · typical mobile`). **No emulation** next to it turns everything off; the cross or Esc closes the picker, and every pick applies at once.

Below the header are three tabs, **Networks**, **Scenarios** and **Region**, each with how many it offers, and on the right the **Session route**: the CDN edge round trip, the nearest server location and the route’s bandwidth (`CDN 18 ms · Frankfurt 34 ms · ↓ 94 Mbit/s`).

### The session’s route

[Section titled “The session’s route”](#the-sessions-route)

**The session’s own route** (in the **Region** tab while no region is picked, and in short next to the tabs) shows what the session’s network already takes before any emulation:

* `CDN edge 23 ms`: the round trip to Cloudflare’s nearest edge;
* `↓ 48 Mbit/s`: the route’s download bandwidth;
* the round trip to each server location (`Frankfurt 31 ms · N. Virginia 112 ms · …`);
* how old a measurement is, when it is over two minutes (`12 min ago`).

Every emulated network comes on top of it: a network adds its delay to these round trips, and can’t be faster than the route’s bandwidth. Round trips are measured every minute; the bandwidth after a location change, or when the last test is over six hours old. A new session starts from the last route measured through its location. Until the first measurement it says **Measuring…**. How the agent measures is described under [Network conditions](/configuration/emulator/#the-sessions-route).

### Networks

[Section titled “Networks”](#networks)

The **Networks** tab is the access link: one row per network with its name, a short description, the delay it adds with its jitter (**RTT**), the download and upload in kbit/s, the packet loss and a **Speed** meter (green, amber or red, from GPRS to 5G on a log scale, less for delay and loss). The picked row has its radio filled. **Filter** narrows the list by name or description. Without a region, hovering a row’s RTT shows the round trip it means to a CDN edge (`≈ 93 ms to a CDN edge`), the route’s plus its own delay, and hovering the loss of a bursty network says how long its runs are.

| Network               | Delay                                       | Download   | Upload     | Loss          |
| --------------------- | ------------------------------------------- | ---------- | ---------- | ------------- |
| **No limits**         | the session’s own network, nothing emulated |            |            |               |
| **5G**                | +25 ±5 ms                                   | 150 Mbit/s | 30 Mbit/s  |               |
| **Good 4G**           | +45 ±10 ms                                  | 30 Mbit/s  | 10 Mbit/s  |               |
| **Typical 4G**        | +70 ±20 ms                                  | 10 Mbit/s  | 3 Mbit/s   | 0.5%          |
| **Weak 4G**           | +150 ±60 ms                                 | 1.5 Mbit/s | 500 kbit/s | 2%, in bursts |
| **3G**                | +200 ±50 ms                                 | 1.5 Mbit/s | 400 kbit/s | 1%            |
| **2G (EDGE)**         | +500 ±150 ms                                | 200 kbit/s | 80 kbit/s  | 2%            |
| **GPRS**              | +800 ±200 ms                                | 50 kbit/s  | 25 kbit/s  | 3%            |
| **Busy public Wi-Fi** | +120 ±80 ms                                 | 3 Mbit/s   | 1 Mbit/s   | 3%, in bursts |
| **Crowded venue**     | +400 ±250 ms                                | 500 kbit/s | 150 kbit/s | 8%, in bursts |
| **Satellite (GEO)**   | +650 ±40 ms                                 | 10 Mbit/s  | 2 Mbit/s   | 0.5%          |
| **Slow upload**       | +60 ±10 ms                                  | 20 Mbit/s  | 300 kbit/s |               |
| **Lossy link**        | +60 ±10 ms                                  | 10 Mbit/s  | 5 Mbit/s   | 10%           |
| **Far away server**   | +300 ±10 ms                                 | unlimited  | unlimited  |               |

Loss is per direction. “In bursts” means lost packets come in runs, as on a weak cell or a busy hotspot, rather than one at a time. The numbers are rough medians from public mobile network reports, rounded to be easy to remember, not measurements of a specific operator. There are no custom values: pick the closest network.

Amber notes under a network say where the route spoils it:

* **The VPN route’s N ms is more than this network’s own N ms**: the route is already slower than the network would be (5G behind a far VPN location), so the delay ends up larger than named;
* **Capped at about N Mbit/s by the VPN**: the network is faster than the route’s bandwidth.

The network can still be picked: loss, jitter and slower links are unaffected.

### Scenarios

[Section titled “Scenarios”](#scenarios)

Scenarios loop through networks, holding each for a random time within the range given. The **Scenarios** tab shows one card per scenario with its loop length (`20–60 s ↻`) and a strip of its steps, each named and roughly as wide as its average hold, with its hold range under it: networks in grey, outages light red and hatched, and the step running now outlined in blue. The running scenario has a **Running** badge.

Picking a card shows its steps on the right: the link of each, its RTT, download and upload, and how long it is held. While that scenario runs, its current step is highlighted, with a bar and how long it has been held (`7 s of 10–20 s, then Outage`). **Start scenario** applies it; **Restart scenario** on the running one starts it again from the first step.

| Scenario                 | Steps                                                                                                              |
| ------------------------ | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| **Satellite (Starlink)** | its own link (+45 ±15 ms, 100 Mbit/s down, 15 Mbit/s up, 0.5% loss) for 14 to 15 s, then an outage of 0.5 to 1.5 s |
| **Subway**               | Typical 4G for 20 to 40 s, 3G for 10 to 20 s, an outage of 5 to 20 s                                               |
| **Driving**              | Typical 4G for 40 to 80 s, Weak 4G for 15 to 30 s, 3G for 10 to 20 s, an outage of 2 to 6 s                        |
| **Elevator**             | Typical 4G for 45 to 75 s, an outage of 8 to 15 s                                                                  |
| **Fading signal**        | Typical 4G, Weak 4G, 3G, 2G (EDGE) and an outage, 20 s each, then from the start                                   |
| **Flapping**             | Typical 4G for 3 s, an outage of 3 s                                                                               |

### Region

[Section titled “Region”](#region)

**Region** stands in for the app’s users in a country. Pick one of Germany, the United States, Ukraine, Kazakhstan, Bangladesh, India, Pakistan, Indonesia, the Philippines, Nigeria, Kenya, Egypt or Brazil (or **No region**) in the list on the **Region** tab; each row shows the region’s typical mobile link, its CDN edge and the edge round trip. A region the route is slower to is marked **VPN slower:** with `CDN`, `servers` or `bandwidth`. Then pick where your servers run under **Servers in** on the right: Frankfurt (the default), N. Virginia, N. California, São Paulo, Mumbai, Singapore or Tokyo. Each server location shows the region’s round trip to it, and the route’s in amber when the route is slower (`160 ms · VPN 210 ms`).

A region splits the device’s traffic into two paths. The **Paths** table shows them:

| Column     | What it is                                                                                                                                                                                                      |
| ---------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| **Path**   | **CDN edge and DNS** (the address ranges of Cloudflare, Fastly and Google, served from the edge the region’s users reach, and every DNS query), or **Servers in …** (your backends and everything not on a CDN) |
| **Region** | the round trip the region’s users have on that path, beyond their access link                                                                                                                                   |
| **Route**  | what the session’s route already takes on it; amber when that is more than the region’s                                                                                                                         |
| **Added**  | what is added: the region’s round trip less the route’s, never below 0                                                                                                                                          |

The access link comes on top of both paths. With **No limits** picked as the access link, the first network becomes **Typical mobile in** the region, the region’s median mobile connection, and that link is used.

When the route is already slower than the region on a path, a warning says so: emulation can only add delay, so a VPN location closer to the servers, or none, gets nearer.

| Region        | Typical mobile link               | CDN edge                                | Edge round trip |
| ------------- | --------------------------------- | --------------------------------------- | --------------- |
| Germany       | +30 ±8 ms, 60 / 12 Mbit/s, 0.2%   | Frankfurt                               | 5 ms            |
| United States | +35 ±10 ms, 100 / 12 Mbit/s, 0.3% | the nearest metro                       | 10 ms           |
