| Ukraine       | +35 ±10 ms, 30 / 12 Mbit/s, 0.5%  | Kyiv                                    | 8 ms            |
| Kazakhstan    | +40 ±12 ms, 35 / 12 Mbit/s, 0.5%  | Almaty                                  | 10 ms           |
| Bangladesh    | +55 ±25 ms, 15 / 6 Mbit/s, 1%     | Dhaka or Singapore, by operator         | 30 ms           |
| India         | +45 ±20 ms, 90 / 10 Mbit/s, 0.5%  | Mumbai, Chennai, Delhi and others       | 15 ms           |
| Pakistan      | +60 ±25 ms, 20 / 9 Mbit/s, 1%     | Karachi or the Middle East, by operator | 35 ms           |
| Indonesia     | +45 ±20 ms, 30 / 12 Mbit/s, 0.5%  | Jakarta                                 | 15 ms           |
| Philippines   | +50 ±25 ms, 30 / 8 Mbit/s, 1%     | Manila                                  | 20 ms           |
| Nigeria       | +65 ±30 ms, 25 / 9 Mbit/s, 1.5%   | Lagos                                   | 20 ms           |
| Kenya         | +55 ±30 ms, 25 / 9 Mbit/s, 1.5%   | Nairobi or Mombasa                      | 15 ms           |
| Egypt         | +50 ±20 ms, 20 / 8 Mbit/s, 1%     | Cairo                                   | 25 ms           |
| Brazil        | +40 ±15 ms, 45 / 12 Mbit/s, 0.5%  | São Paulo and other metros              | 10 ms           |

Round trips from each region to the server locations, in milliseconds:

| Region        | Frankfurt | N. Virginia | N. California | São Paulo | Mumbai | Singapore | Tokyo |
| ------------- | --------- | ----------- | ------------- | --------- | ------ | --------- | ----- |
| Germany       | 10        | 90          | 150           | 200       | 120    | 160       | 230   |
| United States | 100       | 30          | 50            | 130       | 220    | 190       | 130   |
| Ukraine       | 35        | 120         | 180           | 230       | 150    | 180       | 250   |
| Kazakhstan    | 75        | 160         | 220           | 270       | 120    | 160       | 220   |
| Bangladesh    | 170       | 240         | 230           | 340       | 60     | 50        | 110   |
| India         | 120       | 200         | 220           | 300       | 20     | 50        | 120   |
| Pakistan      | 130       | 210         | 260           | 310       | 50     | 90        | 160   |
| Indonesia     | 180       | 230         | 180           | 330       | 70     | 20        | 90    |
| Philippines   | 200       | 220         | 160           | 330       | 90     | 40        | 60    |
| Nigeria       | 100       | 160         | 220           | 230       | 200    | 260       | 300   |
| Kenya         | 130       | 210         | 270           | 280       | 110    | 180       | 260   |
| Egypt         | 60        | 140         | 200           | 230       | 110    | 150       | 220   |
| Brazil        | 200       | 120         | 170           | 15        | 300    | 330       | 260   |

These are rounded estimates from public speed reports and latency maps, plausible rather than measured per operator.

### Backends behind a CDN

[Section titled “Backends behind a CDN”](#backends-behind-a-cdn)

An API behind Cloudflare has a CDN address, but its requests go through to your servers. List such hosts under **Backends behind a CDN**, one per line (or separated by commas): a host name, `*.example.com` for every name below it, or an IPv4 address. **Save backends** appears when the list changed.

Their traffic then takes the servers’ path. The agent answers the device’s DNS, so it picks up the addresses the device gets when it looks a backend up, and shapes them about a second later; the addresses found so far are listed under the field. Other hosts on the same CDN addresses take the servers’ path too.

The list is kept per app: in your account when the portal’s [database](/configuration/database/) is persistent, in this browser otherwise. It is filled in when you pick a region in the app’s next session.

## Common tasks

[Section titled “Common tasks”](#common-tasks)

**Check the app on a slow network.** Pick **3G** or **Weak 4G** and go through the main screens: loaders should show, and nothing should be tapped twice while a request is slow.

**Check that the app survives drops.** Pick **Subway**, **Elevator** or **Flapping**. Requests made during an outage hang until they time out; the app should retry or say what happened. The [WebSockets](/session-tools/websockets/) tab shows each reconnect of a socket as a new row.

**Test for users in a country.** Pick the country as the region, your servers’ location in **Servers in**, and list your API under **Backends behind a CDN**. A [VPN location](/concepts/vpn/) in or near the same country keeps the route short, so the region’s full round trips can be added; the IP address then also matches the country.

**Find out why the emulated network is faster than promised.** Read the amber notes: the route is already slower than the network, or the network faster than the route’s bandwidth. Pick a closer VPN location.

**See how long requests took.** The picker only sets the conditions; the timings are elsewhere (see [Measuring the effect](#measuring-the-effect)).

## Measuring the effect

[Section titled “Measuring the effect”](#measuring-the-effect)

Holtdroid has no separate load-speed report. Request timings are in these places:

* live, in the **DevTools** tab’s Network panel: Chrome’s own timing for each request of the WebView;
* in a [recording](/concepts/recordings/#network-console-and-websockets), a request’s **Timing** on the Network tab: queued and stalled, DNS, connect (with TLS), send, **Waiting (TTFB)**, download and the total;
* in a recording’s [Routes](/session-tools/routes/) tab, the median connect, TLS and waiting times of the WebView’s requests to each name, and how many of them opened a new connection;
* the Network row’s **Device traffic**: download and upload of the whole device every two seconds over the last minute.

## In recordings

[Section titled “In recordings”](#in-recordings)

A [recording](/concepts/recordings/#the-player) keeps the conditions as they changed: the player’s **Network** card shows the VPN location, **Throttling** with the network’s name and numbers (or **Full speed**), the **Region** with what it added to the CDN and the servers (`CDN +5 ms · Frankfurt +40 ms`) and the device’s traffic, each as it was at the moment you are at.

## Limits

[Section titled “Limits”](#limits)

* Only emulator sessions with VPN locations have network conditions; phones don’t.
* Emulation can only add delay and take bandwidth away, never make the session’s route faster.
* Addresses are IPv4 only; the CDN ranges are Cloudflare’s, Fastly’s and Google’s published lists.
* There are no custom networks: the networks and scenarios are fixed.
* The step shown for a running scenario is the agent’s; the portal reads it again when the step’s shortest hold is over, so it can lag a step’s change by a couple of seconds.

# Overview

> The tool tabs to the right of a session's screen, what each one is for and when it appears.

To the right of a session’s screen is the tools card with a row of underlined tabs. Each one looks at the device or the app from another side. DevTools, Logcat, DNS, Routes, Files and Terminal are in the row; WebSockets, Cache and Pixel perfect are under **More** at its end, and the one picked from there joins the row while it is open. Tabs stay open in the background while you look at another one, so DevTools keeps its state and the terminal its shell.

Not every tab is there in every session: a tab appears only when the session can use it. [Network conditions](/session-tools/network/) are not a tab: the **Network** row of the Device panel on the left opens them in a picker.

| Tab                                                | What it is for                                                                      | When it appears                                          |
| -------------------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------- |
| **DevTools**                                       | Chrome DevTools for the app’s WebViews: Elements, Console, Network, Sources         | always ([WebView DevTools](/concepts/devtools/))         |
| [**Pixel perfect**](/session-tools/pixel-perfect/) | lay a design mockup over the screen and find where the app differs                  | unless the server turned it off (`pixelPerfect.enabled`) |
| [**WebSockets**](/session-tools/websockets/)       | the WebViews’ sockets and event streams, frame by frame                             | when the app has a WebView DevTools can reach            |
| [**Cache**](/session-tools/cache/)                 | how the WebViews’ requests use the HTTP cache and a CDN                             | same as WebSockets                                       |
| [**DNS**](/session-tools/dns/)                     | every name the device looks up, and rewrites of names to other addresses            | in sessions with a [VPN](/concepts/vpn/)                 |
| [**Routes**](/session-tools/routes/)               | where the connections go: servers, countries, networks, the VPN exit and slow paths | in sessions with a VPN                                   |
| [**Logcat**](/session-tools/logcat/)               | the device’s log, with the app’s lines and crashes                                  | when the session has ADB                                 |
| [**Files**](/session-tools/files/)                 | the app’s private data and the shared storage                                       | when the session has ADB                                 |
| [**Terminal**](/session-tools/terminal/)           | a shell on the device                                                               | when the session has ADB and the device a shell          |

Logcat, Files and Terminal talk to the device over ADB straight from your browser (see [ADB tools](/concepts/adb/)). The connection opens when you first open one of them; if it drops, the tab offers **Reconnect**.

## In recordings

[Section titled “In recordings”](#in-recordings)

A [recording](/concepts/recordings/) keeps what most of these tabs show: its player has Logcat, the WebViews’ Network, Console and WebSockets, Cache, DNS, Routes and Pixel perfect, each as it was at the moment you are at. Files and Terminal aren’t recorded.

# Pixel perfect

> Lay a design mockup over the device screen, find where the app differs from it and export a report.

The **Pixel perfect** tab next to DevTools lays a design mockup over the device’s screen, the way the PerfectPixel browser extension does for web pages, and goes a step further: it finds where the screen differs from the mockup, explains each difference and makes a report to send to whoever owns it.

## References

[Section titled “References”](#references)

A reference is an image: SVG, PNG, JPEG or WebP, up to `pixelPerfect.maxFileSize` (25 MiB). Add one by dropping it on the tab, choosing a file, or pasting it with ⌘V / Ctrl+V while the tab is open.

From Figma, paste the link

For a Figma frame, paste its link instead of an exported image (see [Import from Figma](#import-from-figma)): it comes with its layers and components, rendered by Figma itself. Keep the frame the size of the phone’s screen in dp (for example 360 × 800); Holtdroid fits it to the work area. An exported image still works: a PNG at 3× or 4×, or an SVG for a flat frame (Figma’s SVG export loses corner smoothing and background blur).

An SVG needs a size: `width` and `height` on its root, or a `viewBox`, which Figma always writes.

## Import from Figma

[Section titled “Import from Figma”](#import-from-figma)

A frame can come straight from Figma, together with its layers: select it, **Copy link to selection** (⌘L / Ctrl+L), and paste the link into the tab, or use **Figma** in the reference list. Figma renders it as a **PNG at 4×** (less for very tall frames, to stay under 24 megapixels): its own rendering, exact for corner smoothing, shadows, blurs and text, and the same as the components it is split into. There is no format to choose.

### Components

[Section titled “Components”](#components)

The import also renders up to 20 parts of the frame on their own, so you can leave some out of the reference, such as a placeholder where the app shows a video, a camera picture or a map. The parts are the frame’s children; while there is room, the largest group or frame that adds nothing of its own (no fill, stroke, effect, clipping, mask or opacity) is replaced by its children, so a wrapper is split and a card stays whole. What is meant as one thing stays one part:

* a component **instance** (a button, a timer, a card), unless it covers at least half of the frame;
* anything smaller than 5% of the frame;
* a **list or grid**: a group whose items, looking through plain rows, are mostly (three quarters or more) instances of one component or layers of one name.

A frame with more than 20 children keeps them as they are, up to 60. References imported before these rules get them on **Update from Figma**.

The **Components** tab lists them, top first, with a picture each; pointing at one outlines it on the screen and the eye hides it. Hidden components are kept with the reference. With all of them shown, the overlay is the frame’s own rendering; with some hidden, the browser draws the frame again from its background colour and the visible components, in order. **Skip hidden components** (on by default) also leaves their place out of the comparison, so the video under a hidden placeholder isn’t a difference.

Parts with an image or video fill over at least half of them (a photo or a player, not an icon), or whose name says video, player, stream, camera, preview or map, are marked **live?**, and **Hide live content** hides them at once.

Redrawing works when the frame’s own fill is plain colour and no mask spans its parts; otherwise the tab says so and ignored areas are the way to skip them. A redrawn frame can differ from Figma’s rendering where hidden and shown parts interact: background blur over a hidden part, or blend modes between them. The pictures count towards your quota (usually a few MB) and are fetched again by **Update from Figma**, which keeps the hidden ones that still exist.

Importing needs a Figma **personal access token**. The server may have one for everyone (`pixelPerfect.figma.token`); otherwise add yours on the **Pixel perfect** page (the frame icon in the dock), under **Account** in the `users` sign-in mode, or right in the import form. Each of them has the same step-by-step guide:

1. In Figma, click your name or avatar in the top left corner → **Settings** → **Security**.
2. Under **Personal access tokens**, **Generate new token**, name it `holtdroid` and pick the longest expiration Figma offers.
3. Scopes: **File content** read-only and **Current user** read (Holtdroid checks the token with it and shows whose it is); nothing else.
4. Copy the token (it starts with `figd_`, Figma shows it once), paste it and **Check and save**.

The token reads only the files your Figma account can open. Where it is kept depends on the server:

* **With your account** when the database is `sqlite` and `auth.sessionKey` is set: the api checks it with Figma, encrypts it (AES-GCM with a key derived from `auth.sessionKey`) and never sends it back, so it works in every browser you sign in with. Changing `auth.sessionKey` makes saved tokens unreadable; everyone then saves theirs again.
* **In this browser** otherwise (an in-memory database would lose it on the next restart): the api only checks it, and the browser sends it with each import or update.

When the token expires, imports say Figma refused it: generate a new one and **Replace** it.

## Pixel perfect page

[Section titled “Pixel perfect page”](#pixel-perfect-page)

The frame icon in the dock opens the page for your references outside a session: all of them grouped by app, with search, the space they take and when they will be deleted; import from Figma or add an image, rename, download, delete, open a Figma reference’s frame in Figma or update it, and show or hide its components (the layers button). It also holds your Figma token and how the tab starts in this browser (opacity, blend, and which of the switches below are on).

The import keeps the layers under the frame: their boxes, the top fill and stroke, corner radius, opacity, font (family, weight, size, line height, letter spacing) and auto layout padding and gap. They move with the reference when you move or scale it, and the comparison uses them (see [Elements](#elements)). **Update from Figma** (the arrows next to a reference) fetches the frame again, keeping where it lies and its ignored areas.

A phone frame drawn at the screen’s width in dp (360, 393, 412) has its measures in dp; a wider frame is in pixels, and the tab says so. References belong to you, not to a session, so they are there in every session; the ones added for the current app come first.

Double-click a name to rename it. Each reference also remembers where you put it over the screen and which areas the comparison skips.

They live in the server’s storage (S3 or a folder). Each user has `pixelPerfect.quota` (1 GiB by default; per user in the `users` auth mode), and a reference nobody opened for `pixelPerfect.maxAge` (30 days) is deleted; laying it over a screen counts as opening it, its thumbnail in the list doesn’t.

The list shows small previews (160 px wide, the top of tall frames) that the browser makes when you add an image, so opening the tab doesn’t download the full images; the server makes them for PNG, JPEG and WebP it got without one.

## The tab

[Section titled “The tab”](#the-tab)

The toolbar at the top holds what is used all the time: the reference (click it for the list, search, import from Figma or add an image), the eye that hides the overlay, its opacity and blend, **Freeze**, the settings and **Find differences**. Below it, three tabs:

* **Layout**: the work area, the position, the grid and the guides;
* **Components** (or **Skip areas** for an image): the Figma components to hide and the ignored areas;
* **Differences**: the result, which **Find differences** switches to.

When the panel is wide (DevTools stretched across the window), the three are shown side by side as columns instead of tabs.

The same panel is in a recording’s player, over the recorded video (see [Recordings](/concepts/recordings/#pixel-perfect)).

Nothing of Pixel perfect is drawn over the screen while another tool tab (DevTools, Logcat, …) is open: the reference, a frozen frame, the differences, the work area, the grid and the guides come back as they were when you return to the tab.

## Over the screen

[Section titled “Over the screen”](#over-the-screen)

Picking a reference lays it over the device screen. By default it fills the work area’s width without going past its height, top-aligned, so a mockup at any density (1×, 2×, 3×) fits as is.

* **Opacity** and the **blend**: *Normal* is the mockup see-through; *Difference* is the classic “negative” check, where matching pixels turn black and anything off lights up; *Invert* shows the inverted mockup, so matching areas fade to grey.
* **Position**: X and Y in the mockup’s own pixels and a scale, where 100% is the fit above. Turn on **Move** to drag it over the screen or nudge it with the arrow keys (Shift for 10 px). While dragging, its edges and centre snap to the work area, the grid’s columns and the guides; hold Alt not to. The device stays usable while Move is off: taps go through the overlay.
* The eye button hides the overlay without losing its settings.

## Work area

[Section titled “Work area”](#work-area)

The work area is the part of the screen you work in, for example the app without the status and navigation bars, or a single card. The reference is fitted to it, the grid and the guides start at its corner, and the comparison skips everything outside it. The area outside is dimmed and the area outlined in amber.

* **Whole screen**, the default.
* **Insets**: top, right, bottom and left in dp, so the same area fits any screen size and density. **Without system bars** sets 24 and 48 dp.
* **Drawn**: drag a rectangle over the screen; it is kept as fractions of the screen.

**Detect** takes a screenshot and reads the views, and offers what it finds as insets: **Content by colour** cuts off plain bars along the edges (black bars above and below a letterboxed game; a camera hole or a few status icons in them don’t stop it), a large **WebView**, **SurfaceView**, **TextureView** or player view, and the **App window**. Point at one to see it outlined on the screen, click to use it. When the content reaches the screen’s edges and fills it, there is nothing to find.

While drawing the work area, an ignored area or a guide, a **loupe** next to the pointer shows the screen magnified with its pixel grid. Corners land on pixel boundaries and snap to the nearest contrasting edge within four pixels, such as a card’s border; hold Alt to place them freely. The loupe uses a picture of the screen taken when the tool is turned on, or the frozen frame.

Each reference keeps its own area, grid and guides. **Save as a preset** (the bookmark button) keeps them under a name for your other references and devices, and the list above the switch applies one; presets live with your account in the server’s storage.

## Grid and guides

[Section titled “Grid and guides”](#grid-and-guides)

The **grid** is drawn inside the work area, in dp: a number of columns with a margin on each side and a gutter between them, like Material’s layout grids, and rows every so many dp for a baseline. **4 columns**, **8 columns** and **8 dp rows** fill in common values.

**Guides** are lines at a distance in dp from the work area’s left or top edge. Turn on **Rulers** and drag from the ruler at the top of the screen for a horizontal guide, or from the left one for a vertical guide; drag a guide to move it (it snaps to the area and the columns) and drag it out of the area to remove it. They are also listed with their positions to type in exactly.

**Grid and guides on the screen** in the settings hides them without losing them.

## Freeze frame

[Section titled “Freeze frame”](#freeze-frame)

**Freeze frame** keeps the current picture of the screen over the live one, so a toast, a ripple or an animation that is gone in a second can still be compared: freeze it while it is on the screen, then line the mockup up and look for differences at leisure. **Live** (on the screen or in the tab) goes back to the stream.

## Finding differences

[Section titled “Finding differences”](#finding-differences)

**Find differences** compares the screen with the mockup as it lies:

1. The screen is taken from a lossless screenshot of the device, or from the frozen frame. A frozen frame comes from the stream, so a higher stream quality makes it sharper.
2. Pixels are compared perceptually (pixelmatch, YIQ colour distance), with anti-aliased edges left out. Transparent parts of the mockup are not compared, and lone stray pixels (video compression, dithering) don’t make a region.
3. Differing pixels are grouped into regions, and each region gets a guess at what is wrong: **shifted** by so many pixels in which direction (the mockup is moved around the region to find where it fits), **colour** (same shapes, another colour, with both colours), **missing** on the screen, **not in the reference**, or simply **differs**. Sizes are in the device’s pixels.

The match is the share of compared pixels that agree. Regions are outlined and numbered on the screen (**Differences on the screen** in the settings turns that off) and on the **Differences** tab, which offers the views that image diffs on code review sites use: **Side by side**, **Swipe** (a line to drag across), **Onion skin** and **Difference** (black where equal, the size of the error otherwise, with the differing pixels in red). Pointing at a region in the list highlights it everywhere; a click opens a magnified crop of the reference, the difference and the screen.

While a frame is frozen, moving or scaling the mockup or changing the ignored areas runs the comparison again at once, which helps line a mockup up.

### Interfaces over video

[Section titled “Interfaces over video”](#interfaces-over-video)

An interface drawn over a video, a camera picture or a map would differ from any mockup everywhere the video is. Three things keep that out:

* **Skip what moves** (on by default) takes a few frames a moment apart before comparing, marks the parts of the screen that changed between them and leaves them out: video and animation under the interface are skipped, the still interface over them is compared. The skipped area is shaded blue. Freeze frame takes these frames right after the frozen one.
* **Ignored areas**: on the **Components** tab (**Skip areas** for an image without components), turn on **Draw** and drag over the screen to mark areas the comparison always skips for this reference, such as a player that may be paused.
* **Skip video, canvas and frames in WebViews** (with **Name differences by WebView elements** on, see below): in a WebView page, the boxes of `<video>`, `<canvas>`, `<iframe>`, `<embed>` and `<object>` elements are left out, paused or not (see below). They are hatched violet.

### Elements

[Section titled “Elements”](#elements)

A difference found by pixels says where; elements say what is there. Both switches are in the settings (the sliders icon in the toolbar).

**Name differences by native views** (on by default) reads the app’s views with Android’s `uiautomator`, the way Appium does, without touching the app: each difference names the view that fits it, with its class, resource id, text or content description, and its size in pixels and dp; pointing at a difference outlines the view over the screen. Compose screens show their texts and descriptions, and their test tags as ids when the app sets `testTagsAsResourceId`. It adds a second or two, and doesn’t work while the screen keeps animating: the tab then says so and compares by pixels alone. With a frozen frame, the views are read the moment it is frozen.

With a reference **imported from Figma**, each difference also names the design layer there (`◆ Card › Pay`, outlined in pink when you point at it) and what the design asks of it: size, fill, stroke, radius, font, padding and gap; for a colour difference, the fill next to the colour on the screen. The view or page element drawn where that layer is (outlined in amber) is measured against it, so the list says `width 320 dp instead of 328` and the magnified crop has a table of the edges and sizes that are off.

### WebView pages

[Section titled “WebView pages”](#webview-pages)

This part is **experimental** and **off by default**: turn on **Name differences by WebView elements** in the settings; the choice is remembered in the browser.

When the screen shows a WebView that DevTools can inspect, the comparison also asks the page about itself, through its own DevTools connection next to the DevTools tab (Chrome serves several at once):

1. It reads the visible elements of each open page: their boxes, a CSS selector, their own text and a few computed styles, and takes a screenshot of the page.
2. It finds where that screenshot sits on the device’s screen, which places the page on it exactly: under the status bar and the app’s own toolbar, or wherever the app put its WebView. A WebView that isn’t on the screen, or a page in a background WebView, doesn’t match and is left out. The page found is outlined violet on the screen.
3. Each difference gets the element that fits it best: the list shows `button.submit “Pay”` under the difference, and the magnified crop adds its selector (with a copy button), its size in CSS pixels, a shift in CSS pixels as well as device pixels, and the styles that matter for that kind of difference: margins, padding and transforms for a shift, colours and borders for a colour difference, sizes and fonts otherwise.
4. Pointing at a difference in the list highlights its element on the device the way DevTools does, with margins, padding and its info box.

With a frozen frame, the page is read the moment the frame is frozen, so a toast that is gone by the time you compare still names its element. Highlighting needs the element to still be there.

## Report

[Section titled “Report”](#report)

**Report** downloads a PNG with the project’s logo, the reference name, the app, its version, the screen and the time, the match, three columns (the reference, the difference with ignored areas, the screen) with the regions numbered on them, and the list of differences with their sizes, positions, their elements or views, and the Figma layer with what is off.

## Configuration

[Section titled “Configuration”](#configuration)

```yaml
pixelPerfect:
  enabled: true # the tab and its API; on by default
  quota: 1GiB # per user; 0 = no limit
  maxAge: 720h # deleted this long after it was last opened; 0 = never
  maxFileSize: 25MiB # largest image
  sweepInterval: 1h # how often retention runs
  figma:
    token: env:FIGMA_TOKEN # a personal access token for everyone; empty = each user gives theirs
    url: https://api.figma.com
  storage: # optional: where references go; default is the shared storage under pixel-perfect/
    type: s3
    s3:
      endpoint: https://s3.example.com
      bucket: holtdroid
      prefix: pixel-perfect
      accessKey: env:S3_ACCESS_KEY
      secretKey: env:S3_SECRET_KEY
```

Without a storage of its own the references go to `storage`, which the Helm chart puts on the cache volume, an `emptyDir`: give them an S3 prefix or a persistent folder to keep them across restarts.

# Routes

> Where a session's connections go — the servers behind each name, their country and network, the VPN location they left through, and what makes a path slower than it needs to be.

Sessions with a [VPN](/concepts/vpn/) know every connection the device opens: the sidecar that carries its traffic reports them to the session’s agent. The **Routes** tab next to DevTools turns them into the path the app’s traffic takes, from the device through the VPN location to each server, and points out what looks off.

## The path

[Section titled “The path”](#the-path)

The line at the top is the session’s route: the device, the VPN location, its exit address with the country and network it belongs to, then the servers. Below it, one row per name the app connected to (or per address, for a connection without a name):

* the **address** of the server, and how many others the name led to;
* **where** it is: the country and the network (autonomous system) the address belongs to; for Cloudflare, Fastly and Google, **anycast** and the site that answered (see [CDN sites](#cdn-sites));
* **via**: the VPN location (or `bypass`) the traffic left through;
* how many **connections** it took, open ones in brackets, and the bytes received.

In a narrow panel the table drops **via** first, then the **address**, and shows the flags next to the name; click a row for everything about it. Names whose connections all closed are greyed. The list survives a reload (the agent keeps the open connections and the last 2000 closed ones).

## What is flagged

[Section titled “What is flagged”](#what-is-flagged)

* **far**: the server is on another continent than the session’s exit, so every round trip crosses an ocean or two. A CDN edge is never far: its address is anycast, and the site that answers is the nearest one, whatever country the address is listed in.
* **no reuse**: six or more TCP connections to one port within a minute. Each pays a TCP and a TLS handshake; keep-alive or HTTP/2 would carry them over one connection.
* **bypass**: some of the traffic left past the VPN location (the addresses in `vpn.bypassCIDRs`).
* **HTTP**: unencrypted HTTP on port 80.

**Flagged** shows only the names with a flag.

## CDN sites

[Section titled “CDN sites”](#cdn-sites)

A CDN announces the same address from hundreds of sites, and the one nearest to the session’s exit answers. Geolocation databases list such an address where it is registered (for Cloudflare often Canada or the United States), which has nothing to do with where it answers, so the tab never shows that country. It shows **anycast**, the CDN and, when it is known, the site that answered, such as `Vilnius, Lithuania VNO`:

* for a Cloudflare address, the agent asks Cloudflare once per address and VPN location, through the same location: `/cdn-cgi/trace` from that address as `www.cloudflare.com`, or else from the connection’s own name. Cloudflare answers it at the edge; the app’s servers never see it;
* in a recording, from the headers of the WebView’s responses: Cloudflare’s `cf-ray`, CloudFront’s `x-amz-cf-pop` and Fastly’s `x-served-by`.

Sites are named by their airport code; the city comes from Cloudflare’s list of sites, which covers most of Fastly’s and CloudFront’s too. A CDN address is never flagged **far**.

## A name’s details

[Section titled “A name’s details”](#a-names-details)

A click on a row shows the name’s servers with their places, its DNS answers (asked through the VPN location, so a geo-DNS service answers for that location’s country), and every connection: when it opened, how long it lasted, the protocol and port, the outbound and its bytes. In a recording, the details also show the median connect, TLS and waiting times of the WebView’s requests to that name, and how many of them opened a new connection.

The [DNS](/session-tools/dns/) tab places the addresses it answered the same way and marks a lookup **far** when every address in it is on another continent than the exit.

## In recordings

[Section titled “In recordings”](#in-recordings)

[Recordings](/concepts/recordings/) keep the connections, and the player has the same tab: it shows the connections as they stood at the playhead. Places are looked up when the recording is watched, so they are where the addresses are now.

A name’s details in a recording also show how fast the WebView reached it: the median **connect**, **TLS** and **waiting** (time to first byte) of the WebView’s requests to that name up to the playhead, and how many of them opened a new connection. Slow TLS or many new connections point at the connection setup; a long wait points at the server.

## Limits

[Section titled “Limits”](#limits)

* Emulator sessions see every connection as it opens and closes, however short, with its final bytes. On [phones](/configuration/phones/) the open connections are read four times a second, so one shorter than that may be missing, or shown without its last bytes.
* Places are per country, from the [DB-IP Lite](https://db-ip.com) databases in the portal’s image (`geoIP` in the [configuration](/configuration/overview/#ip-geolocation)); a portal without them shows no countries or networks, only CDN sites.
* Holtdroid doesn’t trace the hops to a server: from inside the session a trace stops at the tunnel, and the exit belongs to the VPN.
* Sessions without a VPN sidecar have no Routes tab.

# Terminal

> An interactive ADB shell on the session's device, in a tab of the session page.

The **Terminal** tab is `adb shell` in the browser: a full terminal on the session’s device, with colours, line editing and full-screen programs such as `top`. Use it to poke at the device the way you would with a cable on your desk: read a property, list processes, run `am` or `pm` by hand, look at a file with `cat`. It works over [ADB in the browser](/concepts/adb/), so you need nothing installed on your computer.

## When the tab appears

[Section titled “When the tab appears”](#when-the-tab-appears)

The tab sits after **Logcat** and **Files**. It needs everything the other ADB tabs need:

* the server allows ADB in the browser (`adb.browser`, on by default);
* with `adb.ownerOnly` (the default), the session is yours or you are an admin;

and on top of that, the device must allow **any** shell command. That is off by default: emulators show the tab only with `redroid.shell: full` ([Emulator provider](/configuration/emulator/#users-adb-inside-android)), phones only with `adb.shell: full` ([ADB on phones](/configuration/phones/#adb-on-phones)). With the default `allowlist` the device runs only the commands behind the other tabs, and the Terminal tab isn’t shown at all.

There is nothing to click or allow. The page connects to the device’s ADB once the device is first ready, and the tab shows **Connecting to ADB…** until then. If the connection fails or drops, it shows **Could not reach the device over ADB** with the reason and a **Reconnect** button.

## What you see

[Section titled “What you see”](#what-you-see)

A dark terminal that fills the tab, with the shell’s prompt. The shell starts the first time you open the tab and gets the focus, so you can type right away. The terminal follows the size of the tab, and full-screen programs redraw when you resize the window or the split between the device and the tools.

Who the shell runs as depends on the device:

* **Emulators**: root. redroid’s adbd runs as root, so the shell can read and change anything in Android, and because redroid shares the node’s kernel, root there reaches the node too. That is why the tab is off by default; see [Security](/operations/security/).
* **Phones**: Android’s `shell` user, the same as `adb shell` on your own phone. On a phone in root mode, `su` works from this shell.

The terminal keeps the last 5000 lines; scroll up with the mouse wheel.

## Common tasks

[Section titled “Common tasks”](#common-tasks)

* **Type and edit commands** as in any terminal: arrow keys, history, tab completion and Ctrl+C to stop a command all go to the device’s shell.
* **Paste** with the browser’s paste shortcut.
* **Copy** by selecting text with the mouse and using the browser’s copy shortcut (Cmd+C on macOS). Ctrl+C is sent to the shell as an interrupt, not a copy.
* **Switch tabs.** The shell keeps running while you look at DevTools, Logcat or Files, with its output and history, and is where you left it when you come back.
* **Start over.** Type `exit` (or press Ctrl+D): the terminal prints `[the shell exited]` and shows a **New shell** button that opens a fresh one.

The `adb` commands that only make sense on your computer (`adb push`, `adb pull`, `adb install`) don’t exist inside the device’s shell. Move files with the [Files](/session-tools/files/) tab and install builds from the portal.

## Compared with your own adb

[Section titled “Compared with your own adb”](#compared-with-your-own-adb)

The [holtdroid client](/concepts/ssh/) gives each of your devices an ADB port on your computer, so your own `adb`, Android Studio and scripts work against it. Use it when you need `adb push`, `adb pull`, port forwards, scripted runs or your usual terminal. The Terminal tab needs nothing installed and is one click away, but it is one interactive shell in one browser tab.

Both go through the same policy: what the Terminal tab can’t run, your own `adb shell` can’t run either, and requests that would cut the session off from its device (`reboot`, `unroot`, `remount`, `tcpip`, `usb`, `sideload`, `disable-verity`) are refused in both; see [ADB tools](/concepts/adb/).

## Recordings

[Section titled “Recordings”](#recordings)

[Recordings](/concepts/recordings/) don’t keep anything of the terminal: the player has no Terminal tab, and neither the commands nor their output are recorded. Only what a command does to the screen shows up in the recorded video.

## Limits

[Section titled “Limits”](#limits)

* The shell lives in this browser tab. Reloading the page, closing it or leaving the session ends it, along with whatever runs in the foreground; each browser tab gets its own shell.
* When the ADB connection drops, the shell is gone; after **Reconnect** the tab opens a new one.
* Everything you change on the device is gone when the session ends, like the rest of the device.
* A device without the shell protocol (very old Android) gets a shell that doesn’t learn the terminal’s size, so full-screen programs may draw in the wrong size.

# WebSockets

> The WebSockets and event streams of the app's WebViews, frame by frame, with JSON and common protocols taken apart, kept for the whole session.

Chrome DevTools shows a socket’s messages only while its Network panel is open, and forgets them when you reload. The **WebSockets** tab doesn’t: the agent follows every WebSocket and event stream (`EventSource`) of the app’s WebViews for the whole session, whether or not anyone is looking, and the tab lists them with every message sent and received. Use it to check what a live chat, a price feed or a push channel actually sends, and in what order.

## When the tab is there

[Section titled “When the tab is there”](#when-the-tab-is-there)

The tab sits next to DevTools whenever the session has WebView DevTools: always on emulators, and on [phones](/configuration/phones/) only for debuggable builds (see [WebView DevTools](/concepts/devtools/)). The agent watches every page, iframe, worker and service worker of every WebView process from its first request, so a socket opened while the app starts is there too.

The tab keeps no state of its own. Reload the portal page, or open the session in another browser, and it fills again with what the agent kept (see [Limits](#limits)).

## What you see

[Section titled “What you see”](#what-you-see)

### The toolbar

[Section titled “The toolbar”](#the-toolbar)

* **Pause** stops updating the tab; **Resume** catches up on what came in the meantime, as long as the agent still keeps it.
* **Clear** empties the tab. It clears only this view: reloading the page brings back what the agent kept.
* **Filter** keeps the frames of the picked socket whose payload contains the text, ignoring case.
* **Hide under 15 B** hides frames shorter than 15 bytes, such as pings and heartbeats. The browser remembers the choice.
* On the right, how many sockets there are and how many frames the picked one has (`3 sockets · 128 frames`).

### Sockets

[Section titled “Sockets”](#sockets)

The list on the left has one row per WebSocket or event stream, in the order they appeared; the newest one is picked until you pick another. Each row shows:

* the host and path it connected to (hover for the whole URL), or **opened before Holtdroid attached** when the socket existed before the agent could see its address;
* its state: `connecting`, `open`, `error`, `closed`, or **media stream, not shown** (see below), and how many frames the tab has of it;
* a radio icon, green while the socket is up, red after an error and grey once it closed.

An event stream is listed like a socket: each event it receives is a frame.

### Frames

[Section titled “Frames”](#frames)

The table on the right lists the picked socket’s frames, oldest at the top. It follows new frames as they come; scroll up and it stops following, scroll to the end and it follows again.

| Column     | What it shows                                                                                     |
| ---------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| (arrow)    | a green ↑ for a frame the app **sent** (the row is tinted green), a red ↓ for one it **received** |
| **Data**   | a one-line preview of the payload (see [How payloads are read](#how-payloads-are-read))           |
| **Length** | the payload’s size in bytes, decoded for binary frames                                            |
| **Time**   | when the agent saw it, to the millisecond, in your browser’s time zone                            |

Click a frame to open it below the table: **Sent** or **Received**, its time, and the payload with a toolbar on top:

* what the payload is: **JSON**, **Socket.IO**, **Engine.IO**, **SignalR**, **Server-Sent Events**, **JSON Lines**, **Form**, **Binary** or **Text**, with the number of packets when there are several;
* **binary · UTF-8** when the bytes came in a binary frame but are text;
* the size, and **cut at the recording limit** in amber when the payload was longer than the agent keeps;
* **Pretty** and **Raw**, to switch between the parsed view and the text as it was sent;
* the copy button (**Copy as base64** for binary payloads).

A frame that looked like video or a picture has no payload: **The payload looked like media and isn’t kept.**

### How payloads are read

[Section titled “How payloads are read”](#how-payloads-are-read)

The preview and the details take apart what they recognise:

* JSON is a tree you open and close, also when it sits in a string field;
* **Socket.IO** events get their name as a label, other packets their type (`socket.io connect`, `engine.io ping` and `engine.io pong` for `2` and `3`);
* **SignalR** messages and Engine.IO polling records, separated by `\x1e`, are split into their packets, SignalR ones labelled `handshake json`, `invoke SendMessage`, `ping` and so on;
* **Server-Sent Events** blocks get their `event:` name as a label and their `data:` parsed;
* **JSON Lines** (several lines, each a JSON value) are split per line.

In the list, a binary frame carries a **bin** mark. One that holds UTF-8 text shows that text, parsed like any other; one with real bytes shows its size, and its details show a hex dump of the first 4 KB.

Values that look like a point in time (Unix seconds, milliseconds, microseconds or nanoseconds, ISO 8601 and HTTP dates) get two chips: how far they were from the device clock when the frame came, and how far they are from it now. Hover one for the same moment in UTC, in the device’s time zone and in yours. The [recordings page](/concepts/recordings/#network-console-and-websockets) explains the chips in full.

### Media streams

[Section titled “Media streams”](#media-streams)

A socket that carries video, audio or pictures would fill the tab with bytes nobody reads. The agent drops payloads whose first bytes look like H.264, MP4, WebM, Ogg, JPEG, PNG, RIFF (WAV, WebP, AVI) or FLV, and once a socket has sent three of them, or has moved 1 MB or 60 binary frames within the last four seconds, it marks the socket **media stream, not shown**. From then on the agent counts its frames but sends none to the tab.

## Common tasks

[Section titled “Common tasks”](#common-tasks)

**Find the message behind a wrong value on screen.** Pick the socket, type the value or a field name into **Filter**, and open the frame. The time chips show whether a timestamp in it was already old when it arrived.

**Check that the app reconnects.** Turn on a scenario such as **Subway** or **Flapping** in the [Network](/session-tools/network/) tab and watch the list: every reconnect is a new row, the old one turns `closed`.

**See only what the app sends.** Sent frames are the green rows with ↑; **Hide under 15 B** removes the heartbeats around them.

**Read a binary protocol.** Open a **bin** frame: text inside binary frames is decoded as UTF-8; anything else is a hex dump you can copy as base64.

**Mark the moment for a bug report.** While the session [records](/concepts/recordings/), click a frame’s time to pin a marker at that moment of the recording. Hover the time instead to pick the marker’s icon (Pin, Bug, Flag, Star, Warning or Done) or **Open the recording from here**, which opens the recording half a second before the frame, on its WebSockets tab with that socket picked. A frame that came while nothing was recording says so.

## In recordings

[Section titled “In recordings”](#in-recordings)

A [recording](/concepts/recordings/#network-console-and-websockets) keeps every socket and frame within the same limits, and its WebSockets tab shows them up to the playhead. It adds what the live tab doesn’t have: **All**, **Sent** and **Received** filters, whether a row is a **WebSocket** or an **Event stream**, the iframe or worker it came from, and for a media stream the moment it was marked and how many frames and bytes it moved. Each frame’s time seeks the video there, and [markers](/concepts/recordings/#markers) show on the timeline. **Export → Network (.har)** saves the messages with the requests.

## Limits

[Section titled “Limits”](#limits)

* Only text and binary data frames are shown; ping, pong and close frames are not.
* Event streams are `EventSource` connections. A response read as a stream with `fetch()` is a request, which DevTools’ Network panel shows, not a socket.
* The agent keeps a text frame up to 128 KB and a binary one up to 16 KB; longer payloads are cut and marked.
* For a reload or another browser the agent keeps about 16 MB of socket traffic; once there is more, the oldest goes first.
* The tab keeps the last 5000 frames of each socket and lists the last 500 of them that pass the filters.
* **Filter** matches a frame’s one-line preview, and a text frame’s whole payload. A binary frame that holds text is matched by its decoded text.
* The live tab doesn’t show a socket’s handshake status or error message; the [DevTools](/concepts/devtools/) Network panel does, while it is open.

# Browsers from release archives

> Keep Opera, Firefox and other browsers in a source with holtdroid-archive-sync, from the public archives their makers publish.

[holtdroid-archive-sync](https://github.com/holtdroid/holtdroid-sync/blob/main/docs/archive.md) is a separate job (`job: archive` in the chart `deploy/helm/holtdroid-sync`). It reads public release archives that are plain HTTP directory listings and copies the newest versions into a folder or S3 prefix, which Holtdroid lists as a read-only source.

## Opera and Firefox

[Section titled “Opera and Firefox”](#opera-and-firefox)

Opera publishes every Android build at `get.opera.com`, Firefox at `archive.mozilla.org`. This config keeps the five newest versions of each:

```yaml
job: archive
existingSecret: holtdroid-archive-sync # S3_ACCESS_KEY, S3_SECRET_KEY
config:
  archives:
    - name: opera
      title: Opera
      url: https://get.opera.com/pub/opera/android/
      versionDir: '^\d+$'
      fileVersion: "Opera_([0-9_]+)_Generic"
      include: ["*_arm8_*.apk", "*_x86_*.apk"]
    - name: opera-gx
      title: Opera GX
      url: https://get.opera.com/pub/opera/android/opera-gx/
      fileVersion: 'opera-gx-([0-9.]+)\.apk'
    - name: firefox
      title: Firefox
      url: https://archive.mozilla.org/pub/fenix/releases/
      versionDir: '^\d+\.\d+(\.\d+)?$'
      fileVersion: 'fenix-([0-9.]+)\.multi'
      depth: 2
      include: ["*arm64-v8a.apk", "*x86_64.apk"]
  target:
    type: s3
    s3:
      endpoint: https://s3.example.com
      bucket: holtdroid
      prefix: archive
      accessKey: env:S3_ACCESS_KEY
      secretKey: env:S3_SECRET_KEY
```

And the source in Holtdroid:

```yaml
sources:
  - name: browsers
    type: s3
    readOnly: true
    s3:
      endpoint: https://s3.example.com
      bucket: holtdroid
      prefix: archive
      accessKey: env:S3_ACCESS_KEY
      secretKey: env:S3_SECRET_KEY
```

The job sends its own name as the User-Agent and doesn’t try to pass bot checks. Brave and DuckDuckGo publish APKs on GitHub, so [holtdroid-github-sync](/sources/github/) covers them; for Brave, set `releaseName: "^Release "`, since its Nightly and Beta builds are normal releases there.

# Chromium versions

> Keep Chromium browser builds of many milestones in a source with holtdroid-chromium-sync, to reproduce bugs on the version they were reported on.

## Prebuilt releases

[Section titled “Prebuilt releases”](#prebuilt-releases)

[chromium-builds](https://github.com/holtdroid/chromium-builds) publishes Chromium browser and WebView APKs for every milestone from 83 on, built from the release tags with proprietary codecs, for x86_64 and arm64. [holtdroid-chromium-builds-sync](https://github.com/holtdroid/holtdroid-sync/blob/main/docs/chromium-builds.md) (`job: chromium-builds` in the chart `deploy/helm/holtdroid-sync`) copies them into a folder or S3 prefix. It takes a release only when all four APKs are uploaded, and shows the date Google released that version to Android, not the date the build was published.

```yaml
job: chromium-builds
existingSecret: holtdroid-chromium-builds-sync # S3_ACCESS_KEY, S3_SECRET_KEY
config:
  target:
    type: s3
    s3:
      endpoint: https://s3.example.com
      bucket: holtdroid
      prefix: chromium-builds
      accessKey: env:S3_ACCESS_KEY
      secretKey: env:S3_SECRET_KEY
```

Then list `chromium-builds/browser` as a read-only source and `chromium-builds/webview` as `webview.storage`, as in [Installation](/start/installation/). All releases take about 55 GB.

Without a job in the cluster, run one pass from any computer with Docker, with the `config:` part above in `config.yaml` and the S3 keys in the environment:

```sh
docker run --rm -e S3_ACCESS_KEY -e S3_SECRET_KEY -v "$PWD/config.yaml:/config.yaml" \
  ghcr.io/holtdroid/holtdroid-sync:<commit sha> holtdroid-chromium-builds-sync --config /config.yaml --once
```

A browser APK downloaded from a release page can also be uploaded with **Upload** like any build. A WebView APK uploaded that way is only a build in the list, not a choice in the launch dialog: the catalog lists builds by their sidecars’ tags (`version`, `milestone`, `minSdk`, …), which the job writes.

These builds are Chromium, not Google Chrome: no Google sign-in, sync, Safe Browsing or Widevine. The WebView is `com.android.webview`, so phones, whose Android only accepts Google’s signature, can’t use it. On redroid, the browsers of Chromium 96 and older crash at startup, and 104 crashes on Android 16. They stay in the list.

## Snapshot builds

[Section titled “Snapshot builds”](#snapshot-builds)

[holtdroid-chromium-sync](https://github.com/holtdroid/holtdroid-sync/blob/main/docs/chromium.md) is a separate job (`job: chromium` in the chart `deploy/helm/holtdroid-sync`). It copies Chromium browser builds, one per milestone, into a folder or S3 prefix, which Holtdroid lists as a read-only source. Launch one like any other build to open a page in that browser version.

## Where the builds come from

[Section titled “Where the builds come from”](#where-the-builds-come-from)

Chromium’s x86_64 snapshot builds in the public `chromium-browser-snapshots` bucket, the same ones the [WebView catalog](/concepts/webview-versions/) uses: `ChromePublic.apk`, Chromium as `org.chromium.chrome`, one APK with no splits. It is Chromium, not Google Chrome, so Google sign-in, sync and Play services features are missing. Builds go back to Chromium 129 (mid-2024), about 420 MB each.

## Which milestones

[Section titled “Which milestones”](#which-milestones)

Not all of them: the job keeps many recent milestones and fewer older ones. Counting the available milestones newest first, it keeps:

* the milestones on Android’s Stable, Beta, Dev and Canary channels;
* the newest `milestones.latest` (default 10);
* every milestone divisible by `milestones.every` (default 2);
* past the newest `milestones.older.after` (default 24), only milestones divisible by `milestones.older.every` (default 5) instead;
* `milestones.extra`.

In October 2026 the defaults pick 149–158, the even milestones 136–148 and 130: 18 builds, about 7.5 GB. Builds that stop matching as new milestones come out are deleted, but only after a pass in which Chromium Dash and the bucket answered. Each build is the milestone’s last Canary, give or take a few commits, and the current Canary milestone moves with every new Canary release.

Each build is `chromium-{milestone}.apk` with a sidecar: the title `Chromium {milestone}`, the version and snapshot revision as the note, and the tags `milestone`, `version`, `channel`, `revision`, `minSdk`, `targetSdk`, `requiresSdk` and `frontend`. Chromium 149 to 156 are tagged `requiresSdk: 34`: they abort at startup on Android 11 to 13. Chromium 157 and later are tagged `requiresSdk: 35`, see below. The launch dialog greys out the Android versions below `requiresSdk`, offering the newest Chromium that runs there instead, and the api refuses them.

## Deploying

[Section titled “Deploying”](#deploying)

```yaml
job: chromium
existingSecret: holtdroid-chromium-sync # S3_ACCESS_KEY, S3_SECRET_KEY
tmpSize: 2Gi # one unpacked APK at a time
config:
  interval: 6h
  target:
    type: s3
    s3:
      endpoint: https://s3.example.com
      bucket: holtdroid
      prefix: chromium
      accessKey: env:S3_ACCESS_KEY
      secretKey: env:S3_SECRET_KEY
```

And the source in Holtdroid:

```yaml
sources:
  - name: chromium
    type: s3
    readOnly: true
    s3:
      endpoint: https://s3.example.com
      bucket: holtdroid
      prefix: chromium
      accessKey: env:S3_ACCESS_KEY
      secretKey: env:S3_SECRET_KEY
```

The job needs outbound HTTPS to `chromiumdash.appspot.com` and `storage.googleapis.com`. Every option is in the job’s [docs](https://github.com/holtdroid/holtdroid-sync/blob/main/docs/chromium.md#configuration).

## Notes

[Section titled “Notes”](#notes)

* Snapshot builds report no DevTools frontend of their own. Holtdroid passes the build’s `frontend` tag (the milestone’s Canary commit) to the session, so the DevTools panel opens the browser’s tabs with that frontend. It can differ from the build by a few commits.
* Sessions skip Chrome’s welcome screens (`--disable-fre` in `chrome-command-line`) and make the browser the default one, so links from other apps open in it. Runtime permissions are granted at install.
* Two builds of the same package can’t be installed side by side: to compare milestones, start one session per milestone.
* Chromium 157 and later draw only through Vulkan 1.3 features. The Android 15 image of holtdroid-redroid ships newer Mesa Vulkan drivers for that; on Android 11 to 14 these builds abort with “GPU process isn’t usable”, hence `requiresSdk: 35`. Chromium 148 and older run on every version.

# Writing your own

> Principles for a sync job that publishes builds from CI, releases or anywhere else into a source.

There is no plugin API for sources. The contract is the file layout: a job that writes `*.apk` files and their [sidecars](/sources/overview/#the-metajson-sidecar) into a folder or an S3 prefix is a source integration. It can be written in any language and deployed and released apart from Holtdroid. [holtdroid-slack-sync](/sources/slack/) and [holtdroid-github-sync](/sources/github/) are examples.

The simplest integration is a CI step:

```sh
key="ci/$CI_PIPELINE_ID/app-release.apk"
cat > meta.json <<EOF
{"origin":"ci","link":"$CI_PIPELINE_URL","uploadedBy":"$GITLAB_USER_NAME",
 "changelog":"$(git log -1 --format=%s | sed 's/"/\\"/g')",
 "tags":{"branch":"$CI_COMMIT_REF_NAME","commit":"$CI_COMMIT_SHORT_SHA"}}
EOF
aws s3 cp meta.json "s3://holtdroid/$key.meta.json"
aws s3 cp app/build/outputs/apk/release/app-release.apk "s3://holtdroid/$key"
```

## Principles

[Section titled “Principles”](#principles)

**Own a prefix.** Give each job its own prefix (`slack/`, `ci/`, `releases/`) and point a separate `readOnly` source at it. A job never touches files outside its prefix, and portal users can’t delete what it manages.

**Use keys built from IDs the origin already has.** Examples are `{channel}/{file id}/{name}.apk`, `{pipeline}/{job}/{name}.apk` and `{tag}/{asset}.apk`. Then “is this build already here?” is just a listing, and the key never collides with another build.

**Let the listing be your state.** Don’t keep a database or state file. Before copying, list your prefix and skip what’s there. A restart, a crash halfway through or a second copy of the job then does nothing wrong. In-memory caches are fine as an optimisation, never for correctness.

**Write the sidecar first, then the APK.** The api lists whatever exists at that moment. With the sidecar in place first, a build never shows up without its owner, visibility and changelog. If the job dies between the two writes, it is left with a stray sidecar that the next pass overwrites.

**Add an icon if the APK’s own can’t be rendered.** For example, when the launcher icon is a vector with gradients or an animated drawable. Put it in `app.apk.icon.png`, written before the APK.

**Replace in place to publish a new build under the same name.** The api notices the new ETag or modification time, parses the file again and treats it as a new revision. Sessions already running keep the old one.

**Don’t modify APKs.** Holtdroid installs them exactly as published. Anything that needs repackaging is out of scope.

**Fill what you know.** Every sidecar field is optional:

* `origin` tells users where a build came from;
* `link` adds a button back to the pipeline or message;
* `changelog` and `tags` (branch, commit, flavor) make builds searchable;
* `owner` together with `visibility: private` keeps a build to one portal user and the admins.

**Clean up on your own schedule.** Holtdroid never deletes from read-only sources. If storage matters, prune old builds by age in the job, and keep the retention longer than the window the job scans, or pruned builds come back.

**Keep secrets out of the files.** Tokens for the origin and the bucket belong in the job’s environment. Nothing secret goes into keys or sidecars: everything in a sidecar is shown to every user who can see the build.

**Link back into the portal.** To announce a build (chat message, PR comment), use a [launch link](/sources/overview/#launch-links): `{portal}/?source={source name}&launch={base64url(key)}`.

## Checklist

[Section titled “Checklist”](#checklist)

* [ ] own prefix, `readOnly: true` source in the api config
* [ ] stable keys from origin IDs; skip what the listing already has
* [ ] sidecar before APK; `origin`, `link`, `uploadedAt` set
* [ ] safe to run twice at once and after a crash
* [ ] secrets from the environment, never logged
* [ ] tests against a fake origin and a fake bucket (e.g. `gofakes3`)

# GitHub releases

> Copy APKs attached to GitHub releases into a source with holtdroid-github-sync.

[holtdroid-github-sync](https://github.com/holtdroid/holtdroid-sync/blob/main/docs/github.md) is a separate job (`job: github` in the chart `deploy/helm/holtdroid-sync`). It polls the releases of one or more repositories and copies their `.apk` assets into a folder or S3 prefix, which Holtdroid lists as a read-only source.

## What it copies

[Section titled “What it copies”](#what-it-copies)

For each repository, the job walks the releases newest first:

* drafts are skipped;
* pre-releases are skipped unless `prereleases: true`;
* only the newest `releases` releases count (`0` = all);
* [`include` rules](/sources/overview/#include-rules) pick assets by `{tag}/{asset name}`, e.g. `!*-debug.apk`.

Each asset lands at `{owner}/{repo}/{tag}/{asset}` with a sidecar:

| Field        | Value                                              |
| ------------ | -------------------------------------------------- |
| `note`       | the release name, or the tag, plus “(pre-release)” |
| `changelog`  | the release notes                                  |
| `uploadedBy` | the GitHub login that uploaded the asset           |
| `uploadedAt` | when the asset was last updated                    |
| `link`       | the release page                                   |
| `tags`       | `repo`, `release`, `target` (branch), `prerelease` |

The launcher icon is extracted and written as `x.apk.icon.png`. A re-uploaded asset is copied again. Copies of assets that are gone, fall out of the newest `releases` or no longer match the rules are pruned, but only after every repository was listed.

## Rate limits

[Section titled “Rate limits”](#rate-limits)

Without a token, GitHub allows 60 API requests an hour. A pass costs one request per repository plus one per new asset, so the default 15-minute interval fits a handful of public repositories. Set `github.token` for more repositories, shorter intervals or private repositories.

## Deploying

[Section titled “Deploying”](#deploying)

The chart is in the sync repository (`deploy/helm/holtdroid-sync`); `job` picks the GitHub sync:

```yaml
job: github
existingSecret: holtdroid-github-sync # S3_ACCESS_KEY, S3_SECRET_KEY, NOTIFY_URL
persistence:
  enabled: false # an S3 target needs no volume
config:
  repos:
    - repo: WebView-CG/CanIAndroidWebView
      releases: 5
  interval: 15m
  target:
    type: s3
    s3:
      endpoint: https://s3.example.com
      bucket: holtdroid
      prefix: github
      accessKey: env:S3_ACCESS_KEY
      secretKey: env:S3_SECRET_KEY
  notify: # optional: announce new builds with launch links
    urls: [env:NOTIFY_URL] # shoutrrr, e.g. slack://xoxb:<bot token>@C0123ABCD
    portalURL: https://holtdroid.example.com
    source: github
```

And the source in Holtdroid:

```yaml
sources:
  - name: github
    type: s3
    readOnly: true
    s3:
      endpoint: https://s3.example.com
      bucket: holtdroid
      prefix: github
      accessKey: env:S3_ACCESS_KEY
      secretKey: env:S3_SECRET_KEY
```

Every option is in the job’s [docs](https://github.com/holtdroid/holtdroid-sync/blob/main/docs/github.md#configuration).

# Overview

> Folders and S3 buckets with APKs, the optional .meta.json sidecar, change tracking, uploads and launch links.

A **source** is a folder or an S3 bucket (or a prefix in one) with `*.apk` files. The api lists it directly — there is no separate source service. How the files get there is up to you: copy them by hand, let CI publish them, run a sync job such as [holtdroid-slack-sync](/sources/slack/) that pulls builds out of Slack or [holtdroid-github-sync](/sources/github/) that copies GitHub release assets, keep [Chromium builds of many milestones](/sources/chromium/) from the project’s chromium-builds releases (browsers here, WebViews in the [WebView catalog](/concepts/webview-versions/)) or Chromium’s snapshots, copy other browsers from their [public release archives](/sources/archives/), [write your own](/sources/custom/), or upload them in the UI.

```yaml
sources:
  - name: local # default when `sources` is not set
    type: filesystem
    filesystem:
      dir: /var/lib/holtdroid/apks
  - name: slack
    type: s3
    readOnly: true
    pollInterval: 1m
    s3:
      endpoint: https://s3.example.com
      bucket: apks
      prefix: slack
      accessKey: env:S3_ACCESS_KEY
      secretKey: env:S3_SECRET_KEY
```

| Key            | Default      | Meaning                                                                                          |
| -------------- | ------------ | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| `name`         | –            | Unique, lowercase letters, digits, `-`, `_`; shown in the UI                                     |
| `type`         | `filesystem` | `filesystem` or `s3`; the backend options are the same as for [storage](/configuration/storage/) |
| `readOnly`     | `false`      | Nobody can delete or change files through the portal; a read-only mount works                    |
| `pollInterval` | `30s`        | How often the source is listed to notice new, removed or replaced files and push it to the UI    |
| `include`      | everything   | Only list APKs whose keys match these [rules](#include-rules); not allowed on the uploads source |

Every `*.apk` (any depth, case-insensitive) is an artifact; other files, hidden files and directories that can’t be read (`lost+found`) are ignored. Newest first, by `uploadedAt` from the sidecar or else the file’s modification time. An app’s page orders its builds by version code instead, highest first.

## Include rules

[Section titled “Include rules”](#include-rules)

`include` picks builds from a source that holds more than you want to show, e.g. a shared bucket. It is a gitignore-style list:

```yaml
include:
  - /releases/* # anchored: releases/ and everything below it
  - "!/releases/night/*" # ...except nightly builds
  - "*-qa.apk" # a name pattern matches at any depth
```

* Keys are relative to the source’s directory or S3 prefix.
* `*` matches within one path segment, and `**` spans directories.
* A pattern that matches a directory matches everything below it.
* `!` excludes, and the last matching pattern wins.
* A list that starts with an exclusion starts from “everything”.
* Lines starting with `#` are ignored.

Excluded builds aren’t listed and can’t be launched.

## The `.meta.json` sidecar

[Section titled “The .meta.json sidecar”](#the-metajson-sidecar)

Next to `app.apk` you may put `app.apk.meta.json`. It is optional, every field in it is optional and unknown fields are ignored, so a sync job can add what it knows:

```json
{
  "title": "Checkout redesign",
  "note": "Build for the QA round on Thursday",
  "changelog": "- New payment sheet\n- Fixed crash on Android 15",
  "uploadedBy": "Jane Doe",
  "uploadedAt": "2026-10-16T09:30:00Z",
  "link": "https://example.slack.com/archives/C0123/p1760607000",
  "origin": "slack",
  "tags": { "branch": "feature/checkout", "commit": "3f2a9c1", "flavor": "staging" },
  "owner": "jane",
  "visibility": "public",
  "temporary": true,
  "lastUsedAt": "2026-10-17T08:00:00Z"
}
```

| Field        | Meaning                                                                                           |
| ------------ | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `title`      | Display name instead of the APK’s label                                                           |
| `note`       | Short description, shown under the title                                                          |
| `changelog`  | What changed, plain text; shown collapsed and searchable                                          |
| `uploadedBy` | Display name of whoever published the build                                                       |
| `uploadedAt` | RFC 3339 time; defaults to the file’s modification time                                           |
| `link`       | Link back to the origin (Slack message, pipeline, release)                                        |
| `origin`     | Free-form label of where it came from: `slack`, `ci`, `upload`, …                                 |
| `tags`       | String key/values shown as badges and searchable; `requiresSdk` is also a launch limit, see below |
| `owner`      | Portal user ID (as in `/api/v1/me` → `user`) who may delete it and change its visibility          |
| `visibility` | `public` (default) or `private`: only the owner and admins see and launch it                      |
| `temporary`  | `true`: deleted once unused for `uploads.temporaryTTL`; ignored in `readOnly` sources             |
| `lastUsedAt` | RFC 3339 time of the last launch; the api updates it for temporary builds                         |

A build runs on Android versions at or above its APK’s `minSdk` and, when the sidecar sets it, the `requiresSdk` tag (an API level, e.g. `"35"` for Android 15): for builds that declare an older `minSdk` but break on older Android. The launch dialog greys out the Android versions below that (the tooltip says why). When another build of the same app runs on such a version, the card stays clickable, names the newest of those builds and switches the dialog to it, keeping the other choices. Quick launch picks a version that fits or stays disabled, and the api answers 422 for them.

Write the sidecar **before** the APK when the visibility matters — the api lists whatever is there at that moment. A sidecar that isn’t valid JSON is ignored (and logged); the APK is still listed.

## The icon sidecar

[Section titled “The icon sidecar”](#the-icon-sidecar)

The api takes the launcher icon from the APK. It uses the densest bitmap, renders a vector drawable, or composes an adaptive icon from bitmap and vector layers. Gradients, clip paths and theme colours inside vectors are skipped, so such icons may come out incomplete. A publisher that knows better can put `app.apk.icon.png` next to the APK, before the APK itself.

The sidecar may contain PNG, JPEG or WebP data, up to 4 MiB and 4096 px per side. Icons are untrusted input wherever they come from. The api checks the dimensions before decoding, decodes them with Go’s memory-safe decoders, and re-renders them as a 256 × 256 PNG, so only pixels reach the browser. A sidecar that fails any of this is ignored and logged, and the extracted icon is used instead. An icon is optional: without one the UI shows a placeholder.

The icon is read when the APK is first cached, and again after an upgrade that improves icon extraction. Replace the APK, not just the icon, to change it.

## Change tracking

[Section titled “Change tracking”](#change-tracking)

Each file gets a **revision** — its ETag on S3, size + modification time on a filesystem. The APK cache is keyed by it, so replacing `app.apk` with a new build under the same name is picked up on the next listing: the new file is downloaded and parsed again, while sessions started from the old one keep using the copy they started with. Sidecar edits show up on the next listing too. Each api replica polls its sources every `pollInterval` and tells open browsers through `/api/v1/events` (`event: artifacts`), so lists refresh by themselves.

## Uploads

[Section titled “Uploads”](#uploads)

```yaml
uploads:
  enabled: true # default
  source: "" # default: the first source
  prefix: uploads
  maxSize: 1GiB
  temporaryTTL: 168h # temporary builds are deleted 7 days after their last launch
```

With uploads enabled every signed-in user gets an **Upload** button (and can drop an `.apk` onto the list). The file is checked to be a valid APK and stored as `{prefix}/{random}/{file name}` in the uploads source with a sidecar that records the uploader as `owner`, the chosen visibility, and an optional note and changelog. The owner and admins can make it public or private and delete it; admins can also delete builds without an owner in writable sources. The uploads source can’t be `readOnly`.

Uploads are **temporary** by default (untick the box to keep one). Each launch, and each install into a running session, moves the build’s `lastUsedAt`; once it has gone unused for `temporaryTTL` the api deletes it. The owner and admins can make a build permanent or temporary later from its menu. A sync job can set `temporary: true` in its own sidecars for the same cleanup in any writable source.

Uploads live in the source, not in the cache, so the source has to be persistent: the chart mounts a PersistentVolumeClaim at `/var/lib/holtdroid` for the default `local` source. A `ReadWriteOnce` claim limits the api to one replica — use an S3 source for uploads to run more.

## Downloads

[Section titled “Downloads”](#downloads)

```yaml
downloads:
  adminOnly: false # default: everyone who can see a build can download it
```

Each build in the list has a **Download** button that saves the APK as it is in the source. With `adminOnly: true` only admins see the button; everyone else gets 403 from the endpoint and can still launch the build. Every download is audited as `artifact.download`.

## Launch links

[Section titled “Launch links”](#launch-links)

`https://holtdroid.example.com/?source={source}&launch={artifact ID}` opens the portal with the launch dialog for that build. The artifact ID is the base64url (no padding) of the file’s key inside the source, e.g. `slack` + `C0123/F0456/app.apk` → `?source=slack&launch=QzAxMjMvRjA0NTYvYXBwLmFwaw`. Add `&quick=1` to skip the dialog: the session starts right away on the provider and location the user launched with last time (or the first provider with a free slot), as the quick launch button in the list does. If nothing is free or the launch fails, the dialog opens instead. Sync jobs use these links to post launch buttons next to the build; a build that is gone or private to someone else shows a notice instead.

# S3 bucket

> Builds from an existing S3 bucket — copied with holtdroid-s3-sync, or read directly with temporary AWS SSO credentials.

If your builds already land in a bucket, for example an AWS bucket that CI writes to, there are three ways to show them in Holtdroid.

| Setup                                   | Use it when                                                                                     |
| --------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| A plain [S3 source](/sources/overview/) | The api can have long-lived keys for the bucket                                                 |
| **holtdroid-s3-sync, copy**             | The bucket needs short-lived credentials (AWS IAM Identity Center), or you want your own copies |
| **holtdroid-s3-sync, broker**           | Short-lived credentials, but no copies: the api reads the bucket directly                       |

For any of them, [`include` rules](/sources/overview/#include-rules) pick the builds, e.g. `/releases/*` without `!/releases/night/*`.

## holtdroid-s3-sync

[Section titled “holtdroid-s3-sync”](#holtdroid-s3-sync)

[holtdroid-s3-sync](https://github.com/holtdroid/holtdroid-sync/blob/main/docs/s3.md) is a separate job (`job: s3` in the chart `deploy/helm/holtdroid-sync`). It reads the bucket with:

* AWS IAM Identity Center (SSO);
* static keys;
* the default AWS credential chain (IRSA, instance role).

It can run in either mode, or both at once.

### Signing in with AWS SSO

[Section titled “Signing in with AWS SSO”](#signing-in-with-aws-sso)

The job uses the OAuth device authorization flow, the same one `aws sso login --use-device-code` uses, so no AWS CLI or local browser is involved:

1. When the job has no usable session, it registers itself with your Identity Center and asks for a device code.
2. It sends a link with the code through [shoutrrr](https://github.com/nicholas-fedor/shoutrrr) (`notify.urls`: Slack, Telegram, Discord, Matrix, ntfy, email, webhooks, …), writes it to its log, and serves it on `/status`.
3. You open the link, check the code and approve. The job then gets role credentials for the configured account and permission set.
4. It keeps the session alive with refresh tokens. The session ends when your Identity Center’s session duration runs out, typically 8 hours to 7 days. Then the job asks again.

A code is valid for about ten minutes. If nobody approves it, the next code, and the next message, comes after `notify.remind` (one hour by default), so the channel doesn’t fill up.

The tokens are kept in `cacheFile` on a small private volume, so a restart doesn’t need a new login.

### Copy mode

[Section titled “Copy mode”](#copy-mode)

Matching APKs are copied into a folder or another bucket that Holtdroid lists as a read-only source. Each copy gets a sidecar with `origin: "s3"`, the object’s time and a link to it in the AWS console, plus the launcher icon. Sidecars already in the bucket are used too. Builds that disappear from the bucket, or no longer match the rules, are removed from the copy.

With `notify.builds`, each copy pass that brought something new sends one message through shoutrrr, for example to a Slack channel. It lists the builds with their version and package, and adds **Quick launch** and **Launch** links into the portal. Builds older than `maxAge` (24 hours by default) are left out, so copying an existing bucket for the first time doesn’t flood the channel.

Copies don’t depend on the session. If nobody approves a new login, the builds that were already copied stay launchable.

```yaml
# holtdroid-s3-sync
source:
  bucket: work-apks
  prefix: android/
  region: eu-west-1
```
